articles.title: Threat from China looms large over Taiwan’s local elections
articles.summary:
Taiwanese officials raise alarm over interference by China in elections that will shape fortunes of ruling party

Taiwanese voters go to the polls on Saturday in closely watched local…
articles.byline: Amy Hawkins and Yu-chen Li in Taipei

blocks.text: Taiwanese voters go to the polls on Saturday in closely watched local elections that will shape the fortunes of the ruling Democratic Progressive party (DPP) as it navigates an increasingly precarious set of relationships on the global stage.

Saturday’s vote will choose mayors, council members and other local leaders across 22 districts. Unlike the presidential elections, in which foreign policy is often a key issue, the local elections, held every four years, are largely focused on bread-and-butter issues such as housing affordability and wealth distribution.

Nevertheless, China looms large over the vote, which takes place against the background of intense military pressure from Beijing. China claims Taiwan as part of its territory despite never having ruled the self-governing island. Taiwanese officials have raised the alarm over thousands of incidents of suspected misinformation or election interference, and certain candidates have been subjected to harassment from the Chinese authorities. There have also been reports of hundreds of China-linked AI-generated videos spreading disinformation about Taiwanese politicians disliked by Beijing.

Beijing calls the allegations of election interference “completely fabricated”. Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for China’s Taiwan affairs office, said the allegations “stir up anti-China sentiment to win votes”.

Wei-Ting Yen, a political scientist at Academia Sinica, Taiwan’s national research academy, said: “Even though local elections are not about China, the outcome of local elections will have huge implications for cross-strait relations.”

Most races are a tight competition between a candidate from the ruling DPP and the main opposition party, the Kuomintang (KMT). The KMT promotes closer ties with Beijing, and its chair, Cheng Li-wun, travelled to China this year to meet Xi Jinping, China’s leader. Xi has vowed to unify China with Taiwan, and has not ruled out using military action to achieve that aim.

blocks.caption: Cheng Li-wun travelled to China to meet Xi Jinping. Photograph: CTI/Reuters

blocks.text: Yen said if the KMT loses some of its traditional strongholds, Beijing “may need to reconsider what is the most effective strategy for influencing Taiwanese people”.

One of the most contentious votes is the race for Taipei mayor, an office that has been held by the KMT for three decades. The DPP has selected as its challenger Puma Shen, a national legislator whom Beijing declared a “diehard separatist” in 2024. It is the first time a candidate under sanctions by Beijing has run to be mayor of Taiwan’s capital city. In the neighbouring New Tapei City race, the DPP’s Su Chiao-hui is also proving to be a ferocious challenger to the incumbent KMT.
Shen said in a recent interview that even if he didn’t win, the capital’s mayoral race was “a slap to China” because it proved that “democracy works here in Taiwan”.

Huang Bo-kai, a 23-year-old law student, said his top concern was cross-strait relations and how US-China relations were evolving. “The world’s three major powers are increasingly willing to flex their muscles: the US attacking Iran, Russia attacking Ukraine. I think Taiwan could very well be the next target [of China],” he told the Guardian.

Taiwan’s president, the DPP’s Lai Ching-te, is detested by Beijing and has taken a bolshier stance on cross-strait relations than his predecessor, Tsai Ing-wen, who was admired for her ability to drum up support in Washington while walking a delicate tightrope to avoid angering China.

blocks.caption: Taiwan’s president, Lai Ching-te, is detested by Beijing. Photograph: Ann Wang/Reuters

blocks.text: Lai has pushed for greater spending on weapons to deter military aggression from China. The government has proposed a record 18% increase in defence spending for next year, including for drones and missiles, taking it above 1tn Taiwan dollars (£23bn) for the first time.

But many Taiwanese voters would rather that money was spent on more immediate economic issues. Lev Nachman, a political scientist at National Taiwan University, said the national leaders of the DPP and KMT had been notably absent from the mayoral races, reflecting the extent to which campaigns were focused on local issues.

Going into the campaigns for the 2028 presidential elections, Lai would “try to take advantage of the momentum that [Shen] and Su have built for the DPP,” Nachman said, noting that support for those candidates would not necessarily translate into support for Lai.
Tony Yeh, a Taipei man in his 70s, said: “To put it simply, the authorities should do more to boost the economy and buy fewer weapons.”

Taiwan’s economy has boomed this year, largely thanks to the pivotal role that its semiconductor industry plays in the global artificial intelligence rally. The economy grew by more than 14% in the first nine months of the year, the fastest rate in 50 years. But nearly 70% of workers earned less than the average monthly wage of 49,152 Taiwan dollars (£1,137) in the same period.
Yeh said: “Most traditional industries are having a really tough time.”

William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “The issues that really are going to determine their votes are livelihood issues including the stagnant wage, the astronomically high housing price, the affordability issue, and how the government can better make sure Taiwan’s incredible economic boom fuelled by the global AI growth is going to be distributed more evenly.”
Other voters have more niche concerns. Walking her dog in a park, Kuo Wei-tong, a nail salon worker, said policies affecting pets were among her top concerns.
“People are having fewer children and getting more cats and dogs,” she said. “I think that’s something worth giving serious consideration to as well.”

articles.title: Met Police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly sentenced over attack on UK couple
articles.summary: Evidence from a British police officer helped convict Ali Kololo over a 2011 attack in the Kenyan resort of Lamu.

blocks.text: A Kenyan woodcutter who was wrongly sentenced to death over an attack on a British couple has told the BBC that actions by London's Metropolitan Police involved in the case destroyed his life.
Somali gunmen broke into David and Judith Tebbutt's beach bungalow on the Kenyan coast in 2011. They shot David dead and abducted Judith, holding her captive in Somalia for six months.
Met detectives flew to Kenya to assist the investigation. Their evidence helped convict Ali Kololo, who spent more than a decade in prison before his conviction was overturned.
Kololo is suing the Met, claiming a senior officer, former Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, gave misleading evidence at his trial and acted unlawfully to secure his conviction.
In his first media interview, he told the BBC about his 15-year ordeal and his fight for compensation, which the Met is challenging in court.
We meet on Lamu, a small island off Kenya's northern coast, once a thriving Swahili port. People and goods are still carted through its narrow stone streets by donkey rather than car.
It was here, in 2013, that Kololo was sentenced to death.
Standing at the jetty, where police once brought him ashore in handcuffs, he relishes being free. But he is struggling to rebuild his life.
"Everything was taken from me. I'm starting from zero. I don't think I'll ever go back to who I was before," he says.

Before his arrest, Kololo lived with his wife and their three young children. He had once worked as a groundskeeper at the resort where the Tebbutts were staying, but by 2011 he earned his living felling trees in a local forest and selling the wood.
"My life was very good," he says. "I was fending for myself, taking good care of my family."
Within 24 hours of the attack, Kenyan police had arrested him.
"I was beaten with clubs and thrown into a car," he says. "They beat me for days, burning me with cigarettes, forcing me to confess to things. They subjected me to torture like no other."
Kololo could not read or write. He says police made him put his thumbprint on a statement claiming he had led the attackers to the Tebbutts.
"I didn't understand anything," he says, calling the statement "a mountain of lies". "I signed it without knowing what it was because of the state they had put me in".
The Kenyan police told us it "at all times strives to work within the law". Kololo is not suing them.

Within days of the attack, a team of Met officers, led by then Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, arrived to support the Kenyan investigation. The UK government had instructed the officers not to accept information from the Kenyan authorities that had been obtained by interrogating detainees.
But Hibberd requested Kololo's statement and later relied on it when giving evidence for the prosecution at his trial.
In court, Hibberd also presented evidence linking Kololo to the attack. He told the Kenyan court Kololo had been wearing a type of shoe that matched footwear marks found in the sand at the resort.

The officer who had arrested Kololo said he was barefoot when he was handed to police. Hibberd did not disclose that the Met's own forensic examination could not establish whether the shoe in question had made the marks.

At the trial, Kololo did not initially have a lawyer. He had to cross-examine all the prosecution witnesses himself, including Hibberd, through an interpreter who spoke Swahili, which was not Kololo's first language.
"I believe I was framed because I am a poor man and I did not have the strength or means to fight for myself," Kololo says.

Kololo was convicted of kidnap and robbery with violence - the only person ever convicted in connection with the attack. He spent three years on death row before his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.
He recalls seeing his prison file. In the space for the expiry date, someone had written "death".
"I was completely heartbroken. I believed I could be executed at any moment, and I would never see my family, my children, ever again."

Years later, the UK's Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) established that Hibberd had omitted significant forensic evidence at the trial. It found that he would have had a case to answer for gross misconduct, but he could not face disciplinary proceedings because he had retired from the force. At the time, his lawyer said Hibberd absolutely disagreed with the report's findings.

In April 2023, Kenya's High Court quashed Kololo's conviction, because of doubts over the prosecution's evidence. This followed years of work by the legal charity Reprieve and a Kenyan lawyer, Alfred Olaba, who represented him for free.
They were supported by Judith Tebbutt, who believed Kololo was innocent. In an interview with the BBC in 2022, she said he had been scapegoated by Scotland Yard.
"He was not there on the night. He was not part of the group that held me. They've put this man in prison without any real evidence."

More than three years after his release, Kololo says he is still living with the effects of his torture and decade in prison. As we walk the narrow streets of Lamu's old town, his thin frame moves stiffly. He is on edge. "My mind is not good," he says. "I have not recovered."
He remembers being kept in a filthy, bedbug-ridden cell with up to eight other inmates, which he thought he would never leave. Twice he contracted tuberculosis and nearly died.
Kololo is now too frail to do the woodcutting he once relied on to make a living. He tries to grow enough to eat on the land around his home, but erratic rain makes it difficult.
"I have nothing. On the days I get food, I eat, and on the days I don't, I endure."

He lives alone in a mud hut. His wife divorced him after he went to prison, and their children went to live with his mother. They dropped out of school because the family could not pay the fees. Kololo says they were not allowed to visit him in prison. When he was released, they barely remembered him, especially his youngest.
"They were too young. Only now are they starting to regain the memory that 'this is our father who disappeared'," he says. "If it weren't for my mother, my children might have died."
For much of our time together, Kololo is remarkably upbeat. He trusts that his lawyers and God will deliver him justice. But when we talk about the Met, his demeanour shifts.
"I am extremely angry with the police," he says. "I'm also angry with the Kenyan Police. They collaborated to incriminate me. What [Hibberd] said destroyed my entire life and my children's lives."
The Met has not apologised to Kololo or admitted wrongdoing. The force is contesting his compensation claim, which his lawyers say could take years to resolve.
"These people falsely accused me. Do I not deserve something?" he asks.

The Met told the BBC that neither they nor Hibberd wanted to comment on Kololo's claim, but it said: "Our thoughts are with Mr Kololo, Mrs Tebbutt, her family and all those who have been affected by this terrible crime. The Metropolitan Police remains committed to supporting the Kenyan authorities in any way that may be possible, in order to get justice for Mrs Tebbutt and her late husband."
Preetha Gopalan, Reprieve's head of UK litigation, describes the Met's behaviour in Kololo's case as "egregious".

"They've spent 10 years trying to evade accountability in every way possible, now dragging him through the courts," she says. "It's possible for them to do the right thing, but they are unwilling, and so this ordeal continues to haunt Kololo and his family."
"Even if I get a billion shillings, I will never be the same," Kololo says. "But if I get the justice I deserve, I can help my children and take care of myself when I am an old man."

articles.title: Death-sentenced Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind
articles.summary: The ousted prime minister's December homecoming plan deepens Dhaka-Delhi tensions and risks fresh unrest.

blocks.text: Death-sentenced Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind

blocks.caption: Image caption, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi with Sheikh Hasina in Delhi in 2024 - Hasina was a close ally of India during her years in power

blocks.text: Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty Images
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi with Sheikh Hasina in Delhi in 2024 - Hasina was a close ally of India during her years in power
Sheikh Hasina has repeatedly vowed to return to Bangladesh.
Now the ousted prime minister has put a date on her homecoming - 16 December - and even outlined how she intends to make the journey.
The government in Dhaka, which had previously dismissed the prospect, is taking her latest declaration more seriously.

Hasina, 79, who fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule, plans to go back on Victory Day, the anniversary of Bangladesh's triumph over Pakistan in the 1971 liberation war, her spokesperson said.

She was sentenced to death after being convicted of crimes against humanity for her role in the crackdown, in a trial held in her absence that raised questions about due process. Her Awami League party is banned in Bangladesh. The UN says as many as 1,400 people were killed by security forces during the uprising.
The government says she would be arrested immediately if she returned and has promised to carry out the death sentence.
Hasina now wants the Bangladesh government to arrange a flight from Delhi. If that fails, she could travel commercially or cross the land border.
"She is even prepared to walk into Bangladesh," Abu Obaidha Arin, a key aide to Hasina, told the BBC.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Sheikh Hasina fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Sheikh Hasina fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule

India and Bangladesh share a 4,096km (2,545 mile) border across five Indian states - West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Her supporters, Arin said, had identified nine possible crossing points. "This is a carefully thought-out, precise plan. This is serious."
Dhaka has responded with defiance, insisting Hasina must be extradited.

"Reality and desire are different things," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs, told reporters in Dhaka. "[The reality is] she's not a regular commercial passenger. She can only be brought back in handcuffs."
India's foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Hasina's extradition request was being examined through the "established process", adding that a voluntary return would be a separate matter.

items: Sheikh Hasina: The pro-democracy icon who became an autocrat
Hasina's conviction for crimes against humanity is testing India-Bangladesh ties

blocks.text: Many in Dhaka believe Hasina's declaration is more than a promise of homecoming.

They believe it is an attempt to test the government's authority, force her way back into the political conversation and exploit divisions among the parties that united to oust her. It also threatens to turn India's unresolved problem of sheltering a former ally into a more immediate diplomatic crisis.
The date is significant. Hasina is invoking Victory Day to reclaim her place in Bangladesh's founding narrative. Aides say she has spent months trying to keep her party alive in exile.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India, his neighbour, since becoming prime minister in February

blocks.text: Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images
Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India, his neighbour, since becoming prime minister in February

Arin says Hasina has been in regular contact with party leaders and workers through interactive audio conversations on Telegram, keeping alive a network that might otherwise have been difficult to sustain from exile.

Over the past 18 months, he says, she has held more than 300 such meetings, reaching supporters across all 64 districts and the country's 300 constituencies. They are organised through the Awami League's 78 units and "can last four or five hours".

The meetings allow Hasina to listen directly to party workers, hear their grievances and understand what is happening on the ground, Arin says. He insists the response has been substantial and claims the party "could mobilise five million people to welcome her along the route from the border to Dhaka, forming a human chain".
"We have the organisational capacity to make that happen," he says.

That may be an ambitious claim. The Awami League remains a mass party with millions of supporters, but it is banned and largely shut out of mainstream politics. Much of its leadership is abroad, in jail or underground. Police have arrested supporters and filed thousands of cases against party workers.
Yet its supporters have continued to take to the streets, staging flash protests that have grown more frequent and confrontational in recent months.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Awami League supporters have staged flash protests across Bangladesh in recent months

blocks.text: Awami League supporters have staged flash protests across Bangladesh in recent months
Several districts have reported bomb attacks, arson and vandalism, though responsibility for some incidents remains disputed.
Gopalganj, Hasina's ancestral district, has proved particularly difficult for the authorities to control.

Awami League supporters have attacked police stations, external, torched vehicles and targeted homes and offices belonging to ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) leaders, reports say. Highways have been blocked, external with felled trees and burning tyres, bringing traffic to a standstill. In some areas, police have withdrawn, external amid fears of further attacks.

Supporters have staged 40 demonstrations and more than 140 riots up to 23 November, according to data from conflict monitoring group Acled (Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project). At least 11 people, including two civilians, have been killed in political violence this month, six directly linked to the unrest, the group says.
The party's ability to cause disruption, however, is not necessarily evidence of a broad resurgence.
Many in Dhaka remain sceptical that Hasina will actually return, viewing the announcement as a means of galvanising a demoralised party.

Yet the Awami League has achieved something politically: it is back in the conversation. Immediately after Hasina's fall, even mentioning the party was taboo. Now its future is being debated across the political spectrum.

Shafiqul Alam, editor of the English-language daily Daily Waadaa and former press secretary to the Muhammad Yunus-led interim government, believes the party is "exploiting cracks in the unity forged during the uprising".

He told the BBC that "disagreements" over the July Charter, external, proposed constitutional changes and the referendum have "widened divisions" between the elected BNP government and rivals Jamaat-e-Islami and the youth-led National Citizen Party (NCP).

blocks.caption: Image caption, Fire engulfs a police station in Gopalganj on 17 November amid unrest following the arrest of Awami League activists

blocks.text: Fire engulfs a police station in Gopalganj on 17 November amid unrest following the arrest of Awami League activists

"The Awami League sees an opening," Alam told the BBC. "The party believes this is an opportune moment to take to the streets, exploiting a weakened police force and divisions among the forces of the July uprising."

Analysts say if Hasina returns it could just as easily deepen hostility as revive her party's fortunes. The government has framed the sporadic recent violence as terrorism, while supporters insist their demonstrations are peaceful and accuse the authorities of repression.
The larger question is whether Bangladesh can sustain the exclusion of a political constituency as substantial as the Awami League without creating another source of instability.
For India, the dilemma is increasingly difficult to manage.

Delhi has sheltered Hasina, but her public remarks have angered Dhaka, which wants her extradited. India has sought to repair ties through diplomatic outreach and talks on trade, border security and other bilateral issues, but relations remain strained.
The chill is striking: nearly 10 months into his tenure, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India.

blocks.caption: Image caption, NCP members stage a motorcycle rally in Dhaka on 24 November, protesting against violence allegedly carried out by the banned Awami League

blocks.text: NCP members stage a motorcycle rally in Dhaka on 24 November, protesting against violence allegedly carried out by the banned Awami League
A trip was reportedly in the offing in August, but Hasina's press conference in Delhi proved a setback to efforts to reset relations.
Avinash Paliwal, who teaches politics and international studies at SOAS University of London, argues that Hasina's latest announcement has "shifted the burden of choice to Dhaka rather than Delhi".

Delhi, he says, "feels it has tried its best" to work with Rahman's government over the past 10 months - "from appointing a political heavyweight as high commissioner, external with cabinet rank to offering fresh talks on security and trade".

"The failure of this outreach has left India disillusioned with Dhaka. India seems to have decided that bilateral relations will likely remain tense whatever it does, so there is little reason to stop Hasina from stirring the political pot."
Delhi has the leverage to restrain Hasina from making political statements on Indian soil, Paliwal argues, but may not want to exercise it.
Nor, in his view, is it in India's interest to see the Awami League permanently excluded from Bangladeshi politics.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Bangladesh security forces patrol and conduct drills in Dhaka's Shahbagh area on the Awami League's founding anniversary

blocks.text: Bangladesh security forces patrol and conduct drills in Dhaka's Shahbagh area on the Awami League's founding anniversary

"The political party still enjoys pockets of support across Bangladesh and is weaved into the social and political fabric of the country," he says. "So, yes, it is in India's interest, and also in Bangladesh's long-term interests, to rehabilitate the Awami League and take the path of political reconciliation."
That view is increasingly contested in Dhaka.

"There is a perception in Bangladesh that India wants to rehabilitate the Awami League. There are issues India has not resolved, including the extradition of Hasina. India has also not renewed the transit facilities that could benefit Bangladeshi garment exporters, while the Ganges water treaty, external is nearing expiry without much progress. But has India done enough to win back trust?" says Alam.
"For now, only tourist and medical visas have resumed. Everything else remains in limbo."
A Dhaka-based foreign-policy expert, who asked not to be named, says the two countries remain locked in "mutual frustration".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Vehicles pass a mural of Sheikh Hasina near Dhaka University

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Vehicles pass a mural of Sheikh Hasina near Dhaka University
Hasina, he says, remains central to the impasse. "She remains the elephant in the room, but we also have to find a way to move beyond Hasina."
Paliwal argues that the least damaging outcome for India would be Hasina returning to face a fresh trial, with the Awami League rehabilitated under a different operational leadership.
"It will reintroduce a degree of balance in Bangladeshi politics, and will afford India space to protect its long-term interests and equities better," he says.
For now, 16 December is not yet a confirmed journey. But Hasina has already succeeded in making her return a question that neither Dhaka nor Delhi can ignore.

"December could be chaotic. Everyone in Dhaka is on edge," says the foreign-policy expert, warning of protests and confrontation as Hasina's proposed return date approaches - and the possibility that it could be postponed yet again.
"Hasina is unlikely to return, as she would face a death sentence. But her comments have clearly galvanized her supporters," says Pearl Pandya, Acled's South Asia analyst.

But the impasse is also complicating India's ties with Bangladesh. As Paliwal puts it, the "next window of serious negotiations will now open only after Hasina returns to Dhaka, or Dhaka relents under pressure and returns to the table".

articles.title: Major Thanksgiving storm brings flooding, flight delays across US
articles.summary: Massive storms are descending on both US coasts, with wind gusts, heavy rain, downed trees, and power outages for hundreds of thousands of customers.
articles.byline: Ana Faguy, James FitzGerald, Sareen Habeshian

blocks.text: On Thursday, a powerful storm hit the eastern US, bringing damaging winds of up to 70mph, torrential rain, and major coastal flooding.
New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency, as several communities along the Jersey Shore saw widespread flooding.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul also declared a state of emergency for New York City, Long Island and Westchester County.
In New York City, organisers of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have postponed the event to Saturday.
Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds and waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk.
In Maryland, almost two million customers have been asked by the water utility to use water for essential use only due to "intermittent power disruptions".
On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington DC, tidal waters surged and soaked all runways at Reagan Washington National Airport, according to the National Water Prediction Service.
More than 900,000 households were reporting power outages by Thursday evening, with Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey hit particularly hard.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said that utility providers were working tirelessly to restore power. Meanwhile, energy companies in Virginia and New Jersey warned it may take some time, even days, for power to return, as crews had to wait until it was safe to access damaged areas.
Across the US, severe weather is also descending on the West Coast. The NWS has warned of a series of Pacific storms that are expected to bring rain, mountain snow and strong winds.
On Thursday afternoon, President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds for the east coast as it faces down the holiday storm.
In Miami, some travel delays persisted into Thursday after a FedEx plane overshot the runway the night before, which prompted the closure of all but one runway at the airport for a brief period.
A statement FedEx provided to US media confirmed that one of its flights had "experienced an issue upon landing".

It added: "We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries. We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA."
An airport employee who spoke anonymously to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, raised the possibility that rainy conditions had been a factor.

"They tried as hard as they could to stop, but I don't know if it was the weather because the rain and the wind were really bad, and they just couldn't stop in time and went right off the runway and veered off into the grass," they said.
Wednesday's incident in Miami came 11 weeks after a cargo plane crashed on landing at the same airport, killing five people and injuring five others in vehicles on the ground with which it collided.

The airport is among the top five domestic destinations for travellers in the country over Thanksgiving, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for the Thanksgiving holiday over a seven-day period.
Rebecka Pieder contributed reporting.

articles.title: Residents skate the streets as freezing rain blankets Fort St. John, B.C.
articles.summary: Warned to stay home due to hazardous roads, some northern British Columbians strapped on their skates instead Thursday morning, as freezing rain blanketed Fort St. John.

image.caption: Some Fort St. John residents took to the streets on skates and sleds after freezing rain blanketed roads the morning of Nov. 26, 2026. (Chris Boehm/Leann Muggeridge/Nicole Marshall)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Warned to stay home due to hazardous roads, some northern British Columbians strapped on their skates instead Thursday morning, as freezing rain blanketed Fort St. John.
Warned to stay home due to hazardous roads, some northern British Columbians strapped on their skates instead
Chris Boehm didn't let hazardous weather keep him indoors Thursday morning.
After freezing rain coated the streets of Fort St. John in northeast B.C., he decided to strap on his skates and take a spin around his neighbourhood.
"I saw a couple people skate by our house, I'm like, what the heck, I've never done this in my lifetime. I'm 50 years old, now I've done it," he said.
He wasn't alone. Around the city people took out their sleds, skates and hockey sticks to take advantage of the unusual conditions.
Residents skate and sled the icy roads of Fort St. John
"It was super fun, I felt like a kid again," said Leann Muggeridge, whose kids stayed home from school after bus runs were cancelled due to the slippery streets.
She said the roads were surprisingly smooth, likely due to a lack of snow, while Boehm said it was as if they had been flooded specifically for skating.

Throughout the morning, highway warnings were posted encouraging people not to drive unless absolutely necessary. The City of Fort St. John also urged people to avoid unnecessary travel as crews worked to clear and sand main routes.
Muggeridge didn't mind the delays.
"I know we have our ups and downs ... but I feel like when something like this happens you'll see even adults, their personalities come out," she said.

articles.title: Qantas and Air New Zealand planes too close at Sydney airport as ‘mental models’ of crews to be investigated
articles.summary:
Aborted descent on Wednesday morning is latest in a series of landing incidents at Sydney airport

  • Get our

blocks.text: The Australian Transport Safety Bureau is investigating flight crews’ “mental models” after a Qantas plane aborted its landing at Sydney airport on Wednesday after noticing another aircraft crossing the runway while on its descent.
The ATSB said Qantas flight 426 from Melbourne was due to land just before 10.15am on Wednesday, with the Boeing 737 jet told to expect a late landing clearance due to aircraft crossing the runway.
As the Qantas plane continued to approach the airport, and before it received a clearance to land, the crew reported seeing an Air New Zealand plane crossing the runway.
The Qantas crew decided to conduct a go-around, aborting the landing before trying again.

The ATSB said it would investigate what it called an “aircraft separation issue”. The agency will gather evidence, including interviewing flight crew, looking at flight data and monitoring air traffic control audio and any available CCTV into the incident.
“In particular, the investigation will seek to ascertain what information was provided to the crews of both aircraft, and what mental models those crews held,” the agency said in a statement.
“The ATSB notes that, during the occurrence, important safety defences were in place and operated, such as the flight crew’s go-around decision.”
A preliminary report should be complete in about eight weeks, the ATSB said.
Qantas did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
“Our pilots were following air traffic control instructions and elected to conduct a go-around as the other aircraft was crossing the runway,” the airline told the Sydney Morning Herald.
Sydney airport has seen a series of near-miss incidents this year, including when a Jetstar plane narrowly avoided a collision with a Qatar Airways plane on the tarmac in August.
In another incident, a Virgin plane was forced to abort takeoff when a Qantas plane began to cross the runway in front of it.

Angus Mitchell, the ATSB chief commissioner, released preliminary investigation reports in September that found staffing levels at Sydney airport had “emerged as a recurring area of inquiry”, with a review finding runway incursions and near misses at 20% above national averages there.
“This should be viewed in the context of Sydney airport being the most complex in the country,” Mitchell said at the time.

The ATSB stressed it “has yet to determine whether staff resourcing factors directly contributed to any occurrence, or whether they were simply underlying conditions that were recognised and being effectively managed by Airservices, Australia’s air traffic services provider”.

The ATSB added Friday its examination of the recent incident would seek to look at safety defences in place “and to establish or rule out any underlying safety issues and contributing factors common across the other occurrences at Sydney airport currently under investigation”.

articles.title: Water firms to identify 250,000 vulnerable households in England eligible for discounts
articles.summary:
Department for Work and Pensions to provide data about households missing out on WaterSure support scheme

Water companies will use government data to identify as many as 250,000 vulnerable…

blocks.text: Water companies will use government data to identify as many as 250,000 vulnerable households in England eligible for discounts, after criticism that not enough people are aware of the £428 support for their annual bills.

The Department for Work and Pensions will provide information to identify and contact a quarter of a million households who are missing out on support to which they are entitled under the WaterSure scheme.
The scheme is open to people on benefits who need to use a lot of water either for medical reasons or because their household has three or more children under 19.

The government said that 300,000 customers are signed up to WaterSure, but fewer than half of eligible households claim it because either they are unaware or they may have difficulty proving they qualify.

The Labour government has sought to portray itself as tough on the water industry. However, Andy Burnham has yet to outline his plan for the sector, despite saying he would bring in “more public control” of companies.
Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, said it was “common sense” to share information about eligible households with companies.

“Hundreds of thousands of the most vulnerable people aren’t getting help with their water bills because they don’t know how to access it,” she said. “That’s not right. By sharing data across government and water companies, we’re fixing that problem – meaning getting that help will be far easier for those who need it.”
The changes received the backing of Martin Lewis, founder of the MoneySavingExpert advice website.

He said: “Too many people miss out on help they desperately need and are entitled to. Water companies shoulder some blame for confusing applications and underpublicising support. Yet it is important the government joins the dots too. If one part of the state knows someone needs help, another shouldn’t leave them in the dark. Help is only effective if it actually reaches those who need it.”

Eagle also announced that the Consumer Council for Water, which helps households with complaints, will be given new powers to investigate water companies’ customer service and work with regulators to rectify problems. It will be named the Water Watchdog.

A spokesperson for Water UK, a lobby group for the industry, said: “Water companies have long called for government to automatically provide us with the information needed to give people heavily discounted water bills. As a result, hundreds of thousands more people will now benefit from WaterSure.”

articles.title: Nearly half of ethnic minority people in UK have faced racism at work in last year, survey finds
articles.summary:
Figures show impact on mental health, with majority having no confidence HR will take their concerns seriously

Nearly half of people from minority ethnic backgrounds have experienced racism…

blocks.text: Nearly half of people from minority ethnic backgrounds have experienced racism at work and the majority have no confidence that HR would take their concerns seriously, a survey has found.

It also found that 75% of people from the UK’s five largest minority ethnic communities had experienced racism or unfair treatment linked to their race, ethnicity or religion in the previous year, and three-quarters of those who had experienced racism said it had affected their mental health to some degree.

Susan Solomon, a senior research manager and lead author of the Centre for Mental Health’s report, said: “When three-quarters of people who have experienced racism report an impact on their mental health, it is clear that racism is not just an equality issue. It is a public mental health issue.”
The findings of the survey of 2,506 adults come amid reports that racial equality is worsening and discrimination is becoming more common in the UK.

Jabeer Butt, the chief executive of the Race Equality Foundation, said the research demonstrated “how widespread racism remains in everyday life and the cumulative toll it takes on the mental health of Black, Asian and minoritised ethnic people”.

In the workplace, 45% of ethnic minority workers said they had experienced racism at work in the past year, most often passed off as “banter”, while 56% had no confidence that HR would take them seriously.

The research also revealed that 42% of ethnic minority people who had faced racism linked it to anti-immigrant protests and demonstrations, 57% saw negative posts about immigrants or minorities on social media every week, and 46% heard politicians blaming immigrants for the UK’s problems just as often.

Butt said the results showed that “racism does not occur in a vacuum”. He said: “Hostile anti-immigration rhetoric, amplified in politics and across social media, can legitimise racist attitudes and behaviour, echoing our findings following the racist riots of 2024.

“The response cannot be to ask people to become more resilient or simply to report individual incidents. Political leaders, employers, public institutions and social media platforms must challenge the narratives that fuel racism and take effective action to prevent it.”

The research highlighted a gap between experiencing racism and seeking support and help. Of the respondents who had experienced racism or unfair treatment, half said they felt they had to be constantly “on guard” and ready for racist encounters, while only 5% of people who experienced racism sought professional mental health support.

Solomon said: “Our findings show that the harm does not come only from overt acts of discrimination but from the constant effort of anticipating, managing and responding to racism in everyday life. People described living in a state of vigilance, weighing decisions about where they go, how they behave and whether it is safe to speak up.”

She added: “The research also shows that the mental health impact of racism is not limited to personal experiences of discrimination. It is compounded by exposure to anti-immigration and discriminatory rhetoric in political speeches, newspaper coverage and social media. If we are serious about protecting mental health, action must be taken to prevent the harm caused by racism before it reaches crisis point.”

articles.title: Ombudsman orders graft raps vs 3 ex-Landbank officials, businessman
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman has ordered the filing of graft charges against three former officials of the Land Bank of the Philippines and a private businessman over alleged irregularities in the…

blocks.text: November 27, 2026 | 7:30am
Philstar.com / File

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman has ordered the filing of graft charges against three former officials of the Land Bank of the Philippines (LBP) and a private businessman over alleged irregularities in the approval and renewal of loans extended to American Boulevard Trading Corp. (ABTC).

In a statement on Thursday, November 26, the Ombudsman said it found prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction against former LBP First Vice President Lolita Silva, former Assistant Vice President Danilo Dayanghirang, former Account Officer Ronaldo Robles, and ABTC President and Chairman Alberto Ching for allegedly violating Section 3(e) of Republic Act No. 3019, or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act.
The case stemmed from a complaint filed by LBP’s Loan Recovery Department following a February 2022 letter from then-Assistant House Majority Floor Leader Rowena Niña Taduran.
The letter flagged Ching’s disclosure that bank "insiders" had allegedly fast-tracked the approval and subsequent renewals of ABTC's loans in exchange for a 10% commission.

ABTC initially secured a P50-million short-term loan facility in August 2017, which was later increased to P100 million in February 2018 and eventually reached P115 million in September 2018, according to the Ombudsman.
According to the Ombudsman, an internal investigation and special audit conducted by LBP uncovered multiple violations of bank lending policies.

These included the diversion of loan proceeds for purposes other than those approved, the renewal of promissory notes despite existing past-due accounts, and the failure to properly assess the borrower’s financial condition and creditworthiness.

Investigators also found that the financial projections used to justify the loan approvals were significantly higher than historical figures, while material information regarding ABTC's financial obligations and outstanding loans was neither properly disclosed nor evaluated.

The Ombudsman also pointed out that Silva, Dayanghirang, and Robles, acting in conspiracy with Ching, allegedly disregarded established lending requirements and failed to exercise due diligence in facilitating the credit facilities.

“The investigation revealed that the respondents' actions gave unwarranted benefits, advantage, or preference to ABTC. The company also had outstanding loan obligations to LBP amounting to P141,305,054.24,” the Ombudsman said.

articles.title: This birdwatching expert tracked down every single bird in Grand Theft Auto VI
articles.summary: If you get tired of slinging drugs, stealing cars and running from the cops in Grand Theft Auto VI, you can always give birdwatching a try. The experience of trekking through different habitats to…

image.caption: A screengrab from Grand Theft Auto VI shows seagulls on the beach. Players can track down and log more than 60 birds in the new game, a side-quest that birders say is surprisingly accurate. (Rockstar Games/Grand Theft Auto VI)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

If you get tired of slinging drugs, stealing cars and running from the cops in Grand Theft Auto VI, you can always give birdwatching a try. The experience of trekking through different habitats to track down the game's dozens of species is impressively realistic, says one birdwatching expert.
If car chases are losing their thrill, players can track down dozens of birds to log instead
Getting tired of slinging drugs, stealing cars and running from the cops in Grand Theft Auto VI? You can always give birdwatching a try.

When the news dropped a week before its release that arguably the most anticipated video game of the decade would feature 62 bird species to log, birdwatching expert Nick Lund took notice — and vowed to be the first to find them all.
"I've played video games my whole life, but I'm a birder first and foremost," he told CBC's As it Happens.
"It's not often in real life that I get to rob a bank and then look at some parrots on the way out as I'm escaping."

items: Grand Theft Auto VI is the video game event of the decade

blocks.text: In the smash-hit release from Rockstar Games, players can alternate between the perspectives of characters Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos as they roam a fictionalized Miami and south Florida.

As with previous games in the series, the central plotline dives into the criminal underworld. But for those who want to take their time with the crime, players can do chores, buy flowers — or go looking for avian species from roseate spoonbills to house sparrows.
Birders working to fill out their GTA VI wildlife checklists should know something I just found out: THERE’S A ZOO https://t.co/2xN0joPKcR—TheBirdist
Players can simply use in-game binoculars to look at a bird and the game automatically logs its information. Other forms of wildlife can also be logged, adding another dimension for completionists.

For Lund, the most tantalizing illegal activity the game offers isn’t smuggling or high-speed chases: it’s being able to pull his car to a screeching halt in the middle of an intersection just so he can get out and look at a cool bird in the sky.
"[It’s] something that as a real life birder I’ve wanted to do my entire life," said Lund, who lives in Maine and works for a state conservation organization.
Nick Lund, who has been birding for more than 20 years, says the birding experience in GTA VI is surprisingly accurate. (Nick Lund)
'Actual species you'd find in south Florida'
Not only do the birds in GTA VI look accurate enough for most to be identified without binoculars, Lund said, but you also have to trek to their habitats to find them.

"It's set in a fictional version of south Florida and I've birded in Florida a lot. And so I was actually able to use my experience in real Florida to figure out where to go to find birds in fake Florida GTA," he said.

items: Carly Rae Jepsen reacts to her song's 'mind-blowing' boost from GTA VI
GTA VI lets you buy flowers for your girlfriend. Some streamers say it's too woke

blocks.text: Wading birds and herons creep through the game's version of the Everglades. Sanderlings and terns are found flitting around the beaches. Birds known to be in the north of Florida are found in the northern part of the game’s map, while bird populations that make Miami their home in real life, including tropical birds, are also found in the heart of the game’s city.
But there’s a few hiccups.
"There’s a whole bunch of whooping cranes around," Lund said. "It's a very rare bird that lives mostly in Texas."
Golden eagles are also a common sight in the game, despite being rarely spotted in south Florida.
incredibly healthy populations of critically-endangered Whooping Cranes across Vice City. Huge if true. https://t.co/doe6oMOvBX—TheBirdist
Overall, though, the game "does a great job of presenting actual species that you’d find in south Florida," Lund said.

Before the game’s release it was reported there would be 62 bird species to find — a fraction of the real number found in Florida — but the official in-game compendium only includes 60 slots for gamers to log their birds.
Lund said he’s found 63 in total so far, including three not listed in the official bird count. He’s since written a guide to the game’s birds for Audubon magazine.
He isn’t the only GTA player going gaga for gulls — many have taken to social media to share their birding excitement. One user on X suggested players "make a GTATwitter Birdwatching club!"
What makes the release of Grand Theft Auto VI so special?
"It's really wild that birding is such a prominent part of such a huge cultural phenomenon," said Kyle Horner, an engagement co-ordinator at Birds Canada.
He noted that some other games, like Rockstar’s Red Dead Redemption 2, have included birding, and said he hopes it catches on.
"Hopefully people who enjoy it in the game maybe take it up in real life. Maybe they realize there's birds outside in their own world that they can go and explore, too."
Considering the game is for entertainment and not for education, "they really nailed it," Horner added.
Players can use the in-game binoculars to automatically log birds. (Rockstar Games/Grand Theft Auto VI)
Lund doesn’t know if he was actually the first player to find all the birds, but a designer from Rockstar gave their seal of approval.
When Lund shared a video of him finding his 60th bird — an owl — senior technical designer Alec McNamara wrote "History!" in response.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca

articles.title: Defence minister 'very concerned' after Poilievre claims constituent's job was threatened
articles.summary: Defence Minister David McGuinty says he's asked his deputy to raise concerns about a Wainwright, Alta., nurse's job being threatened after she was photographed with Conservative Leader Pierre…

image.caption: Minister of National Defence David McGuinty, left, and deputy minister Christiane Fox prepare to appear at the defence committee on Thursday, where McGuinty commented on Poilievre's point of privilege. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Defence Minister David McGuinty says he's asked his deputy to raise concerns about a Wainwright, Alta., nurse's job being threatened after she was photographed with Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre.
Poilievre said nurse scrutinized for photo with Conservative leader after Wainwright fire

The minister told MPs on the House defence committee that the issue was brought up with the government contractor that employs the nurse, but beyond that there is little more that he could do at this point.

"This is a matter of privity of contract between her and her employer, which is a contractor to the federal government. So obviously you can imagine I can't involve myself in that private sector contract," he said.
"I did ask my deputy to speak to the company involved to at least raise the issue. It was raised."
This photo of nurse Maureen Carpenter was posted online by Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre on Oct. 20. (Pierre Poilievre/Facebook)
In an unusual speech in the House of Commons on Wednesday evening, Poilievre said his parliamentary privilege is being breached because of the incident.

Last month, Maureen Carpenter — a nurse who helped treat soldiers burned in the CFB Wainwright fire — was photographed speaking to Poilievre following the tragic incident that killed five soldiers and wounded 38 others on Oct. 17. Poilievre said she is under contract with Calian Health, a government contractor.

"Maureen spoke to me on base, with the permission of the unit commander. I had the permission of the base commander to be there. She talked about caring for our men and women on the shift that night, that horrendous night," said Poilievre.

items: Poilievre claims constituent's job was threatened after meeting at CFB Wainwright

blocks.text: An online post from Oct. 20 shows Poilievre meeting with medical staff at CFB Wainwright Health Services. Online comments identify the woman in the photo as Carpenter, which was confirmed by Poilievre's office.
The base is part of Poilievre's federal riding of Battle River-Crowfoot.

He said, following the meeting, Carpenter was subject to a complaint and threatened — told by her boss that if her term contract was not already coming to an end, she would be put under the microscope by the company's legal department.
McGuinty said during the committee meeting that he agrees with Poilievre "that constituents should always feel free — and MPs should always be able to speak to their constituents."
"I've been on this file, on this issue, because I'm very concerned. It's not right that a member of Parliament should not be able to speak to a constituent."
Now that Poilievre has raised the matter as a point of privilege, the minister said he needs to wait for the Speaker's ruling as well.

"I can't cross a certain other line, which is the question of now this claim that Mr. Poilievre's own privileges have been affected. That's now residing with the Speaker and I'm hoping for a good outcome in terms of the decision there."
McGuinty said he has been in contact with Carpenter's brother.
CBC News has reached out to Calian Health and Carpenter for comment but has not yet received a response.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.
With files from Kate McKenna

articles.title: Chance of snow forecast for northern England and Scotland in next few days
articles.summary:
Met Office warns of icy roads and risk of freezing rain on higher ground as weather turns cold and unsettled

Parts of England could see snow in the coming days as cold and unsettled weather…

blocks.text: Parts of England could see snow in the coming days as cold and unsettled weather continues into the weekend, forecasters have said.
Heavy rain sweeping eastwards on Friday could turn to snow over higher ground in northern England and Scotland.
The Met Office has issued a yellow ice warning for parts of northern England and the Midlands from 4am to 2pm on Friday.
Freezing rain could leave roads and pavements icy, particularly on higher routes across the Pennines, with up to 3cm of snow also possible, the warning states.
Forecasters also said there is a small chance of road closures, public transport disruption and injuries from slips and falls.
The Met Office meteorologist Honor Criswick said: “The cold is here to stay over the coming days.
“Not only this but it’s set to be rather unsettled at times, with heavy outbreaks of rain, possibly even some hill snow.”
Criswick added: “Also, a chance we could see some freezing rain towards high ground in northern England.
“This can lead to some slippery surfaces, so do take care if you’re out and about early first thing on Friday.”
Temperatures could plummet to -10C in parts of Scotland on Friday night, while widespread frost is also expected across Northern Ireland.

Heavy rain and hill snow are possible in northern England and Scotland on Saturday, with temperatures largely in single figures, although parts of the south-west could reach unseasonable highs of 14C.
The Met Office said that Saturday is expected to be wet and breezy for most of the UK with a brighter showery interlude on Sunday before more rain bands sweep through on Monday.

articles.summary: Sen. Erwin Tulfo interpolated during the hearing, citing the earlier hearing with the Department of Tourism, where accidents and drowning events at beaches caused by lacking safety signs were…

blocks.text: November 27, 2026 | 7:00am
Sen. Panfilo "Ping" Lacson at the Senate budget hearing on the Department of the Interior and Local Government on Thursday, November 26.
YouTube / Senate of the Philippines

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of the Interior and Local Government is seeking to add P176.89 million to their rescue and safety allocations to help local government units respond to tourist emergencies more efficiently.

During the budget hearing on Thursday, November 26, Sen. Erwin Tulfo asked if local government units had dedicated task forces to ensure the safety of tourist, especially in beaches, falls and other bodies of water.
Tulfo cited the earlier budget hearing with the Department of Tourism, where accidents and drowning events at beaches caused by lacking safety signs were discussed.
Sen. Panfilo “Ping” Lacson answered that police are stationed in major tourist stations, but local government units also employ rescue personnel.
These personnel have completed their safety training, and the P176.89 million requested will complement existing funds, Lacson said.

Various water-related accidents have been reported in tourist spots around the country throughout the year. In November 2026, five tourists were rescued after being caught in a rip current while swimming in Baler, Aurora.
The DILG also led the high-profile investigation into the deaths of Ateneo de Manila University basketball players Rene Baterbonia and Divine Adili.

The department’s Criminal Investigation and Detection Group recommended filing charges for violation of the Anti-Hazing Act against former Ateneo men’s basketball coach Tab Baldwin and 10 members of his coaching staff.

articles.title: [Market Rider] PSE’s 2027 rebalancing: Will it unlock broader market activity?
articles.summary: The message is clear: Size alone is no longer enough for a sure spot of a company’s stock in the PSEi.

blocks.text: The message is clear: Size alone is no longer enough for a sure spot of a company’s stock in the PSEi.

In the search for new catalysts that could lead to unlocking broader market activity and growth, the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE) is implementing its biggest index management overhaul since 2011 starting with the February 2027 rebalancing, using the whole-year trading data of 2026.
The revised framework applies to the PSEi, PSE MidCap, PSE Dividend Yield, and sector indices. (READ: What is the PSEi, and why does it matter?)

Unveiled last July, the new rebalancing framework radically departs from the pure market cap methodology by introducing three core changes in the rules for eligibility and liquidity for inclusion in the bourse’s index as it shifts toward free-float trading velocity.

As evaluated, many of our large conglomerates have a high total valuation, but a huge portion of their shares are locked up with founding families or strategic insiders. Under the old rules, a large company could enter or stay in the PSEi simply because of its sheer size and overall peso trading volume, even if its actual public float rarely changed hands.

The first of the three pivotal changes made in the rule is that the PSE instituted a 98% cumulative market capitalization screen. Before even undergoing liquidity evaluations, companies must fall within the top 98% of cumulative total market capitalization among eligible securities. This also effectively filters out the exchange’s smallest listed names from the outset.

Second, the exchange replaced its legacy single liquidity metric with a rigorous dual liquidity test combining the Median Trading Activity Ratio (MTAR) and Monthly Average Daily Value Turnover (MADV). MTAR measures how fast a stock’s publicly available shares are being bought and sold relative to its size, rather than just looking at the raw amounts of pesos traded, while MADV is a liquidity metric that measures the average monetary value of a stock traded per day over a given month.

For the PSEi, MidCap, and Dividend Yield indices, prospective entrants must achieve an MTAR of at least 15%, whereas existing constituents need 10% to retain their spots, a buffer designed to prevent excessive index turnover while sector indices require 7%. Simultaneously, both new and current members of the primary indices must rank in the top 25% of all listed stocks by MADV for at least nine of the 12 months in 2026. For sector indices, the bar is looser. A stock only needs to rank in the top half by daily traded value in at least eight of the 12 months.

Third, the PSE introduced a P250-billion mega-cap float carve-out. While the standard minimum public float remains 20%, corporate giants valued at P250 billion or more can now qualify with a 15% float, provided they satisfy all liquidity tests.

blocks.caption: [Market Rider] Essential market insights on the recent GCash IPO

blocks.text: Despite these sweeping updates, several foundational eligibility rules remain intact for the 30-member PSEi. Companies must still maintain a PSE Main Board listing tenure of at least 12 months, or six months for early inclusion if they rank among the top 25 firms by market value.

Once candidates clear the market cap screen, public float minimum, and dual liquidity filters, the top 30 eligible companies ranked by full market capitalization secure their places in the index. Furthermore, the exchange retains its semi-annual rebalancing cadence every February and August.

Ultimately, these revisions carry profound implications for market participants. Under the 2011 framework, tightly held conglomerates could qualify through size and sporadic block trades, creating liquidity bottlenecks for institutional funds trying to execute large orders without distorting prices.

The message is clear: Size alone is no longer enough for a sure spot of a company’s stock in the PSEi. A company can be worth hundreds of billions of pesos, but if its public shares sit idle without regular trading turnover, it risks being dropped from the benchmark index. Shares need to trade under the new rules.

For domestic institutional investors, including Unit Investment Trust Funds (UITFs), mutual funds, pension systems, and exchange-traded funds (ETFs), enforcing MTAR reduces execution friction and tracking error. Because trading large institutional blocks in large-cap stocks with tightly held floats or thin turnover can push prices sharply against a fund, requiring active trading relative to free float ensures deeper tradable liquidity during rebalances. This allows funds to buy newly added and sell deleted index stocks cleanly at or near benchmark prices and weights, preventing their returns from diverging from the benchmark index. (READ: EXPLAINER: How mutual funds and UITFs make investing beginner-friendly)

Additionally, the P250-billion carve-out creates an immediate pathway into the PSEi for tightly held utility giants. Conversely, the strict nine-month MADV requirement mathematically delays late-2026 mega-IPOs like Mynt (GCash) from immediate entry, ensuring that new additions prove sustained trading depth before attracting passive institutional capital.

By transitioning from static size metrics toward dynamic free-float trading velocity, the PSE is aligning domestic index construction with international institutional standards and mitigate structural illiquidity — standards that is followed by major global stock indexes like the Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) index and the Financial Times Stock Exchange Russell (FTSE Russell) index. – Rappler.com

articles.title: US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough, Zelensky tells BBC
articles.summary: Ukraine's president voices frustration with US and says it is "strange" Trump has described Vladimir Putin as a friend.
articles.byline: Sarah Rainsford, Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent

blocks.text: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying that delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough during peace talks.

In an interview with the BBC at his office in central Kyiv, Ukraine's president also said it was "very strange" that Donald Trump had posted a picture of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend".
"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, suggesting it was like hugging Adolf Hitler during WWII.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.
Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.
He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it wasn't clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.
The Kremlin appears to be resisting.
In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.
Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.
But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Amercians were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.
"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.
"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."
He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.
So whose decision was that?
"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."
Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.
On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.
Zelensky defended the strikes, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".
He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without coordinating with its partners.
He declined to be more specific.
But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.
Recent strikes on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.
Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.
They've also plunged much of the city into darkness.
"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.
"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

articles.title: Bill C-39, Bill C-22 and Quebec's Bill 21: What you need to know
articles.summary: In Parliament, a bill is a written proposal for a new piece of Canadian law. Those proposals make the news because they're typically about big-ticket issues that affect Canadians across the entire…

image.caption: Peace Tower on Parliament Hill is seen on Wednesday. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

In Parliament, a bill is a written proposal for a new piece of Canadian law. Those proposals make the news because they're typically about big-ticket issues that affect Canadians across the entire country, like everyday affordability or personal privacy. Here's what to know about those in the headlines this month.
From major infrastructure to online privacy, federal bills have been up for debate in November
Almost daily, bills make the news across Canada. Stories are often about the bills you have to pay on a regular basis, but November has brought plenty of updates about the bills that can become law.

In Parliament, a bill is a written proposal for a new piece of Canadian law or changes to an existing law. Those proposals make the news because they're typically about big-ticket issues that affect Canadians across the country, like everyday affordability or personal privacy.
Here's a breakdown of those in the headlines this month.
Bill C-39
Carney's major projects bill faces growing environmental, labour pushback

Bill C-39 is also known as the Building Canada Strong Act. It's a controversial piece of legislation designed to give the federal government the power to fast-track the approval process for major projects in regions deemed to be in the national interest.
Major projects could be mines, pipelines, power lines and other infrastructure.

The bill has been the subject of debate because it contains more than 300 clauses amending more than a dozen existing pieces of federal legislation, including laws to protect species at risk, water quality and fisheries. The bill also includes proposed changes to the Canada Labour Code, which left unions unimpressed.

The special legislative committee voted to approve the bill with some amendments on Monday, bringing a days-long, clause-by-clause debate to an end. The bill is expected to be debated in the House of Commons again soon and could become law before the holiday break in December.
Bill C-22
Liberals propose new police search powers bill after privacy concerns thwarted 1st attempt
Known as lawful access legislation, Bill C-22 is a deeply divisive legislative proposal that would make it easier for police and intelligence agencies to access Canadians' private information.

If the bill becomes law, tech companies would be compelled to adapt their systems to preserve data and then turn that information over to law enforcement and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS) if either had a warrant.

The bill would also give the federal public safety minister the power to issue confidential orders requiring electronic service providers to retain user metadata, which can include the sender, recipient and timing of communications, for as long as six months.

The government and security community argue the bill is essential for investigators to keep pace in a digital age. Privacy proponents, civil liberties groups and some of the world's largest tech companies, on the other hand, have raised concerned about opening up access to encrypted information.
This week, senators on the national security committee said they wanted to see some changes to the bill after another clause-by-clause review.
Bill 21
Why all Canadians’ rights are at stake in the Supreme Court challenge of Quebec’s Bill 21

This is Quebec's controversial secularism law, which bars some public-sector workers from wearing religious symbols on the job. The law, which applies to teachers and police officers, among others, quickly faced a constitutional challenge from civil liberties groups arguing that it discriminates against Muslim women who wear head coverings.
The law is technically no longer a bill because it was adopted by the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) government in 2019, but has been commonly referred to as Bill 21 in media coverage for years.
That convention will continue when the Supreme Court of Canada issues its decision about the legislation Friday morning.

articles.title: Strobe Talbott, Time magazine reporter and deputy US secretary of state, dies aged 80
articles.summary:
After 21 years at Time, Talbott joined the Clinton administration and later headed the Brookings Institution

Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy…

blocks.text: Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.
His son, Devin Talbott, confirmed he died peacefully after a long illness in his East Hampton, New York, home.

The elder Talbott was educated at Yale and Oxford, where he bunked with Clinton. While at the British university, after interning for Time in Moscow, the magazine asked Talbott to help translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former first secretary of the Communist party of the Soviet Union.
Talbott did, and it landed him a job at the magazine.
After 21 years at Time, where he focused on Soviet-American relations and held positions including Washington bureau chief and a foreign-affairs columnist, he joined the Clinton administration.

Talbott joined the US state department in 1994, swiftly becoming deputy secretary of state. In that role, he was the architect of the administration’s approach to Russia and other formerly Soviet countries and conducted negotiations between the US and India after the latter’s nuclear tests in 1998.

He served as the president of the Brookings Institution, one of the US’s most prominent thinktanks, from 2002 to 2017. In that time, he also chaired the US state department’s foreign affairs policy board.
Talbott authored over a dozen books. His last book was titled Our Founders’ Warning: The Age of Reason Meets the Age of Trump, which was published in 2020.

He was born in Dayton, Ohio, in 1946, and is survived by two sons, Devin and Adrian; stepdaughter Rebecca Ascher-Walsh; siblings Kirk, Marjo and Page Talbott; and eight grandchildren, according to the New York Times.
His first wife, Brooke Shearer, died in 2009, and he later married author Barbara Lazear Ascher.
