articles.title: ‘Food insecurity, poor sleep linked’
articles.summary: Older Filipino adults with insufficient access to nutritious food are sleeping poorly, according to local and foreign experts.

blocks.text: November 27, 2026 | 12:00am

Studying almost 3,600 people aged 60 and older nationwide, researchers found that “the prevalence of food insecurity was 13 percent among community-dwelling older Filipinos and the prevalence of sleep deficiency was 80 percent.”
STAR / File
MANILA, Philippines — Older Filipino adults with insufficient access to nutritious food are sleeping poorly, according to local and foreign experts.
Food insecurity is linked to poor sleep as it mainly increased the chances of depression and physical weakness , they said.
Depressive symptoms and frailty among older Filipinos living independently were two plausible explanations for sleep deficiency when suffering from food insecurity, authors noted.

“Tackling depression and frailty may help improve sleep among older adults who experience food insecurity. Supporting mental health, preventing frailty and ensuring food security could therefore play a big role in helping older people live healthier and more restful lives,” researchers said.

articles.title: Sandigan to NBI: Bring Romualdez co-accused to court
articles.summary: The Sandiganbayan Third Division has ordered the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) to bring to court on Dec. 4 Felicito Guevarra, a co-accused of former speaker Martin Romualdez in the…

blocks.text: November 27, 2026 | 12:00am
Guevarra surrendered to the NBI on Nov. 19 after state prosecutors moved to cancel his passport.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — The Sandiganbayan Third Division has ordered the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) to bring to court on Dec. 4 Felicito Guevarra, a co-accused of former speaker Martin Romualdez in the P7.4-billion plunder case in connection with alleged kickbacks from government infrastructure projects.
He is currently in the NBI’s detention facility.
His arraignment will coincide with the last day of the hearing of Romualdez’s petition for bail.

Third Division Clerk of Court Dennis Pulma said the anti-graft court issued a produce order for the arraignment of Guevarra, president of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corp., a firm allegedly used to funnel the alleged kickbacks for Romualdez.
State prosecutors asked the court to exclude Guevarra as accused in the plunder as they seek to substitute him for former public works secretary Manuel Bonoan in the bail hearing.
The Office of the Ombudsman is seeking to make Guevarra a state witness after he returned P343 million in alleged proceeds in connection with the plunder case.
Pulma said the court has yet to issue a resolution on the motions filed by state prosecutors.

articles.title: JV eyes restoration of P130 billion for 2027 infra projects
articles.summary: Senate finance committee chairman JV Ejercito is pushing for the restoration of some P130 billion in the proposed 2027 budget to fund railway, bridge and highway projects.

blocks.text: November 27, 2026 | 12:00am
Senator JV Ejercito on February 25, 2026.
STAR / Ryan Baldemor
MANILA, Philippines — Senate finance committee chairman JV Ejercito is pushing for the restoration of some P130 billion in the proposed 2027 budget to fund railway, bridge and highway projects.

“The P130 billion cannot be compromised. It cannot be compromised as far as the Senate is concerned,” Ejercito said in an interview over dzBB yesterday. He added multipurpose building projects should be given smaller allocations.
Ejercito said the government must prioritize long-term infrastructure investments to help the Philippines attract more foreign investments and catch up with its Southeast Asian neighbors.

He said the P130 billion that he was pushing to restore should cover foreign-assisted projects, including the North-South Commuter Railway, Metro Manila Subway, Bataan-Cavite Interlink Bridge and Laguna Lakeshore Highway.

Ejercito acknowledged that reducing allocations for district projects could upset congressmen. But he said the government must strike a balance between addressing local needs and attracting investment that would generate jobs and boost economic growth.

He defended his decision to realign nearly P20 billion from the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations or AICS and the Department of Health’s Medical Assistance Program to Philippine Health Insurance Corp. (PhilHealth).

He said the move would increase the state health insurer’s subsidy from P74 billion to P94.2 billion – from the P100 billion target – so it can expand its coverage and improve benefits under the Universal Health Care Law. He said the subsidy is short of the target due to what he called limited fiscal space.
Delinquent payment
Health Secretary Edwin Mercado noted a decline in the number of direct PhilHealth members regularly paying contributions, a situation that may require granting them incentives.

“What happened was because of what we call ‘immediate eligibility,’ there has been a drop in the number of paying members even though they have the capability to pay. That is why we thought of giving incentive if you are a regularly paying direct member,” Mercado said.
The DOH chief said their data showed that only one-third of members who have the capability to pay are paying contribution.

He said this was the reason for the recent launch of PhilHealth TAPAT, which aims to provide eligible direct contributors with additional 20 percent incentive in inpatient case rate starting January 2027.

During budget deliberations on Wednesday, P75 million was approved for the establishment by the Department of Labor and Employment of a Labor Attorneys’ Office that will provide free legal assistance to workers. The Senate approved DOLE’s P54.52-billion budget for 2027 during plenary session.

In another development, the Second Congressional Commission on Education reported yesterday that the 2027 budget program provides no funding for 29,588 new scholarship slots under the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority, potentially leaving thousands of learners from the poorest families without scholarship next year. — Christine Boton, Rhodina Villanueva, Bella Cariaso

articles.title: Marcos commits to science, technology investments
articles.summary: President Marcos committed on Wednesday to investing in science and technology as “vital instruments of national development.”

blocks.text: November 27, 2026 | 12:00am
GENERAL SANTOS CITY, Philippines — President Marcos committed on Wednesday to investing in science and technology as “vital instruments of national development.”

“The strength of a nation greatly rests on its ability to understand the challenges of the times, to find lasting solutions through the knowledge and ingenuity of its people, and to strive to continuously improve,” the President stressed in a video message aired at the opening of the 2026 National Science, Technology and Innovation Week of the Department of Science and Technology (DOST).
“For this reason, we continue to invest in science, technology and innovation as vital instruments of national development,” he said.
In making these investments, the President wants a nation with competent people, competitive industries and resilient communities.
“Behind these aspirations are our Filipino scientists, researchers and innovators, whose knowledge and dedication help turn these possibilities into realities,” Marcos said.

The Chief Executive urged the DOST to use the national science week as a platform to advance discoveries and forge partnerships that will benefit the Filipino public. “Let us continue to nurture Filipino ingenuity, advance our research capabilities and transform promising discoveries into practical solutions that will serve our national interests,” Marcos said.
Coconut planting partnership

The government and the private sector yesterday signed a memorandum of agreement (MOU) that aims to plant 10 million coconut trees as part of ongoing efforts to rehabilitate one of the country’s key industries.

President Marcos witnessed the signing of the MOU for a 10-million coconut tree partnership, which is designed to help replace aging coconut trees by distributing quality seedlings to 100,000 farmers in Mindanao and providing training on sustainable farming practices and access to buyers.

The MOU, which supports the government’s goal to plant 100 million coconut trees by 2028, was signed by the Philippine Coconut Authority, Metro Pacific Agro Ventures Inc., Vita Coco Community Foundation, Century Pacific Food Inc. and HOPE.
Marcos said coconut palm has provided food and livelihood for generations of Filipino families, sustained communities and helped establish the Philippines as a leading coconut exporter in the world.
However, he acknowledged that many of Filipino farmers still harvest from palms that their parents and grandparents once tended.

Marcos said the agreement could help farmers earn an additional P30,000 to P65,000 per year, produce more raw materials for processors, generate jobs in rural communities and spur greater opportunities to expand coconut exports.
No funding for vaccine institute
The Virology and Vaccine Institute of the Philippines (VIP) continues to hit a snag after the executive branch failed to allocate a budget for the building’s construction for the third year in a row.
The DOST has requested the full cost of the project at P680 million, but when the 2027 National Expenditure Program was submitted to the House, the item did not appear.

“The project has no budget for 2025 or 2026; there was a proposed one of P680 million for 2027, but this was not granted,” DOST budget sponsor Sen. Bam Aquino said on Tuesday night. “In the NEP, it was not granted; it has not been since, for three years already.”

The five-hectare facility, set to rise in New Clark City, Tarlac, will feature a human and animal virology laboratory, a plant virology laboratory, an animal isolation, biosafety levels 3 and 4 laboratory building, a plant cultivation area, a good manufacturing product building and an administration building.
DOST-Philippine Council for Health Research and Development director Dr. Jaime Montoya said the VIP will house researchers under one roof and accelerate research to prevent another pandemic.

While there’s no budget for infrastructure, attached programs to the VIP still enjoy funding under the DOST’s Grants-in-Aid program, though the allocation declined from P205 million in 2026 to just P65 million in 2027.
Budget scrutiny

Meanwhile, on Tuesday night, during the Senate plenary deliberations on the DOST’s budget, Sen. Imee Marcos asked Secretary Renato Solidum Jr. what concrete interventions the DOST is implementing to arrest the decline in the Global Innovation Index rankings.
“In terms of the input, admittedly it’s low, but they’re committed to really increase the output based on the innovations that the agency is doing,” Senator Aquino said.
The Philippines slipped from No. 50 in 2025 to No. 52 this year in the rankings, as limited resources for innovation endeavors outweigh the country’s growing capacity to produce high-tech outputs.

Aquino urged Congress to increase investments in R&D to prevent the decline, while Senator Marcos told the DOST to set targets in the number of patent applications, technology exports and private sector investment.

The executive branch proposed a P30.47-billion budget for DOST in 2027, a decline of P1.26 billion from the previous year, but the Senate has added P143 million to the agency’s funding. — Alexis Romero

articles.title: Marcos joins AFP boodle fight
articles.summary: President Marcos capped his loaded schedule yesterday by joining a boodle fight with the Armed Forces of the Philippines Council of Sergeants Major, providing him an opportunity to listen to and…

blocks.text: November 27, 2026 | 12:00am

President Marcos joins members of the AFP Council of Sergeants Major yesterday in a boodle fight, a traditional military communal meal that highlights equality, camaraderie and unity among senior enlisted leaders, officers and troops.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos capped his loaded schedule yesterday by joining a boodle fight with the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) Council of Sergeants Major, providing him an opportunity to listen to and speak directly with the soldiers.
The President arrived at Camp Aguinaldo at around 6 p.m. for the boodle fight, a communal way of eating and sharing food piled onto banana leaves, using one’s hands.
Palace press officer Claire Castro said the meal symbolized unity, equality, respect and good relations between the civilian government and the military.
“The President wants to connect, listen, recognize and care for the defenders of the nation,” Castro said in a media briefing.
The event also sought to emphasize the importance of soldiers’ welfare and morale and to acknowledge their efforts to secure Filipinos and the country.

articles.title: Palace: Duterte arrest, ICC turnover in line with Philippines laws
articles.summary: The arrest and transfer of former president Rodrigo Duterte to The Hague was not about sovereignty and was in line with existing laws, Malacañang said yesterday.

blocks.text: November 27, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — The arrest and transfer of former president Rodrigo Duterte to The Hague was not about sovereignty and was in line with existing laws, Malacañang said yesterday.

Palace press officer Claire Castro said Republic Act 9851 enacted in 2009 allows the surrendering of someone accused of crimes against humanity to international bodies, adding that the Supreme Court has ruled that the International Criminal Court has jurisdiction over any crime or act committed before the country’s withdrawal from the ICC.
The Duterte family earlier expressed disappointment over the high court’s decision to junk the petitions questioning the apprehension.

“If we accepted RA 9851 and we are a former member of the ICC, we are not talking about sovereignty because we ourselves became a voluntary member and we created the RA 9851,” Castro said in a media briefing in Baguio City yesterday.

Duterte was apprehended on an ICC warrant on March 11, 2025 for alleged crimes against humanity linked to his bloody war on illegal drugs. He is now detained in The Hague and is set to face trial next week.

His children, Davao City Rep. Paolo Duterte, Mayor Sebastian Duterte and Veronica, had filed petitions for habeas corpus before the Supreme Court, questioning the legality of his arrest and arguing that the Philippines is no longer a member of the ICC.
The former president withdrew the Philippines from the Rome Statute, the treaty that formed the ICC, in 2019.

The high court has dismissed the petitions, saying a writ of habeas corpus is a domestic remedy enforceable only within the Philippines. Since Duterte is now under ICC custody in The Hague, Philippine courts cannot enforce a writ affecting his detention or release, it added.

The high court added that the argument stating that the arrest was invalid because of the Philippines’ withdrawal from the Rome Statute “must be pursued through the appropriate legal proceedings rather than through a petition for habeas corpus.”

On Wednesday, Paolo Panelo, counsel for Veronica, said his client would file a motion for reconsideration, arguing that the decision “effectively reduces the great writ of habeas corpus to a race to remove the person detained outside Philippine territory before the courts can act.”
In a statement, Duterte’s eldest daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte said no foreign court or nation should ever stand above the sovereignty of the Philippines.

“The protection of the life, liberty and fundamental rights of every Filipino citizen must remain paramount. No Philippine court should lightly dismiss a petition as moot, when the underlying issues concern national sovereignty, constitutional accountability and the government’s duty to protect the life and liberty of every Filipino from foreign interference,” the Vice President said.
Defense: No crimes against humanity

Ahead of the start of his trial next week, the defense team of the former president disputed the crimes against humanity charges filed before the ICC, saying the charges should have been tried in the Philippines.

“The case the prosecution has framed against Mr. Duterte is not a crimes against humanity case because the evidence, even taken at its highest, cannot establish the contextual elements,” defense lawyer Peter Haynes said in a 77-page pre-trial filing released on Thursday.

“There was no widespread or systematic attack against the civilian population of the Philippines. There was no State or organizational policy to murder. This is not a crimes against humanity case and, as such, does not belong before this Court,” Haynes added.

The filing, which outlined the defense’s position on the charges, presented Duterte as a leader who has implemented programs aimed at resolving social problems faced by Filipinos, including illegal drugs.

“No sensible analysis of Mr. Duterte’s policy initiatives and achievements in government could possibly conclude that he was attacking ‘the civilian population in the Philippines’,” the defense said in trying to establish the political nature of the case, including his arrest and turnover to the ICC in 2025.
It noted how the Marcos administration changed its position regarding the case after President Marcos’ alliance with the Vice President fell apart.

The defense maintained that Duterte does not bear individual criminal responsibility for the crimes alleged and that this should have been tried in the Philippines instead of bringing it before the international tribunal.

“The Philippines has a functioning criminal justice system, through which killings committed during the campaign against illegal drugs have been prosecuted and continue to be prosecuted as ordinary murders,” the defense claimed, citing the civilian-led Truth Commission and other domestic mechanisms.
The Truth Commission, which was able to identify over 8,000 victims, supports the proceedings at the ICC.
Earlier this week, Human Rights Watch (HRW) reported how Philippine authorities under Marcos failed to investigate extrajudicial killings during Duterte’s drug war.
Despite thousands of reported incidents, only five cases involving nine police officers have resulted in convictions.
Only four cases identified by a Department of Justice task force created in 2024 advanced to trial, while another three are currently under preliminary investigation.

“President Marcos’ pledge to hold police accountable for past and ongoing abuses in its anti-drug campaign has been a failure,” said Lian Buan, HRW Southeast Asia researcher. “The Philippine government needs to prioritize justice for all drug-war victims and provide their families’ adequate redress.”

articles.title: Germany: IG Metall union says deal reached with employers
articles.summary: IG Metall, representing millions of workers in Germany's metal and electrical industry, is the country's largest trade union. The deal came after more than 24 hours of talks with employers.

image.caption: IG Metall was founded in 1949Image: Julian Stratenschulte/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany's powerful IG Metall trade union said Thursday it has reached a pay deal with employers after more than 24 hours of talks.
What is in the deal?
IG Metall and employers agreed on the following points in their agreement:

items: The deal foresees a pay increase in two phases: 2.0% from May 2027 and 2.3% from April 2028
The agreement will also entail one-off payments in March 2027 of between €150 ($164) and €450

blocks.text: What is IG Metal and what are the significance of the talks?
IG Metall represents 3.7 million workers in the German metal and electrical industry. It is Germany's largest trade union.
The talks come amid job cuts across multiple sectors in the German economy, such as the automotive sector.
IG Metall represents workers in major German companies such as Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, Siemens, ThyssenKrupp, and Salzgitter AG, among others.

articles.title: Politician hosts 400,000 guests at daughter’s wedding in India’s poorest state
articles.summary:
Six helipads built and feast prepared by 500 cooks for wedding hosted by Anant Singh, an MP charged with murder

It takes a brave soul to try to match

blocks.text: It takes a brave soul to try to match the mythic opulence of the wedding arranged by the Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani for his son Anant in 2024. Estimates of the cost for the months-long celebration ran to at least $600m, with world leaders and celebrities among those on the guest list.

Smaller fry though he is, Anant Singh, a legislator in India’s poorest state, Bihar, gave it his best shot on Wednesday, albeit in a rustic rural setting, for the nuptials of his daughter Shivangi Singh, and Rishikesh Kumar, an MBA student from Georgia State University in Atlanta.

blocks.caption: Shivangi Singh (left) and Rishikesh Kumar during their wedding.  Photograph: NDTV

blocks.text: About 400,000 guests were hosted across 2.5 hectares at the family home in the village of Nadawa – a staggering figure even by the standards of India’s famed extravagant weddings. Guests were treated to 500,000 pieces of traditional sweets, and a feast prepared by an army of 500 chefs and cooks, Singh’s confidant Munna Singh told Agence France-Presse. One thousand kilos of mutton were reportedly used for kebabs and curries. Six makeshift helipads were erected for VIPs flying in from across India.
Kumar arrived at the venue in sunglasses and waving an orange scarf in a convoy of 151 cars (Hindus consider uneven numbers to be lucky). Among the gifts for the groom was a Land Rover Defender.

The roads leading to the venue were so choked with cars before the wedding that one guest escaped the gridlock, The Times of India reported, by jumping on a tractor and driving across the surrounding fields.
Guests were also treated to elaborate flower arrangements featuring blooms imported from China and a fireworks display.

Instead of a DJ for entertainment, Singh planned a horse race. Gatecrashers clambered up into trees and on to electricity towers to catch a glimpse of the race, but the chaos and tumult was so great it had to be cancelled at the 11th hour. Lying around somewhere amid the wedding detritus was the SUV that would have gone to the winner.

blocks.caption: A screengrab showing crowds at the wedding. Photograph: NDTV

blocks.text: Singh is a controversial figure. Elected five times to the state assembly, he has 28 criminal cases pending against him ranging from murder and attempted murder to extortion and kidnapping. All the cases are listed on the website of the Association for Democratic Reforms, an NGO that is trying to improve governance and strengthen democracy. Singh denies any wrongdoing regarding the charges.

In a television interview before the wedding, he pooh poohed the idea that there was anything unusual about the scale of the wedding preparations. “I laid on exactly the same thing for my elder daughter,” he said.
India’s wedding season has just kicked off. Between now and 15 December, an estimated 5.2m weddings are expected to take place across the country.

articles.title: Sara Duterte can best answer allegations, says House prosecutor
articles.summary: House lead impeachment prosecutor Representative Gerville Luistro on Thursday said she was left wanting more after the defense panel submitted only two names of witnesses it wants to present before…

blocks.text: House lead impeachment prosecutor Representative Gerville Luistro on Thursday said she was left wanting more after the defense panel submitted only two names of witnesses it wants to present before the impeachment court on December 1.
“Medyo nakakabitin (A bit lacking),” Luistro said in an ambush interview.
She also reiterated that Vice President Sara Duterte can best shed light on the allegations that came out during the impeachment trial.
The defense panel asked the impeachment court to subpoena Customs Deputy Commissioner Atty. Agaton Teodoro Uvero and Dr. Lourdes Tingson-Lebosada of Cale88 Foods Corporation.

Luistro said the prosecution had been hoping to receive the complete list of the defense's remaining witnesses, noting that the impeachment court had allotted four days, from December 1 to 4, for the defense's presentation.

“Sana if possible ma-disclose na lahat so that the impeachment court can strategize how to set the date for continuation of presentation of witnesses at yung mga succeeding pa na kailangan gawin for purposes of concluding this trial,” she said.

(Hopefully, if possible, they can disclose the complete list so that the impeachment court can strategize and determine the schedule for the continuation of the presentation of witnesses, as well as the subsequent proceedings that need to be undertaken to conclude the trial.)
Asked why the defense had submitted only two names, Luistro said there could be two possibilities: either the panel was having difficulty producing witnesses or it had no other witnesses to present.
“It's either they are having a hard time producing the witnesses or they really don't have witnesses," she said, adding that the prosecution hoped to see the complete list.
Luistro said that after the defense concludes its presentation of evidence, it will make a formal offer of evidence, which the prosecution will then have the opportunity to comment on.
The impeachment court will subsequently rule on the formal offer before the prosecution and defense deliver their closing statements.
The senator-judges will then vote on the verdict.

When asked how the testimonies of Uvero and Lebosada will impact the defense panel's presentation, Luistro replied, "Yung kay Dr. Lebosada, I think that will be a duplication of what has been testified to already by the previous witnesses. Ang ite-testify ba nila tungkol sa extent ng ownership, registration with BOI and FDA? Sana ang maging testimony nila, on the actual exportation. At pagdating naman dito sa BOC (deputy) commissioner, we look forward na talagang ma-substantiate nila yung alleged exportation ng Cale88."
Luistro said the prosecution panel will seek clarification from Lebosada regarding the P11 million check she received from Vice President Sara Duterte.

When asked why the defense panel seems to be concentrating on Cale88, Luistro replied, "Let us be reminded na ang specific allegation po ng prosecution dwells on the P817 million. This is unexplained wealth, undeclared property, and this Cale88 transaction is just a portion of the same. So sana ma-cover din yung malaking bahagi nitong unexplained wealth and undeclared property, which is the bulk, the substance, the core of the specific allegations of the prosecution."
The lead impeachment prosecutor maintained that Duterte can best answer the allegations.

"Meron na rin namang mga testigong nailatag ang defense. Talagang tayo nafu-frustrate because it does not address squarely the issues raised by the prosecution. And I really maintain my position, tanging si Vice President Sara Duterte lang ang may kakayanang ipaliwanag lahat ng allegations ng prosecution," Luistro stated.

"Palagi niyang sinasabi, she will answer in the proper forum. This is the proper forum. And I believe that this is the last opportunity, in as far as the impeachment process is concerned, para maipaliwanag niya ang kanyang sagot dito sa mga alegasyon ng prosecution. And as a Filipino citizen, hindi na bilang prosecution, I look forward to hearing the answer of the respondent herself," she added.
House impeachment prosecutor Rep. Terry Ridon shared this view.

"For example, doon po sa binabanggit ko lagi na 2023 SALN na walang P80 million pero like past P100 million po yung laman, yung bank, financial, investment at insurance accounts. Yun pong mga external witnesses relating to that like insurance and investment, baka too late in the day na maipasok pa ho sila. So makakapagpaliwanag na lang po talaga diyan, yun pong mag-asawang Duterte Carpio kung bakit yan hindi itinala sa kanya pong SALN for 2023," Ridon said in a separate interview.
"Tingin ko kung wala ho silang maipresenta to rebut the prosecution evidence. The prosecution evidence will, in fact, stand," Ridon added.
The Bicol SARO Party-list representative, however, emphasized the importance of Lebosada's testimony.

"Siyempre mahalaga po itong testimonya po ni Dr. Lebosada kasi siya po yung kalahati noon pong Cale88. Yung "CA" supposedly si Atty Carpio yon. Yung "LE," siya po yung Lebosada roon. So kung meron hong aktuwal na principal na puwede po talaga makapagpaliwanag ng lahat ng mga transaksyon, hindi lang po itong P700 million and yun pong unstated na P500 million doon po sa kanila pong mga transactions at yung China transactions, tingin ko malaki po yung puwede pong maipaliwanag ni Dr. Lebosada dito po sa bagay po na ito," Ridon explained.

When asked about the possibility of the defense panel presenting VP Duterte as a witness, Ridon replied, "If she will be presented there, she will obviously be subjected to cross-examination by the prosecution." —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Is authoritarian Vietnam ready to phase out the death penalty?
articles.summary: Vietnam has voted to abolish the death penalty for six more crimes, continuing a decades-long trend of restricting capital punishment.

image.caption: Vietnam's dealth penalty will now only apply to charges of treason, murder, terrorism and illegal drug production (FILE 2024)Image: AFP

blocks.text: Vietnam, a country once considered one of the world's most prolific executioners, is steadily reducing the number of crimes punishable by death.

On November 20, the country's National Assembly approved a revised Penal Code that abolishes capital punishment for six offenses, including drug trafficking, rape of a person under the age of 16 and crimes against humanity.
When the legislation takes effect next March, just four offences — treason, murder, terrorism and illegal drug production — will remain punishable by death, down from 44 in 1997.

Although Hanoi has given little indication that it intends to do away with capital punishment entirely, few countries that still regularly execute prisoners have narrowed its legal application so considerably.
Authoritarian Vietnam's crime reforms
The reforms are particularly striking given that they come as Vietnam's ruling Communist Party has intensified its crackdown on political dissent and independent civil society.

Minister of Public Security General Luong Tam Quang said the changes reflect humanitarian considerations, the need for more proportionate sentencing and Vietnam's international integration, while maintaining a tough approach to crime, according to the state-run Vietnam News Agency.
Vietnam's gradual reduction in the number of offences punishable by death reflects an evolution in its criminal justice philosophy, said Tran Dai Lam, a lawyer at the ANVI law firm in Hanoi.

"There is a growing recognition that the effectiveness of criminal law depends not necessarily on the severity of punishment, but on the certainty that criminal offences are detected, prosecuted and punished," he told DW.
Moving towards abolishing the death penalty?

Vietnam's latest reforms come barely a year after the National Assembly abolished the death penalty for eight other offences, including embezzlement, bribery, espionage and the illegal transportation of drugs.

The removal of capital punishment for drug trafficking is particularly significant given the prominence of narcotics-related offences in Vietnam's criminal justice system and the country's proximity to the Golden Triangle, one of the world's largest illicit drug-producing regions.
The new legislation also provides for existing death sentences to be commuted to life imprisonment for offences that will no longer carry the death penalty.
Hai Luong, a lecturer in criminology at Griffith University in Australia, told DW that Vietnam has been taking a "retentionist-but-reductionist" approach.
"Vietnam is reforming the death penalty rather than abolishing it," he said. "The trend is towards a more limited and selective use of capital punishment, but not yet towards its complete removal."

According to Luong, the gradual reduction in capital offences reflects Hanoi's efforts to modernize its legal system without relinquishing its authority to severely punish what it considers the most serious crimes.
Why African nations are abandoning the death penalty
Vietnam's integration into international norms
Growing international recognition that capital punishment has little additional deterrent effect is also informing Vietnam's approach, he explained.

Decades of harsh penalties for drug-related offences have done little to stem the international narcotics trade, while the continued expansion of drug trafficking networks in Southeast Asia has raised questions about the effectiveness of executions as a crime prevention measure.

Vietnam's growing integration into the international community, including its participation in international drug control conventions and closer diplomatic ties with Western countries, has also given Hanoi greater incentives to align its criminal justice system with international standards, Luong added.
Vietnam's gradual retreat from capital punishment could also bring it closer to the European Union on human rights.
Brussels has repeatedly called on Hanoi to abolish capital punishment, a subject regularly raised during bilateral human rights discussions.
The EU, one of the world's most vocal advocates of abolition, has long opposed capital punishment as part of its foreign policy.

An EU spokesperson told DW that Brussels welcomes "Vietnam's latest reduction in crimes punishable by capital punishment. This is a positive step and shows a disposition to consider gradual reform, leading towards a moratorium first and finally to the abolition of the death penalty."
"Any concrete step towards this ultimate goal would be very much welcomed by the EU," they added.

However, Vietnam's reforms still fall short of international human rights standards, particularly since the death penalty remains available for drug-related offences that do not involve intentional killing.
Nor is there much evidence that progress on capital punishment is accompanied by improvements in other areas of Vietnam's human rights record, notably freedom of expression and association.
How often is the death penalty used in Vietnam?
It is also difficult to establish whether Vietnam's legislative reforms have resulted in fewer executions.

The authorities classify execution statistics as state secrets. Amnesty International believes Vietnam continues to make extensive use of capital punishment, but it cannot provide reliable annual figures.

Vietnam's capital punishment reform allows the state to continue executing people to fulfil its political and public security goals, "while also managing, or massaging, its international reputation through highly publicized 'reductionist' reforms," Daniel Pascoe, an associate professor of law at the City University of Hong Kong and an expert on capital punishment, told DW

For example, he added, although the recent abolition of the death penalty for drug trafficking is welcome, "it doesn't tell us whether the Vietnamese authorities will now simply charge a higher number of suspects with the drug production offence, which remains death-eligible."
Southeast Asia shifts away from capital punishment
Vietnam's reforms are part of a broader, if uneven, shift away from capital punishment in Southeast Asia.

Cambodia, the Philippines and Timor-Leste have abolished the death penalty altogether. Malaysia abolished mandatory death sentences in 2023, while Indonesia's new Penal Code, which took effect this year, allows for death sentences to be commuted under certain conditions following a 10-year probationary period.

However, Singapore has increased its use of capital punishment in recent years, particularly for drug-related offences, while Myanmar's military authorities resumed executions in 2022 after a hiatus of more than three decades.

Pascoe told DW that although the impact of Vietnam's reforms on execution numbers remains unclear, there is symbolic significance in one of Southeast Asia's most authoritarian governments visibly restricting the death penalty.
"If a one-party state like Vietnam can reduce the scope of capital punishment, why shouldn't Singapore,Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Laos, Brunei and Myanmar also do so?" Pascoe added.

The number of countries actively executing people is close to being at an all-time low, but those that are actively executing, such as Iran and Singapore, seem to be increasing their use, Sara Kowal, co-director of Eleos Justice, a research and advocacy initiative against the death penalty at Australia's Monash University, told DW.
"Vietnam's dramatic reduction of death-eligible offences is another really positive sign that the global trend towards abolishing the death penalty is continuing,” Kowal said.
"It would be great to see Vietnam take the next step to establish an official moratorium on all executions," she added.

articles.title: Iranian drone kills 2 Italian workers in Kuwait, Meloni says
articles.summary: The Italians were employed as technicians for the Italian branch of German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall. One Kuwaiti and one Pakistani national were also injured in the attack. Iran has denied…

image.caption: Iran has frequently targeted Kuwaiti civilian infrastructure, such as its international airport (FILE: April 1, 2026)Image: AFP

blocks.text: An Iranian drone strike on Kuwait left two Italians dead on Thursday, the Italian Foreign Ministry said.
What do we know so far?
The Italians were working for the Italian branch of German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall. Italian news agency ANSA said the victims were two men aged 36 and 65.
It said they had been carrying out maintenance work on detection antennas of the Skyguard air-defense system.
"An explosion caused by a drone attack... occurred at a site where two Italian technicians from the company Rheinmetall Italia were working," the statement from the Foreign Ministry said.
Kuwait's Defense Ministry said a Kuwaiti and Pakistani national were injured in the "criminal attack" on a "vital site" and taken to the hospital.
Iran denied that it had attacked Kuwaiti airspace.
Iran's regime: Inside the system protecting its rulers
Meloni extends 'heartfelt condolences' to victims of families
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she learned of the "tragic" deaths of two Italian citizens in Kuwait during a European Council meeting.

"On behalf of myself and the government, I express my deepest sorrow and extend my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families," Meloni posted on X. "My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also said she was "saddened" by the news.

"We must step up pressure on Iran to put an end to these unacceptable attacks against its neighbors and our partners in the Gulf," von der Leyen said. "Today's events are yet another reminder that security in the Gulf is a matter of security for us all."
Kuwait, a US ally in the Middle East, has been frequently targeted by Iranian attacks since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran in February.

articles.title: Africa's opposition voices face growing pressure
articles.summary: Opposition politicians and government critics say arrests, prosecutions and restrictions on public activity are making it harder to challenge those in power. Is a broader pattern emerging?

image.caption: The leader of Chadema, Tanzania's main opposition party, was sentenced to four years in prison this month for incitement to unrestImage: Ericky Boniphace/AFP

blocks.text: From Cameroon and Tanzania to Mozambique, Nigeria and Zambia, opposition leaders have accused authorities of limiting political freedoms through legal action and restrictions on public activity.
In each case, officials have said the measures are justified under national laws and security provisions.

"Cameroon is very sensitive, and it is important that we know when to criticize the government and when not to criticize the government openly," said Ngam Glory Ani Mbom, a citizen of the central African country.
She said fear of arrest and violence discourage political participation. "You cannot talk about democracy when opposition supporters cannot freely express their minds to the public," she told DW.
For Ndah Grimbald, deputy secretary-general of Cameroon's opposition Social Democratic Front, one of the biggest obstacles is organizing public meetings.

"The first major challenge we face as members of the opposition is the non-authorization of public rallies, public meetings," he said, noting that opposition proposals receive little attention in parliament. "Private members' bills are not even listened to."

Cameroonian law guarantees freedom of assembly but allows authorities to restrict gatherings on grounds of public order or national security. Organizers are also required to notify officials in advance.
Tanzania: Trial and prison

In Tanzania, opposition leader Tundu Lissu was arrested in April 2025 and charged with treason. In November 2026, the High Court acquitted Lissu of treason but convicted him of incitement and sentenced him to four years in prison.

Prosecutors argued that Lissu's remarks were intended to disrupt Tanzania's 2025 general election. In its ruling, the court said it was satisfied that his statements were intended to "disrupt elections and instigate violence."

Lissu rejected the verdict, calling the case "political persecution." He told the judges: "I was not charged with incitement but you judges are convicting me with it just to impress the person who gives you the titles." He added: "Excuses were created to imprison me."
Tanzania's post-election violence: No justice after a year
Gerson Msigwa, Tanzania's chief government spokesperson, directly rejected allegations of political repression and human rights violations.

"Concerns of diminishing civic space and restrictions on political parties to engage in political processes in the lead-up to the general election are unfounded and misleading," Msigwa said in response to Amnesty International's
of a "wave of terror" sweeping Tanzania ahead of the 2025 vote.
Mozambique: Charges disputed

In Mozambique, opposition figure Venancio Mondlane faces five charges linked to protests after the disputed 2024 election, including incitement to terrorism and public advocacy of crime. Prosecutors accuse him of encouraging violence and civil disobedience. Mondlane denies the allegations.

"I have more than enough evidence. There's plenty to go around. Many of my statements were precisely in the opposite direction," he told DW, adding that the protests were intended to prevent violence.

Pedro Sinai Nhatitima, a judge counselor and spokesperson for Mozambique's Supreme Court, defended the court's decision not to allow live broadcasts of Mondlane's trial. He denied that the proceedings are politically influenced, saying the court will decide the case according to the law.
Nigeria: Policing dissent?

In Nigeria, police in Borno State arrested five men wearing T-shirts bearing the slogan "Tinubu Must Go!" The police say the men were not arrested for their political views, but were found with suspected drugs and other items and face allegations including public disturbance and thuggery.
In Kano, police blocked access to a venue for a planned meeting, citing public safety concerns.
What happens when you speak up?
Zambia: Courts and controversy

In Zambia, opposition leader Brian Mundubile has criticized what he describes as a retreat from democratic rights. The courts were closed on August 24, the final day for filing a presidential election petition. The judiciary cited security reasons, while police said intelligence-led security assessments were under way at several government institutions.
State House presidential aide Clayson Hamasaka denied that President Hakainde Hichilema had ordered the closure to prevent an election challenge.

The same month, former opposition lawmaker and cabinet minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was shot dead during a security operation at Mundubile's residence. Authorities said the operation followed intelligence about individuals considered a national security threat, and that officers came under gunfire and returned fire.

Mundubile, who faces treason and sedition charges with other opposition figures, has called for fairness in the proceedings. "We expect an open court process. We are innocent of all the charges against us," he said.
Zambian constitutional lawyer Linda Kasonde has warned: "As you can see, our public institutions are on trial. Democracy in Zambia is on trial."
Cameroonian political analyst Kenang Derek Fay says that despite the setbacks, democratic development across the continent remains a work in progress.
"We are far from getting to the best level," he said. "It is a democracy still struggling to find its way."
'Nothing can prove that I am the one who promoted violence'
DW correspondent Moki Edwin Kindzeka contributed reporting.

articles.title: EU leaders braced for clashes over Ukraine aid at budget talks
articles.summary: Slovakia, Hungary and Czechia want to opt out of €45bn Ukraine loan to fill funding black hole caused by Russia’s relentless attacks

blocks.text: EU leaders are bracing for a clash over long-term financial aid for Ukraine amid an effort to finalise high-stakes budget talks by the end of the year.

Arriving in Brussels on Thursday, the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, reiterated his view that all EU member states should support a €45bn (£38bn) loan for Ukraine for 2027. “When the European Union provides funding, it does so as the European Union – and that union consists of 27 member states, not 23 or 24,” he said.

Merz has previously threatened to veto the bloc’s next seven-year budget unless all countries sign up to the Ukraine loan, which would be a painful outcome for member states that are net recipients of EU funds.
Slovakia, Hungary and Czechia, net beneficiaries, want to opt out of the loan. Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico, who has maintained close ties to the Kremlin, has accused Merz of blackmail.

blocks.caption: From left, France’s Emmanuel Macron, the European Central Bank president, Christine Lagarde, and Germany’s Friedrich Merz, talking in Brussels. Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPA

blocks.text: But Bulgaria, which had been against the loan, said on Thursday it was ready to contribute as long as its share was not linked to weapons.

“Bulgaria is going to ‌take part in the loan of 20bn [for] non-military support ​for Ukraine,” Bulgaria’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, said as he arrived at the summit. “We have a ⁠huge historic diaspora of Bulgarians living ​in Ukraine. Our wish is ​to concentrate our support ​in that ‌area. We are ​going ​to contribute, but no money from Bulgaria for weapons,” he said.

The European Commission last week proposed a €45bn EU loan for Ukraine to fill a funding black hole caused by Russia’s relentless attacks. EU officials proposed €25bn for military spending and €20bn for Ukraine’s civilian needs, such as schools and hospitals.

Arriving at the summit, Czechia’s populist prime minister, Andrej Babiš, was in no mood for compromise. “Cohesion is really the goal of the European Union and [the] Czech Republic. We will fight for this money,” he said, referring to the EU’s cohesion funds, which are intended to help poorer regions catch up with richer ones.

Babiš said his country needed a highway to Austria and more hospitals. “Financing of Ukraine should be negotiated separately. And the most important is the life of our citizens,” he said, adding that the EU should “do everything” to support peace in Ukraine.

But Merz’s stance has won widespread support, especially among western European, Nordic and Baltic states. Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, said: “It’s not acceptable to simply kidnap the support for Ukraine by saying that we will accept the European Union support for Ukraine, but we will not pay for it ourselves. That is not a reasonable way of thinking.”

However, some governments that support Merz’s goal have reservations about his tactics, fearing the public threat to block cohesion funds could make it harder for recalcitrant governments to climb down.
The discussion on support for Ukraine has become entangled in negotiations over the EU’s next long-term budget, which will set the bloc’s spending priorities for 2028-2034.

blocks.caption: Czechia’s populist prime minister, Andrej Babiš, believes financing of Ukraine should be a separate negotiation to the main EU budget. Photograph: Geert Vanden Wijngaert/AP

blocks.text: EU leaders are discussing a €1.78tn proposal presented by the European Council president, António Costa, last Saturday, which represents a 10% reduction on the original €2tn plan from the European Commission.

EU officials want to finalise a budget deal by the end of the year before a sequence of big elections in 2027 complicates finding an agreement. The far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is the frontrunner in next year’s French presidential elections, wants to slash France’s contribution to the budget and cease funding Ukraine.
after newsletter promotion
The Irish taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said it was important to get a budget agreement before the end of the year as “the prospects of doing it in the first half of 2027 are very dim”.

Separately, Germany is seeking to insulate EU funding for Ukraine from a Le Pen victory: Berlin wants to ensure future decisions on funding Kyiv via the EU budget are made by a majority of EU member states. The current system requires unanimity, enabling one country to veto a decision.

Others have pushed back against allowing French elections to dominate the EU budget timetable, and have said making Le Pen the focus gives her ammunition to make a case that the EU is against her political movement. “We should be aware of a self-fulfilling prophecy,” said one senior EU diplomat. “Let’s not be paralysed by elections happening in six months.”

Arriving at the summit on Thursday, Costa said all leaders needed to approach discussions with an “open mind, a constructive approach and a sense of compromise” as he called for the budget to be approved in a “timely” way, adding: “That means by the end of this year.”

The budget has to be agreed unanimously, but countries are deeply split. In one camp are the so-called frugals – net contributors to the EU budget such as Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden – which want to reduce the overall size and shift spending priorities to defence and competitiveness, rather than farm subsidies and regional funds.
In the other camp are 17 countries in southern, central and eastern Europe, which want to ensure the flow of EU funds to traditional policies and oppose cuts.

France sits in neither camp, but has vowed to protect the common agriculture policy (CAP), which benefits French farmers. Maintaining farm payments would make it harder for Le Pen to unravel the budget. On the eve of the summit, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, said “not a single euro of the CAP must be withheld from France in the next European multi-annual budget”.

Le Pen welcomed press reports that Paris was pushing for increased agriculture spending, but said Macron’s position had “nothing to do” with defending French farmers. “The objective would be to dissuade us – if the French entrusted us with the responsibility to govern – from defending French interests in European budgetary negotiations” she wrote on X.

articles.title: Freigang banned — Germany star to miss 2027 World Cup
articles.summary: Germany forward Laura Freigang has been suspended until October 2027 after missing three doping tests, ruling her out of next year's Women's World Cup in Brazil. Freigang denies any intention to…

image.caption: Laura Freigang is already well into her 16-month suspensionImage: Michael Memmler/Eibner/picture alliance

blocks.text: Laura Freigang is set to miss next year's women's World Cup in Brazil after being suspended for missing doping tests, the German Football Association (DFB) said in a statement on Thursday.

Freigang, who has 45 Germany caps and scored 17 goals, will be suspended until October 7, 2027 after reaching a settlement with the DFB, the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) and Germany's National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA). The suspension is for the next 16-months as it began retroactively on June 8, 2026, when she was notified by the DFB.
"It's important to me to emphasize once again that I was never suspected of doping," Freigang said in a statement on Instagram.

"My agreement to a settlement does not mean that I share all the assessments of my case. The past few months have been extremely difficult for me. Another legal process would have entailed significant financial, mental, and emotional strain. This is why I decided to take this path, in the hope of finding some peace, clarity, and perspective for myself," she added.

"It was never my intention to let it get this far. Sports have defined my life since I was little. It breaks my heart that, for now, I won't be able to step onto the field, help my team, or live the daily life that I love so much."
End of an ongoing process for Freigang

This brings to a close a case that has been ongoing for months. The 28-year-old had been accused of not being where she said she would be for a doping control on three occasions between March 2025 and February 2026.

In June of this year, Freigang explained missing the tests "were not deliberately avoided appointments but inconsistencies or misunderstandings in the comprehensive details that have to be updated daily and which we as national team players have to update in the system on a daily and hourly basis."
The ban ends her World Cup hopes, something the DFB has also acknowledged.

"We are simply so sorry for Laura on a personal level because of this situation. The past few weeks have been very stressful for her," said DFB Sporting Director Nia Künzer. "We hold her in high regard both as a player and as a person, and—as we have done in recent weeks—we will continue to stay in touch with her and support her as best we can."
The situation also puts her future at her club, Eintracht Frankfurt, into question. Freigang's contract runs until June next year.

"The agreement that has now been reached provides clarity and planning certainty through a process that is unique to Eintracht Frankfurt—for us as a club, but above all for Laura," Katharina Kiel, Frankfurt's director of women's football.
The club and Freigang, who has played 180 Bundesliga games in her career, are now set to enter talks to determine the shape of her contract moving forward.

articles.title: FIFA says a cyberattack against it targeted a 'limited set of personal and business information'
articles.summary: World football's governing body says the cyberattack targeted personal and business information. They struck at a sensitive time for the under-fire organization and its president, Gianni Infantino.

image.caption: The cyberattack comes at the end of a rollercoaster year for FIFA and its president Gianni Infantino, who is now preparing his bid for reelection at a vote in March [FILE: June 10, 2026]Image: Alfredo Estrella/AFP

blocks.text: FIFA told news agencies on Thursday that it had been targeted by a person or group seeking access to its data.

"FIFA can confirm that it has been the victim of a criminal cyberattack resulting in unauthorized access to a limited set of personal and business information," a FIFA spokesperson told the Reuters news agency, issuing similar comments to other outlets.
Reuters cited a person "with direct knowledge of the matter" as saying that less than 0.1% of FIFA's total data had been compromised.
This person also said that no files from the controversial, abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise project that looked to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors had been accessed.
What else did FIFA say about the cyberattack?
FIFA said that it was working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement, in the aftermath of the event.

It did not say when the attack took place, list the precise nature of the compromised data or specify how unauthorized access to FIFA data had been sought, amid reports of people having posed as FIFA officials rather than actually hacking the organization or otherwise compromising its cybersecurity systems.

"FIFA condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data," the Zurich-based organization said. "Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned."

Last week, a group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club posted a screenshot of what it said were FIFA files. Three days later, it appeared to take credit for the cyberattack when responding to a post saying that more than 12 gigabytes of internal documents had been posted.
FIFA did not explicitly state whether it was talking about the same supposed incident.

The breach comes at a sensitive time for the organization. Still reeling from the scandalfollowing this summer's World Cup of its now-aborted plans to sell off World Cup commercial rights shares, it's now trying to secure another term for its embattled president, Gianni Infantino.

Infantino is the favorite for an election on March 18, when he is expected toface challenges from Kohzo Tashima of Japan and Philippe Diallo of France. But until the turbulence of the last six months, it seemed most likely he would simply stand unopposed and extend his 11-year tenure without a fight.

articles.title: Gérard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged rape of actress in 2018, court rules
articles.summary: A Paris appeals court rules Depardieu will go on trial for the alleged rape of Charlotte Arnould.

blocks.text: French film actor Gérard Depardieu is to stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, a Paris appeals court has confirmed.
Arnould, who was 22 at the time, had reported the alleged rape several days after going to his house in Paris to rehearse a play.
She has waived her right to anonymity and her lawyer said Thursday's ruling was a "first" and the forthcoming trial would be historic.

Depardieu, 77, had contested his indictment on two counts of rape. In a letter published in Le Figaro in 2023, Depardieu strongly denied Arnould's allegations, saying "there was never any coercion or violence between us".

Depardieu was for decades a leading figure in French and international cinema for roles in Green Card, The Man in the Iron Mask and the Asterix films. He was awarded France's Légion d'honneur in 1996.

But in recent years a series of allegations have been made against him over his conduct on film sets and elsewhere in the wake of France's #MeToo movement, known as balance ton porc (call out your pig).

Last year, he was given an 18-month suspended jail term after he was found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set in Paris in May. He was also placed on the sex offenders register and ordered to pay compensation.
He dropped his appeal against the ruling last week and offered "sincere apologies" for his behaviour on the set of director Jean Becker's 2021 film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters).
Depardieu had been a friend of Charlotte Arnould's father and on 7 August 2018 she had gone to his home, where much of what happened was captured on the actor's own CCTV.
Arnould's case was initially dismissed for insufficient evidence, but after she filed a civil complaint, a judicial investigation was opened in the summer of 2020.
Speaking outside the Paris appeal court on Thursday, her lawyer Carine Durrieu Diebolt said the ruling was a victory for her client for whom it was "genuinely a relief".
The appeal court said that while Depardieu should stand trial for what took place on that day, he would not be tried for a further alleged rape at a hotel six days later.

Depardieu's lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski told reporters that court had partly ruled in his favour: "As soon as we get the ruling, we will look into the possibility of appealing to the Court of Cassation."
Meanwhile, Depardieu is under a separate investigation alongside French author Michel Houellebecq for "allegations of a sexual nature".
French authorities confirmed their inquiry last week, following reports of an alleged "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018.

articles.title: Mother of drug war victims set to observe Duterte's ICC proceedings in The Hague
articles.summary: The mother of two drug war victims is set to observe former President Rodrigo Duterte"s trial proceedings at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, Netherlands.

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 10:37pm
The mother of two drug war victims is set to observe former President Rodrigo Duterte’s trial proceedings at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, Netherlands.
In a "24 Oras" report from Oscar Oida on Thursday, members of the group Rise Up supported Llore Pasco, who embarked on a flight to The Hague.

As an observer, Pasco represents the parents of slain drug war victims who could not afford to attend the hearings in The Netherlands. She lost two sons to the drug war on the same day in 2017: Juan Carlos Lozano and Crisanto Lozano.

“Sobrang importante po dahil yung iba po hanggang ngayon ay takot pa rin at sabi ko nga palagi dahil tayo ang naiwan, tayo yung buhay, sino pa ang magtatanggol sa kanila? Sino pa ang magboboses kundi tayong mga buhay,” Pasco said.
(It's very important because the others are still afraid and I always say that because we are the ones left, we are the living, who else will defend them? Who else will speak up but us, the living?)
Pasco brings with her the bag of one of her children. She prayed for strength as her fight for justice continues.
Rise Up covered the expense of Pasco’s trip to the Hague. Members made contributions so that she could make the trip, signifying that they were serious about justice.

“Yung aming paglalakbay, kasama ang pamilya ng biktima, ay talagang napakahaba, mahirap, masalimuot… Pero nang makita namin ang determinasyon ng mga pamilya, lalo na yung mga nanay, yung mga nawalan ng anak, yung mga nawalan ng asawa, yung kanilang determinasyon. Sabi nga ng isang nanay, ‘alam ko dapat may hustisya pero di ko alam kung paano’,” Rise Up Coordinator Rubylin Litaw said.

(Our journey, together with the family of the victims, is so long, difficult, complicated... But when we saw the determination of the families, especially the mothers who lost their children, who lost their husbands, their determination. One of the mothers said ‘I know that there should be justice, but I do not know how to attain it.) — Jean Mangaluz/BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Pregnant US inmate escapes in prison vehicle after medical appointment
articles.summary: Rebecca Taylor had been imprisoned in New Mexico for multiple theft and burglary charges.

blocks.text: A pregnant inmate has escaped from custody in the US state of New Mexico, after taking control of a police vehicle while returning to prison from a prenatal appointment, the state's corrections department has said.
Rebecca Taylor, 26, took control of the Dodge Journey and drove away when the team transporting her and another inmate stopped to pick up food in Albuquerque, local media reported.
The New Mexico Corrections Department said that the vehicle and her prison jumpsuit were later recovered, but Taylor remains on the run.
She had been imprisoned for multiple theft and burglary charges, the department said in a Facebook statement.
Local media reported that another inmate, also travelling back from a prenatal appointment, was able to get out of the car as Taylor took control on Wednesday morning.
The corrections department has said that a multi-agency search for Taylor is under way. The BBC has approached it for an update.

The Albuquerque Journal reported that Taylor is currently in her second trimester of pregnancy. For this reason, she was not restrained during transportation, department spokesperson Brittany Roembach said.
"It is the understanding right now that one officer was with the vehicle but not inside of the vehicle when this occurred," she was quoted as saying.
All prisons in New Mexico went into lockdown following Taylor's escape, but it was lifted at 06:00 on Thursday.
However the prison where she was being held, the Western New Mexico Corrections Facility, will remain on "modified movement", and no visitors are currently allowed.
The public has been told not to approach Rebecca Taylor if they see her, and call police straight away.

articles.summary: “Dapat relentless talaga yung paghahabol sa ilegal na droga. Maraming problema ang nagsisimula sa iligal na droga… Kaya dapat kinokontrol , sinu-suppress at ginagawang almost zero ng gobyerno ang…

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 10:20pm
Vice President Sara Duterte said that she wanted a relentless campaign against illegal drugs.
According to a "24 Oras" report on Thursday, the vice president had an interview with former Communications undersecretary and pro-Duterte vlogger Mocha Uson, who asked about Oplan Tokhang.
Oplan Tokhang is the campaign of former president Rodrigo Duterte, Sara Duterte’s father. The campaign became synonymous with the bloodY drug war, which saw the deaths of at least 6,000 people.

“Dapat relentless talaga yung paghahabol sa ilegal na droga. Maraming problema ang nagsisimula sa iligal na droga… Kaya dapat kinokontrol , sinu-suppress at ginagawang almost zero ng gobyerno ang iligal na droga,” Sara Duterte said.
(The pursuit of illegal drugs should be relentless. There are a lot of problems that start from illegal drugs… Illegal drugs should be controlled, suppressed and made almost zero by the government.)
The fight against illegal drugs was one of the flagship projects of former president Duterte. However, it was widely criticized by both local and international human rights groups.

Rodrigo Duterte is now detained in The Hague, Netherlands, and is awaiting trial before the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity in relation to the drug war. —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Nicholas Ty takes oath as new Deputy Ombudsman
articles.summary: Lawyer Nicholas Felix Ty took his oath on Thursday, November 26, 2026, as the new deputy ombudsman for Luzon.

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 9:47pm
Lawyer Nicholas Felix Ty took his oath on Thursday, November 26, 2026, as the new deputy ombudsman for Luzon.

Before his appointment, he served as an undersecretary at the Department of Justice (DOJ), overseeing legal and inter-agency initiatives, including efforts to address human trafficking and transnational crimes.
Upon taking his oath, Ty expressed gratitude to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. for giving him the continued opportunity to serve in public office.
In his new role, Ty said one of his priorities is to serve as a loyal soldier to Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla to help fulfill the latter’s goal of eradicating corruption in the country.
“Ang mga priorities natin bilang Deputy Ombudsman ng Luzon ay siyempre tulungan ang kasalukuyang nakaupong Ombudsman si Ombudsman Boying Remulla,” Ty said.
(Our priorities as Deputy Ombudsman for Luzon are, of course, to assist the sitting Ombudsman, Ombudsman Boying Remulla.)
“At ako naman ay magiging isang tapat na sundalo dito kay Ombudsman Remulla upang matuloy talaga ang kaniyang hangad na masugpo ang korapsyon dito sa bansa natin,” he added.
(And for my part, to be a loyal soldier to Ombudsman Remulla so that his goal of stamping out corruption in our country can truly be achieved.)
Ty said he believes the experience and insights he gained during his stint at the DOJ will prove useful in his new position at the Office of the Ombudsman.
He vowed to remain faithful to the Constitution and his sworn duties to hold violators accountable.

“Maging tapat talaga sa Konstitusyon, maging tapat sa mga batas, maging tapat sa mga tungkulin ng isang public servant at talagang maging ehemplo sa ibang mga public servant at siyempre tulungan ang ating Ombudsman para panagutin ang mga taong lumalabag sa kanilang mga obligasyon,” the new deputy ombudsman said.

(To truly be faithful to the Constitution, faithful to the laws, faithful to the duties of a public servant, to truly serve as an example to other public servants, and of course, to help our Ombudsman hold accountable those who violate their obligations.)
Ty graduated from the University of the Philippines College of Law.
He earned his Master of Laws in International Economics and Business Law from Kyushu University in Japan.
He has practiced law for more than 20 years and has also taught as an assistant professor at the UP College of Law. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Muni Network: Newsrooms unite against AI disruption
articles.summary: Facing the threats of AI-induced disruption and declining web traffic, Southeast Asian newsrooms unite through the Muni Network for the future of news

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – As artificial intelligence continues to squeeze traffic and revenue from independent media, the question of what path newsrooms need to take to survive the disruption has been at the forefront of many conversations within the industry.

Some independent newsrooms in the Philippines and other Southeast Asian countries are going a step beyond talking. From November 19 to 22, editors, technology leads, and newsroom strategists from these news groups gathered at the Rappler headquarters to confront the issue and explore approaches to addressing the AI enigma that capitalize on their collective strengths and communities.

Organized and hosted by Rappler, the event, Future of News (FON) Laboratory, aimed to build a collective approach to AI disruption, declining website traffic, and unfair policies by tech platforms, striving to secure, as its name suggests, the future of news.

“Since the launch of AI overview, we have seen a 50% to 70% drop in our organic traffic coming from the search engine,” said Wahyu Dhyatmika, CEO of Indonesia’s Tempo Digital. “We have to find other ways to ensure that we still can reach our audience, can still be impactful, and also build a new business model.”Rappler CEO Maria Ressa stressed the need for a shared solution. “It doesn’t matter if one news group is moving ahead because we cannot fight these forces alone,” she said.

Ressa emphasized the need for newsrooms to find new business models and build audiences together. “That’s the other reason I wrote The Fight Back. The fight back literally is building our communities. It is bottom up with our communities, and then we have to work with our governments,” she explained.

“The November 2026 sessions follow many preliminary meetings and one-on-one sessions where we confronted difficult questions that usually got in the way of collaboration,” said Gemma Mendoza, head of strategic programs at Rappler.

blocks.caption: FORGING ALLIANCE. Editorial leaders and representatives from Kiripost (Cambodia), Katadata and Tempo (Indonesia), Malaysiakini (Malaysia), Mizzima (Myanmar), Mountain Beacon and Palawan News (Luzon), Daily Guardian and Sunstar Cebu (Visayas), and MindaNews (Mindanao) pose for a group photo during…

blocks.text: Newsrooms that sent participants to the Future of News Laboratory included Kiripost (Cambodia), Katadata and Tempo (Indonesia), Malaysiakini (Malaysia), and Mizzima (Myanmar), alongside Philippine community newsrooms Mountain Beacon and Palawan News (Luzon), Daily Guardian and SunStar Cebu (Visayas), and MindaNews (Mindanao).

Among matters discussed in preliminary sessions was Meta’s aborted effort to implement a clause in its commercial terms, which treated presence on its platforms as permission for the tech giant to scrape publisher content and use the same as training data for its AI products.

blocks.caption: MUNI-MAXXING. Some representatives from Southeast Asian newsrooms engage in a workshop on how to set up, configure, and maximize MUNI in their workflows. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

blocks.text: “Meta’s recent decision to withdraw the planned website-crawling clause in its updated commercial terms proves that collective pushback works,” said Mendoza, who also leads Rappler’s Future of News initiative.
Representatives of participating newsrooms agreed that they cannot afford to lower their guard.
“They (platforms) steal data, they use data. And the irony is we buy data back from them,” said Redempto Anda, editor-in-chief of Palawan News.

Aryo Widhy Wicaksono from Indonesia’s Katadata also noted that because people now read news straight from social media and AI summaries instead of visiting news websites, fewer brands are buying ads from publishers.
“All the news that we produce, we took effort, we took time, we took a lot of work to do that. And then the AI just took an overview [of] it without really doing anything,” Wicaksono added.

While calling out unfair practices by AI companies, the FON participants also explored ways by which newsrooms can use AI safely to improve and enrich their daily work, as long as human editors stay in control.
At Cambodia’s Kiripost, AI is already helping small teams work faster.
“Recently, our data team, without any coding experience, started a few months ago with vibe coding,” shared Tharum Bun, its co-founder and managing editor.

blocks.caption: THOUGHTS ON AI. Cambodian media company Kiripost managing editor Tharum Bun discusses his newsroom’s unique strengths and the impact of AI in their journalism. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

blocks.text: “Small web tool apps that we have never had before, now we can build in a few months, and we can produce more visual data and stories in a very effective way,” Bun added.
For Mildred Galarpe, editor-in-chief of SunStar Cebu, AI initially felt like a “shining, shimmering tool” that tempted newsrooms to adopt it without enough caution.

blocks.caption: COLLABORATION. SunStar Cebu editor-in-chief Mildred Galarpe suggests community engagement efforts that newsrooms should implement, during the first day of the Future of News Laboratory on November 19, 2026. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

blocks.text: Galarpe noted, however, that moving too quickly led to early mistakes, such as accidentally swapping the family names of the new and old governors in their coverage due to AI use. That experience taught them that while AI is an effective tool to fast-track work, it is not the editor.

“The human eye should always be there. Nothing should be published without your thumbprint,” Galarpe said.Rappler’s Ressa further stressed that AI cannot replace humans because its models operate on probability instead of facts, meaning what many refer to as “hallucination” is actually just the system working as designed.“You will always need a human in the loop…because news is anchored in facts, but the tech that is ruling our lives, they’re anchored in profit, so it’s corrupted the entire world,” Ressa added.

To turn their stand into action, the participating newsrooms are joining forces through the Muni Network, inspired by the MUNI tab on the Rappler app.The Muni Network will officially launch on December 10, coinciding with Human Rights Day, with plans to expand across the region soon.For Anda, this network is essential for small newsrooms like theirs.

“I look at it as a startup venture, because this is something that is pioneering. You have newsrooms gathering together and figuring out a way to go around this problem of AI using our data [and] how we deal with social media platforms inundating and taking over newsrooms,” Anda added.
By combining their audiences and reach, smaller and independent newsrooms hope to achieve greater impact together, if not match the strength of global tech giants.
“AI doesn’t know boundaries,” Wicaksono said. “If we have a collaboration, we add those small sounds or small voices [to] become one.”

blocks.caption: STATUS CHECK. Some Southeast Asian newsroom representatives put their ideas, capabilities, and ways to respond to AI threats on a whiteboard during the first day of the Future of News Laboratory on November 19, 2026. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

blocks.text: The federation wants to change how newsrooms work together across Southeast Asia.
Dhyatmika added that publishers won’t stand a chance if they act individually in the era of AI. For him, newsrooms should not see each other as competitors but collaborators.
He emphasized that acting collectively would enable them to get a fairer share of the value created by their products in the digital ecosystem.

Alongside the workshop, the Future of News Laboratory participants also attended Rappler’s Social Good Summit centered on the theme “We, The Humans” — a timely reminder that humans (the journalists in this situation) must remain in control of technology and use its potential to drive meaningful action instead of being driven by it.
Before the November sessions, the group had also issued a joint statement to sound the alarm on the negative effects of AI on journalism, facts, and democracy.

Released last May for World Press Freedom Day, the joint statement highlighted issues such as algorithmic suppression of news, the economic challenges posed by Big Tech monopolies, and the rise of disinformation, which collectively threaten the survival of independent media.

Early collaborators have already launched public chat channels to strengthen local journalism and held community chats around newsroom-initiated investigations. Among those who participated were Daily Guardian and Sunstar Cebu. Both newsrooms have their branded chat channels embedded on their respective websites.

In September 2025, in time for World News Day, the collaboration also released an experimental video simulating Replica, an “AI-powered journalist.” The video aimed to send a dire warning about what could happen if independent newsrooms die and the only source of news would be AI, ending with a call for citizens to support real journalism. – Rappler.com
