articles.title: EU-Indonesia trade deal opens new markets, but challenges remain
articles.summary: The agreement eyes new export and investment opportunities for Jakarta and Brussels. But can Indonesia turn Europe's growing interest in its markets and critical minerals into sustainable gains at…

image.caption: Economy minister Airlangga Hartarto (2-L) hailed a 'new chapter' in EU-Indonesia tiesImage: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: As the European Union seeks to deepen its presence in Asia and diversify its trade relationships, Indonesia is emerging as an increasingly important partner.

At a signing ceremony in Brussels last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the bloc's trade agreement with Jakarta as one of its "most ambitious deals" in the region, linking markets of 730 million people.

The deal, the culmination of nearly a decade of negotiations, reflects the EU's efforts to diversify its trade partnerships, secure access to critical raw materials and reduce strategic dependencies on China.
For Indonesia, it offers opportunities to attract investment, expand exports and strengthen its position in global supply chains.
The agreement will gradually scrap tariffs on more than 98% of product categories, covering almost the entire value of bilateral trade over 15 years.
Indonesia and EU finally seal landmark trade deal
Indonesia's strategic importance to Europe

For the EU, gaining better access to critical raw materials, particularly nickel, and diversifying its supply chains are central to its strategic partnership with Indonesia, said Philip Schleifer, an associate professor of political science at the University of Amsterdam.

"The main strategic interests are opening up a large and growing market for European companies, diversifying and deepening its economic partnerships, reducing strategic dependencies on China, and securing access to critical raw materials," Schleifer told DW.
Indonesia's mineral resources are particularly important for Europe's green and digital transitions. Nickel, for instance, is a key material for batteries and electric vehicles.
The agreement also creates opportunities for European investment in strategic sectors, including electric vehicles, electronics and pharmaceuticals.

But Indonesia has its own industrial ambitions. The government wants to move beyond exporting raw materials by developing domestic processing industries and retaining more value from its natural resources.

"The challenge for the EU is to reconcile its own interest in securing raw material supply with Indonesia's industrial development objectives," said Eline Blot, a senior policy analyst at the Institute for European Environmental Policy (IEEP).
Trade Reset: How Europe is replacing China and the US
Export opportunities and challenges for Indonesia
For Jakarta, the agreement offers opportunities to expand exports, attract investment and strengthen its position in global supply chains.

Yose Rizal Damuri, an economist at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said his institution's study estimates Indonesian exports could increase by around 60% in the coming years.
"Not only can Indonesia increase exports to Europe, but it can also become more strongly integrated into the global supply chains of European companies," Yose told DW.
Potential beneficiaries include labor-intensive manufacturing sectors such as textiles, garments, footwear and furniture, alongside other Indonesian commodities and manufactured products.

The agreement could also encourage European investment and create employment opportunities. However, Yose stressed that access to the European market does not automatically translate into higher exports.
He identified three priorities for Indonesia: raising awareness of the agreement among domestic businesses, strengthening production capacity and improving the country's business climate.

"Various trade agreements signed by Indonesia have relatively low utilization rates. The value of exports using these facilities remains limited compared with overall export values," he said, emphasizing the need for better information and outreach to producers.

Syafruddin Karimi, an economist at Andalas University, also highlighted the opportunity to diversify Indonesia's export markets and reduce dependence on major trading partners such as China, the United States and regional Asian economies.
However, he warned that Indonesian producers must improve their compliance with European standards.
"Products must be traceable, including whether their production involves environmental damage or labor practices that undermine human dignity," Karimi said.
He added that smaller businesses would need greater government support to meet requirements concerning raw materials, production processes and workers' rights.
Is Europe still a global power? The brutal free trade debate
Environmental costs of economic integration
The expansion of trade and investment could also increase environmental pressures, particularly in nickel mining, palm oil production and manufacturing.

IEEP analyst Blot warned that increased production without stronger environmental safeguards could worsen pollution, ecosystem degradation and industrial emissions. "Nickel mining and processing can contribute to pollution and ecosystem degradation, while palm oil remains closely associated with deforestation," she said.
The growing importance of Indonesian iron and steel exports also raises concerns about emissions from energy-intensive production.

The EU's Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) presents another challenge for Indonesian producers, particularly small-scale farmers who may lack the resources, technical capacity and documentation needed to demonstrate compliance.
Blot acknowledged that these requirements could create disproportionate costs for smaller producers and potentially favor larger companies.
However, she cautioned against using smallholders' livelihoods as an argument to weaken environmental regulations.
Some Indonesian smallholder organisations, she noted, have supported the EUDR as an opportunity to improve accountability in the palm oil industry.
"Rather than weakening environmental requirements, the priority should be to ensure that smallholders receive adequate financial and technical support to meet them," she said.

Professor Schleifer at the University of Amsterdam also warned that growing global demand for Indonesian natural resources could create environmental and social problems previously associated with commodities such as timber, palm oil and coal.

While Indonesia has considerable bargaining power because of its mineral wealth, the challenge is ensuring that increased demand translates into domestic industrial development rather than simply expanding resource extraction.
How a leading EV supplier covered up toxic pollution
Can Indonesia turn market access into sustainable growth?

The agreement includes a dedicated Trade and Sustainable Development chapter covering climate change, biodiversity conservation, sustainable forest management and labor rights. It also provides mechanisms for cooperation and civil society participation.

However, there is no guarantee these commitments will be implemented. "Experience with other EU trade agreements suggests that there is often a big gap between sustainability commitments on paper and outcomes on the ground," Schleifer said.
Blot similarly called for a time-bound roadmap with measurable objectives, stronger monitoring and meaningful participation from civil society and local communities.

For Indonesia, the challenge also lies in preparing domestic industries to compete. Karimi stressed that the government, both at national and regional levels, must work with businesses to improve production standards, particularly among small and medium-sized enterprises.
Yose also emphasized the importance of a predictable business environment, warning that frequent policy changes and regulatory uncertainty could discourage investors.
"Without improvements in the domestic business climate, this will not become a reality. Everything will remain good on paper but will not turn into real momentum for change," he said.
Ultimately, the trade agreement offers Indonesia an opportunity to strengthen its position in international trade and attract investment from Europe.

But whether the agreement delivers broader economic benefits will depend on the country's ability to develop competitive industries, move into higher-value production, and ensure that environmental protection and workers' rights are not overlooked.
DW's Muhammad Athif Aiman contributed to this article.

articles.title: CHR maintains stance vs. abortion except in extreme cases
articles.summary: CHR maintains stance vs abortion except in extreme cases

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 9:32pm

The Commission on Human Rights (CHR) on Thursday stood firm on its pro-life position, saying it opposes abortion except for when a woman's life is at risk, or if she is a rape victim, or there are medical grounds for the procedure.
This was brought up during the Senate plenary deliberations into the proposed P1.285-billion budget of the CHR for fiscal year 2027.
During the session, Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto III asked the CHR of its current stand regarding abortion, considering that there have been efforts seeking to decriminalize it.

“The official stand of the Commission on Human Rights is pro-life. They are anti-abortion, except in extreme circumstances, for example, life-threatening, second, victims of rape, and medical reasons,” budget sponsor Senator JV Ejercito answered.
Sotto said he would no longer propound any more questions if the CHR is maintaining its position against abortion.

“Thank you for that because there is an ongoing hearing. I understand that they are trying to revise the Revised Penal Code. So, hearing that from the CHR, I have no more questions and I have no problem with the budget, Mr. President. I fully support the submission,” he said.
Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel “Migz” Zubiri, meanwhile, also welcomed CHR’s take.
Describing himself as a "Republican" conservative lawmaker, Zubiri said he is "pro-life."

“We appreciate the fact that you came out stating that you will not support legislation to that effect to decriminalize abortion because ayaw po nating mangyari katulad ng Estados Unidos na ano lang, parang pwede kang pumunta ng mall at magpa-abortion [we don’t want to be like the United States where people could just go to a mall and get an abortion],” he said.
“Over my dead body will I allow legislation to that effect, which shall allow decriminalizing of abortion while I’m here in the Senate,” he added.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) earlier maintained that abortion is a crime, but admitted that it was open to proposing exemptions with proposed amendments to the Revised Penal Code (RPC) pending before the House of Representatives.

A DOJ committee reportedly prepared a draft Criminal Code of the Philippines which aims to amend the RPC. A DOJ official also said there were efforts by some progressive lawmakers to decriminalize abortion. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Ex-Cale88 co-owner, BOC official to testify in Sara Duterte impeachment trial
articles.summary: Dr. Lourdes Tingson-Lebosada, who is also the Vice President's dentist, is expected to testify on Cale88's organizational structure, government registrations, business operations, ownership, and…

blocks.text: VEEP. Vice President Sara Duterte talks to supporters as she prepares to leave the Quezon City Regional Trial Court after the postponement of the arraignment for her grave threats case, on October 9, 2026.
Noel Celis/Reuters

Dr. Lourdes Tingson-Lebosada, who is also the Vice President's dentist, is expected to testify on Cale88's organizational structure, government registrations, business operations, ownership, and financial affairs

MANILA, Philippines – A former co-owner of Cale88 Foods Corporation, who is also Vice President Sara Duterte‘s dentist, is expected to testify before the Senate impeachment court when her trial resumes on December 1.

The defense counsel submitted a manifestation dated November 25 asking the Senate impeachment court to issue subpoenas ad testificandum et duces tecum to Dr. Lourdes Tingson-Lebosada and direct her to participate during the proceedings scheduled from December 1 to 4.
Lebosada was also directed to bring certified true copies of the following documents:

items: Registration documents of Cale88 Foods Corporation, including relevant government records;
Documents relating to Cale88’s operations;
Documents relating to the company’s finances and business transactions; and
Other documents relevant to the foregoing.

blocks.text: Cale88, a banana chips production company co-owned by Lebosada and Duterte’s husband, Manases Carpio, came under scrutiny during the impeachment trial after Anti-Money Laundering Council records showed that it received P776 million in cash inflows despite having only P125,000 in paid-up capital and declaring P208 million in sales.

Lawyer Alex Cabrera, who prepared a forensic financial report on Duterte’s bank and financial records, described Cale88’s business model as “implausible” and likened its operations to a “revolving door,” which he said was indicative of money laundering.
Lebosada is expected to testify on Cale88’s organizational structure, government registrations, business operations, ownership, and financial affairs.

The defense also sought a subpoena for Agaton Teodoro Uvero, deputy commissioner of the Assessment and Operations Coordinating Group of the Bureau of Customs. Uvero is expected to testify on Cale88’s exportation records under the custody of the BOC.
The impeachment court confirmed the issuance of subpoenas to both witnesses.

“As of this morning, Thursday, November 26, 2026, the Office of the Clerk of Court has completed service of both subpoenas — serving the Office of Bureau of Customs Deputy Commissioner Atty. Agaton Teodoro O. Uvero personally at 9:05 am, and serving Dr. Lourdes Tingson-Lebosada in Davao City via electronic mail at 9:54 am pursuant to the Court’s electronic service directive,” said impeachment court spokesperson Reginald Tongol.
The impeachment trial is currently on hold to give way to Senate plenary deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget. Proceedings are scheduled to resume on December 1. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘I’m no longer a UAE official’: UN hopeful Lana Nusseibeh tries to shake off Sudan record
articles.summary:
The US and Russia’s candidate for secretary general is on a charm offensive. Can she overcome London’s resistance to her bid?

Lana Nusseibeh is in Britain this week, attempting to present…

blocks.text: Lana Nusseibeh is in Britain this week, attempting to present herself as a potential future UN secretary general, and shift the focus from her past as a United Arab Emirates diplomat who denied the country’s role in arming a militia accused of war crimes and genocide in Sudan’s four-year civil war.
It is a high-risk strategy that involves meeting ministers, MPs, academics and holding a public event with the UN Association.

Labelled by many British NGOs and others as an apologist for war crimes, Nusseibeh is presenting herself as a skilled diplomat with the network to put the UN back at the centre of mediation, development and human rights.

“These are very geopolitical times,” she said in an interview. “You need a geopolitical secretary general, because the fact is these geopolitical ruptures are not going away. These fissures in the international system are not going to dissolve any time soon.”

blocks.caption: Lana Nusseibeh in March, when she was the UAE’s minister of state. Photograph: Abdelhadi Ramahi/Reuters

blocks.text: Nusseibeh had a setback last Friday, when three permanent members of the UN security council, China, France and the UK, all voted to “discourage” her candidature. The UN’s electoral system requires that she secure nine positive votes from the 15-strong security council, and no discouragement from the permanent five (P5) before being recommended to the UN general assembly.

She has the backing of the US and Russia, and thinks her cause is not lost. “Sometimes, the use of the veto is tactical. Sometimes, it’s a holding position, sometimes it’s a leveraging position. There are a number of different theories”.
The centre of the resistance to Nusseibeh’s candidacy is probably London, and specifically the Foreign Office, the penholder on Sudan at the UN, and this may explain the UK political blitz.

When questioned about her role in Sudan, she asked that her candidacy be seen in the round, highlighting her role in forcing humanitarian aid into Gaza, her support for Afghan women and promoting interfaith tolerance.
“Like every candidate, I come from somewhere, but the independence of the incoming secretary general is the key to their credibility.

“I’ve taken a leave of absence from my role in [the] UAE government in order to independently campaign for this role. But I think that if I was secretary general, Sudan would be the litmus test of success for any incoming secretary because it’s such a horrific humanitarian crisis.”

The war in Sudan, which erupted in April 2023 after a power struggle between the ​military and the Rapid Support Forces, has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. Multiple regional powers, including the UAE, have backed different local proxies since the beginning of the conflict in an attempt to win influence and strategic resources.
The UAE has long been accused of supporting the RSF in Sudan, a charge repeatedly denied by Nusseibeh, who has publicly disputed the findings of UN investigators.
A UN panel of experts suggested last month that the UAE had supplied crucial support to the RSF.

Asked if she regretted dissembling during her time as a diplomat, by denying the UAE had armed the RSF, or her personal role in challenging the UN reports critical of the UAE, Nusseibeh said she regretted that “the Sudanese civil war had continued for so long”.

blocks.caption: Fighters who defected from the RSF gathered in western Omdurman, Sudan, earlier this month. Photograph: Marwan Ali/AP

blocks.text: Nusseibeh added: “But I don’t think saying that is enough for the Sudanese people and the people in the surrounding countries where they’ve also felt the impact of this war, or for the victims of sexual violence and in this conflict, the atrocities committed in El Fasher without accountability, and the use of chemical weapons against the civilian population; all of these are a litany of suffering that has been inflicted on the Sudanese people.”

Asked if the UAE had been supplying weapons to the RSF in a breach of a UN embargo, she replied: “I’m aware of the allegations. I haven’t read the last UN panel of experts report, but I’m not going to comment as I’m no longer a UAE official. In this campaign, I am a secretary general candidate.

“As secretary general, I would fully back the findings of all UN panel of experts reports and I’m aware that I think several countries have been mentioned in various reports.”She later added: “I would call out countries that are supplying arms to any of the parties, including those in the RSF … this needs a process that requires accountability for atrocities that have been committed. That it needs to be a process primarily led by the Sudanese people.”

Nusseibeh said she was willing to take risks to mediate and to put UN values, expertise and its development toolkit at the centre of disputes. Her analysis of contemporary diplomacy was that the world had descended into a default setting of non-cooperation, and the UN needed to restate the case for collaboration between nations as being in the self-interest of everyone.

The UN had been missing from too many conflicts, she argued, and she would set up a mediation board to try to use the full UN toolkit, ranging from confidence-building measures to development to secure peace. “What’s missing is this idea of a secretary general that is a strategist and a mediator-in-chief that is looking at the sort of the blips on the dashboard of conflict and saying, ‘How do we deploy to have maximum impact for most effective use of resource and cost?’ Because resources are not going up, they’re going down. I mean, we’re looking at, since 2010, 40% increase in military spending. So we’re using a lot of hard power as countries and systems to deter, but it’s not actually working.”
That would require some prioritisation at the UN – it has 4,000 different open mandates.
Her intelligence and skills as a diplomat are not in question. However, her track record over Sudan is.

One critic said: “It is a very smart strategic play by the UAE that seeks autocratic capture, and then the asset-stripping of the UN and its standards. The UAE would end the UN’s role on climate. It would be a catastrophe.”

The next security council vote is on Monday. By then some of the backmarkers may have dropped out of the race. The diplomats of the P5 may also be clearer on the flexibility of their mandates, in which case the papal conclave may finally produce white smoke.

The public prosecutor's office said the motorist had confessed to driving at 110km/h (68mph) along a section of ring road, to the north of the old city centre, and clipping the tanker with the side of his car as he changed lanes.
Sources close to the investigation were earlier quoted by state media as saying a high-voltage cable had fallen in front of the fuel truck, causing the driver to lose control.
Twenty-one others were injured in the crash in the Warraq neighbourhood on Wednesday evening, with hospitals treating patients for burns and smoke inhalation.
The public prosecutor's office said on Thursday that "upon questioning the suspect and confronting him with the findings of the investigation... he confessed to committing the act".

"He added that, while moving between traffic lanes and overtaking vehicles, the left side of his car collided with the right rear side of the tanker. This caused him to lose control of the steering wheel and his car veered to the far right of the road."

At the same time, one of the fuel tanker's tyres burst, causing it to veer into the highway's central reservation, hit the concrete barrier and overturn, spilling fuel and igniting a fire, the prosecutor's office said.
Egyptian authorities have not named the suspect accused of causing the fatal crash, but they said he had been travelling with his father at the time.

articles.title: So, your personal info was hacked in a breach. Here's how scammers use it against you

image.caption: While it may come as a relief when a breached company says financial information wasn't accessed, cybersecurity experts explain that doesn't mean your bank accounts are safe. (Graeme Roy/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: The hacks just keep coming.

Canadians have been hit with a string of data breaches recently, with companies and organizations such as Bell, Staples Canada's printing website, KPMG, Pattison Food Group and Toronto's Hospital for Sick Children all reporting cybersecurity incidents in the last few months alone.

In many cases, personal — but not financial — information was accessed by unauthorized third parties. Bell and Staples Canada both confirmed no financial information was exposed in their recent breaches.

items: Data breaches are coming fast and furious. Are businesses doing enough to protect your data?

blocks.text: While it may come as a relief to those affected that their credit cards and bank accounts, at least, haven't been compromised, information such as mailing addresses, passwords and phone numbers were.
That's enough to increase the risk of falling victim to identity theft or a financial loss, according to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada.
Bell cyberattack raises fear AI is making data breaches easier

When companies say that no financial data has been stolen, or that the breach was small, people tend to think the breach wasn't that serious, said Ali Dehghantanha, a professor in the school of computer science at the University of Guelph and a Canada Research Chair in Cybersecurity and Threat Intelligence.

But he said criminals can stack and merge the personal information taken from multiple breaches — a piece here from Bell, a piece there from Staples — and use it to try to access your finances, often with the help with AI.
"Once you stack them up, it becomes much easier to scale your attack and targets a much wider and bigger audience," Dehghantanha told CBC News.
"Companies judge each breach alone. But criminals add all of them up. And that's what gives the criminals the upper hand."
How hackers use personal data

While companies at the centre of some of the most recent breaches, such as Bell, said no financial information was compromised, our identity alone can be linked to financial information, said Jeff Horncastle, an outreach officer at the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

"They can potentially have enough information to be able to compromise existing accounts, get into existing accounts or apply for new credit with the information that they've gained," he told CBC News.
"And if they're missing any information, they may be behind a different type of fraud where they're phishing for the information that they're missing."

items: Bell says it's investigating cyberattack that led to potential theft of business customer data
Staples Canada says customer data accessed during 'security incident' on print website

blocks.text: Scammers can use the information they've accessed from breaches to trick victims into handing over their own financial information on scam calls, Dehghantanha said.
Bell's leak, for instance, included the date and amount of customers' last payment, which call centres use to verify their identities.

People walk bast a Bell store in downtown Montreal on May 7, 2025. Bell is one of several Canadian companies who recently warned customers their personal data had been accessed by hackers. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)
If someone has access to a bill you've paid recently, they now have your phone number, and can call you and say your payment for a specific amount on a specific date failed, Dehghantanha said.
If the small pieces of information they repeat to you seem legitimate, they might convince you to give them your card information.
"These bills that have been leaked, have been stolen, are now the gateways," Dehghantanha said.
The scam can also go both ways. Criminals can call companies pretending to be person whose information they now possess, and ask to have their phone number moved to a new SIM card.
So, next time you log into your bank and it texts you an authentication code, the scammer will get it instead, giving them access to your account, Dehghantanha explained.
What to do if your data was breached
Business are required to notify affected customers of a breach.

If you receive a notice about a data breach, contact the organization directly using its official website or phone number, Horncastle said, because sometimes fraudsters will pretend to be a breached company. (Fraudsters have even been impersonating the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre for years).
You need to be suspicious for at least a year, not a week.Ali Dehghantanha

If your information has been exposed, Horncastle says you should change your passwords and contact your financial institution if needed. Some companies will offer credit protection through either Equifax or TransUnion, but he strongly suggests using both.

Try to find out what information was accessed and be cautious for how it may be used, Dehghantanha said. In the recent Staples breach, for example, order summaries and encrypted passwords were accessed by an unauthorized third party.

A customer shops at a Staples Canada store in Richmond Hill, Ont. on Nov. 17, 2026. Staples Canada said there was a 'security incident' on its staplesprint.ca website in early November, which saw a third party get unauthorized access to certain customer data. (Chris Young/The Canadian Press)

That could mean criminals now have access to your print orders, which might include wedding invitations, or funeral programs, or job applications, making you vulnerable to scams that target newlyweds, grieving families and job-seekers.
It's also important to keep in mind that most personal information doesn't have an expiry date, and criminals can wait a long time after the initial data breach before they attempt to use it.
"You need to be suspicious for at least a year, not a week," Dehghantanha said.
How can people protect their information?

Horncastle said you should use strong, different passwords for each of your accounts, turn on multi-factor authentication, and regularly monitor your bank and credit card statements, and credit reports, for unusual activity.

In addition, he suggests always independently verifying the source of an email or text message, no matter how legitimate it looks. When possible, log into your accounts using official apps and websites — avoid clicking on links through messages.
"Never share your passwords, banking information or verification codes with anyone over the phone, especially when you receive that contact unexpectedly," he said.
Always be careful about any personal information you choose to share online, he added.
"It may be the missing piece of information for the puzzle."

items: 'That was my granddaughter's voice': Senior suspects scammers used AI in Regina, Saskatoon
Her grandson's voice said he was under arrest. This senior was almost scammed with suspected AI voice cloning

blocks.text: Dehghantanha suggests contacting your phone carrier to lock your number from being transferred to a new SIM card, if that's a service they allow, and setting a unique a pin representatives are required to ask before they can make account changes.

And don't just rely on text messages for authentication, since scammers may be able to access those, he added. Enable the call-back option, or combine the text message verification with another method, such as the unique pin, or your fingerprints for touch ID, Dehghantanha said.
Cellphone number transfer highlights potential security risks

Dehghantanha also suggests every family has their own unique code word, because AI has made voice-cloning technology so convincing that people are often tricked into thinking they're getting a call from a loved one in distress — commonly known as a grandparent scam.
"If a conversation is uncommon, just quickly ask, 'What is the code word?'" he said.
Finally, Dehghantanha warns people to never underestimate how quickly and convincingly you may be targeted after a breach.
"An AI intruder moves fast," he said.

articles.title: Joshua Kimmich critcizes Bayern bosses over Musiala health comments
articles.summary: Joshua Kimmich has slammed Bayern Munich's leadership over comments about Jamal Musiala's health issues. The bosses have questioned whether the player can return to previous form – and is still worth…

image.caption: Joshua Kimmich feels that Musiala's situation should be dealt with behind closed doorsImage: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Bayern Munich's disappointing 2-1 Champions League defeat at Lille on Wednesday night – in which Jamal Musiala came on for the last quarter of an hour – was overshadowed by comments the club's captain made afterwards.

"It must never happen that something like this is played out at a player's expense. Of course, the club always comes first and is bigger than the player, but it's not bigger than the person," Kimmich told reporters in the mixed zone.
"That's an absolute no-go and not Bayern-like," he added.
Kimmich was responding to recent comments made by Bayern supervisory board members Uli Hoeness and Karl-Heinz Rummenigge.

"If he (Musiala) doesn't return to being the Jamal of old, then we need to have a conversation with his family, with the player, and, above all, with his agency – because, frankly, the current financial figures would no longer be justifiable," Karl-Heinz Rummenigge told Sky on Friday.
Honorary President Uli Hoeness has described the situation as a "dilemma" for the club, while CEO Jan-Christian Dreesen raised the prospect of talks with Musiala's management and family.
Neurological condition

While theGermany player has struggled with a number of injuries over the past couple of seasons, his health came into sharper focus in August, after he collapsed on the pitch in a couple of preseason matches. He subsequently revealed that he had been diagnosed with a neurological condition which causes him to suffer from occasional "absence seizures."
Kimmich added that criticism of a players' performances was legitimate, but that concerns about Musiala's situation should have been dealt with behind closed doors.
"That's something you should sort out internally, around a table, rather than trying to resolve it publicly," he said.
"It's not that he has problems because he's unprofessional. He's there every day trying to get the maximum out of himself."
Talks between two sides ongoing

Meanwhile, Bayern bosses met with Musiala's agents on Tuesday, and clarified the timeline of events, dismissing speculation that the player could have concealed the condition when he signed his last contract extension.

Bayern said the two sides agreed that he was first examined for seizure symptoms in April 2025, two months after he had signed his contract extension, which makes him one of the club's top earners and is to keep him in Munich until 2030. Discussions between Bayern management and Musiala's representatives are reportedly ongoing.

articles.title: Crew member dies after diesel tanker sinks off Ibiza coast
articles.summary: Authorities rescued 17 crew members but one later died in hospital after a diesel tanker sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza. A contingency plan against possible pollution damage is now in place.

image.caption: The chemical tanker Med Emre was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona [FILE: June 8, 2024]Image: Manuel Hernández Lafuente/VesselFinder/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A tanker carrying up to 7,000 metric tonnes (7,716 short tons) of diesel sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza, local authorities said on Thursday.

The ship's 17 crew members were rescued but one later died in hospital and another six suffered from hypothermia when the Maltese-flagged Med Emre capsized overnight, the government of Spain's Balearic Islands, said in a statement.
According to emergency services, the five further crew members were taken to Valencia and the remainig five were in good condition on a ‌rescue ​vessel.
The chemical tanker was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona when it sank about 30 nautical miles (56 kilometers) off Ibiza's northwestern coast.

blocks.caption: The last known position of the tankerImage: Vesselfinder/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The nationalities of the crew or the cause of the sinking was not immediately clear.
Authorities monitor pollution risk

The Transport Ministry said the maritime rescue vessel Guardamar Talia had reported no wreckage, floating debris or signs of pollution at the site as of Thursday morning. It added that another rescue ship was heading to the area to continue monitoring the situation.
Spain's maritime rescue service deployed an aircraft and the Clara Campoamor, a vessel equipped to respond to oil spills, to inspect the area.
Spain's merchant marine authority ​has activated the national maritime pollution contingency plan at level 2, the second-highest.
The Balearic regional government said it was assessing the incident and its potential impact, including the risk of fuel pollution, before deciding on further measures.
The importance of Ibiza for biodiversity
The waters surrounding Ibiza are a critical zone for biodiversity as they host sea turtles, dolphins and the ‌Balearic shearwater, one of Europe's most threatened seabirds.
The area also hosts vast Posidonia oceanica seagrass meadows, which are essential for maintaining marine biodiversity.
Emilio Rodriguez Diaz, a maritime security expert at the University of Cadiz, told Cadena SER radio that the area affected was "particularly vulnerable."

blocks.caption: Any pollution entering the sea could potentially harm Mediterranean seagrass ecosystems [FILE: February 8, 2020]Image: Dietmar Hasenpusch/Hasenpusch-Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: But he said the Med Emre was a modern ship, built in Turkey in 2019, with a double hull to ensure that, "in the event of a leak (or) a collision, that intermediate part between the cargo hold and the outer layer would flood."
"It's a kind of buffer that prevents the cargo... from being released into the environment," he said.

Spain's worst maritime environmental disaster happened in 2022, when the tanker Prestige sank off the northwestern Galicia region. It spilled tens of thousands of heavy fuel oil and polluted beaches across Spain and France.

articles.title: Diesel tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes sinks near Ibiza, killing one
articles.summary: The possible environmental damage is still being assessed by Spain's sea rescue service.

blocks.text: An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has sunk off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.

The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued. However seven were taken to hospital and one was later pronounced dead, Balearic Islands emergency services confirmed.
The six crew receiving treatment reportedly suffered minor injuries, such as hypothermia, Spanish media reports.
The possible environmental damage is being assessed by a plane and Spain's pollution control vessel, Clara Campoamor, which is owned by the country's national maritime rescue service.
"There is still little information available about a possible fuel spill," Balearic Islands' President Marga Prohens wrote on X.
The Med Emre sank 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia. It is unclear what caused the sinking.
The chemical tanker was en route from Algeciras, in southern Spain, to Barcelona in the north-east.

Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call around 22:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday, according to Spanish media. Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle.
The injured crew members have been taken to hospitals in Valencia and Can Misses Hospital in Ibiza, President Prohens said.

Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.

In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline. It spilled more than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil into the sea.

articles.title: What is the US permitting bill and would it actually help the climate?
articles.summary: A sweeping US bill to speed up energy projects has rare bipartisan support. Supporters say it would unlock clean energy and lower bills, but critics say it's a gift to fossil fuels.

image.caption: Will the permitting bill boost renewables or fossil fuels?Image: Caleb Jones/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: While the dust has barely settled on the Democrats' big midterm showing, lawmakers still have business to get done before a new US Congress takes office in 2027: namely, a permitting reform bill with rare cross-party support that could accelerate clean energy or fossil fuels — or both, depending on who's asked.

Permitting reform might sound like a snooze. But the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) could have far-reaching consequences for the country's energy mix, household utility bills and climate goals.

BAAJA, which is backed by US President Donald Trump, has already cleared the Senate and now faces a vote in the House of Representatives. DW breaks down what's in the bill, the political fight playing out on the sidelines and what it could mean for consumers' pockets and the US energy transition.
What does the bill do?
Before many new solar farms, wind projects or power plants can connect to the electricity grid, they must first pass through an arduous and complex permitting process.

Getting the green light for an energy project can often take years and requires permits from multiple government agencies. If it manages to overcome those hurdles, a legal challenge can easily stop new infrastructure in its tracks.

blocks.caption: It can take years until projects get the greenlight due to a complex permitting processImage: Getty Images via AFP

blocks.text: The nearly 500-page bill aims to overhaul that process. It would speed up environmental reviews, simplify the planning and construction of power transmission lines, make permits harder to revoke and require the growing number of data centers to pay for grid upgrades they need.

The bill is mostly technology-agnostic. So, the same reforms that would make it easier to build a lot of green energy infrastructure quickly could, in theory, be used to speed up oil and gas projects whose carbon emissions are warming the planet.

That's what's made BAAJA controversial, with some Democrats saying permitting reform is needed to get energy bills down and others saying they support provisions, like building more transmission lines required for transporting green energy, but not the whole package.
Would the bill cut emissions or raise them?
It's hard to estimate, and there's a lot of contradictory information out there.

The Rhodium Group, an independent research firm, found the bill would lower US greenhouse gas emissions in every scenario it ran, by up to 4% in 2040 compared with no bill. This is a fraction of the emissions reductions targets the US dropped when it withdrew from Paris climate accord this year.

Purdue University engineer Kevin Kircher reached the opposite conclusion. His analysis, which has not been peer-reviewed, estimates that domestic emissions would rise by about 2%, mostly because he assumes the bill would boost US fossil fuel production.
How LA is plugging hidden oil wells

The difference comes down to a bet about what the bill ends up speeding up more: renewables and the power lines to carry them, or fossil fuels. That depends on which administration is issuing the permits.

Under Joe Biden's administration, for instance, renewables got a boost but since Trump took office, his administration has favored fossil fuels and spent billions paying developers to give up their offshore wind leases.
What would it mean for US household energy bills?

The White House Council of Economic Advisers, a team of economists that advises the president, estimates it would eventually cut the average household's electricity bill by $178 to $251 (€162 to €229) a year.

The logic is that long permitting delays discourage investment in infrastructure, which drives up prices. But that estimate considers only one part of the bill, faster environmental reviews, and doesn't say when the savings would arrive.

Independent analyses also found a drop in electricity prices for consumers, though a more modest one. The Rhodium Group estimates the bill's passage would save the average household $41 to $66 a year by 2035. That's largely because new transmission lines would let cheaper power reach customers and the costs of expanding the grid for data centers would no longer be passed on to households.

Critics point to the fact that those savings are relative. Electricity demand from data centers is expected to push up prices regardless, and permitting reform would only slow that rise rather than reverse it.
Data centers face backlash from US communities

Oil Change International, an advocacy group that opposes the bill, argues households will still end up paying more for energy than they do now, especially if the bill mainly speeds up gas projects, since US gas prices are expected to rise sharply over the next decade.
What do environmentalists say about it?

Most major US environmental groups oppose the bill as written, including the Natural Resources Defense Council, League of Conservation Voters and Earthjustice. The Sierra Club called it "fundamentally flawed."
Much of the criticism focuses on provisions making federal permits harder to revoke.

"It would prevent a future administration from reconsidering a prior administration's flawed decisions to authorize activities such as Arctic drilling, deep seabed mining, or development of data centers on public lands," Earthjustice wrote in a critique.
The reverse is also true. That provision also makes it harder for an administration to come in and halt clean energy projects, as Trump did with offshore wind.

Opponents warn the bill could weaken protection for water and habitats, and limit environmental lawsuits. One area that environmental groups praised is the overhaul of how transmission lines are planned and approved.
That matters because the windiest and sunniest places in the US are often far from the cities that need power, and building long-distance power lines to connect them can take a decade or more.

Still, many critics say they would rather wait until Democrats control Congress in January and pass a version more focused on clean energy. Though that approach is risky, any bill would still require Trump's signature to become law.

articles.title: Seven injured, four critically, after Bangkok oil refinery explosion
articles.summary: Black smoke could be seen across Bangkok's skyline after the blast, as officials urged residents to leave the area.

blocks.text: A alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities confirmed that the fire was under control, but urged people to avoid the area.
Eyewitnesses shared video clips on social media of flames and smoke rising above the refinery.
The city-run Erawan Emergency Medical Centre said it was treating four "red" cases and three "yellow" - less severe - cases.

On a visit to the scene, Thailand's energy minister Akanat Promphan said it appeared the impact of the explosion was limited because the fire started in a distillation tower about 100m (330ft) from where oil was being stored.
He said the incident was concerning as the refinery was in a residential area and the government was suspending production until it could be confident that operations would resume without any issues.
Bangchak Corporation said air quality monitoring in the immediate area around the refinery was within normal ranges.

It confirmed that production at the site, which can process up to 120,000 barrels of oil a day had been shut down. The company has a second refinery in Chonburi province, about 50 miles (80km) from Bangkok, handling a daily capacity of about 180,000 barrels.
An explosion occurred at the Bangkok refinery in July 2012, sparking a fire but no reported injuries.

articles.title: Hope for millions as cheaper HIV prevention jab reaches Africa
articles.summary: Lenacapavir, administered as an injection twice a year, is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV infection.

blocks.text: Uganda is set to receive its first supplies of a cheaper version of a ground-breaking injection to prevent HIV, raising hopes of expanding access to the drug across Africa, where the burden of the disease remains highest.
The first global shipment of the generic drug, known as lenacapavir, arrived in Zambia on Wednesday, with deliveries to Uganda expected in the coming days, the Global Fund has said.
The drug, administered as an injection twice a year, is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV infection and is expected to cost just $40 (£30) per person annually.
Zimbabwe is due to receive supplies early next year, with several other countries expected to follow.
The arrival of the generic drug comes just a year after the original version, developed by US pharmaceutical giant Gilead Sciences, became available in sub-Saharan Africa.
The original version cost about about $28,000 annually in the US, putting it beyond the reach of many of those in developing countries.
Lenacapavir works by targeting the protective protein shell of HIV, disrupting the virus's ability to multiply and establish an infection in the body.
In a landmark clinical trial involving more than 5,000 adolescent girls and young women in Uganda and South Africa in 2024, none of those who received the injection contracted HIV.
Health experts say the injection offers a major advantage over existing HIV prevention pills, known as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which must be taken every day and can carry social stigma.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recommended the drug for HIV prevention in July 2025.
The Global Fund described the arrival of the drug in Africa as a "major breakthrough" in the fight against HIV, saying cheaper supplies would help reach millions more people at risk of infection.

"These deliveries mark an unprecedented acceleration and expansion in access to a highly effective, quality-assured generic HIV prevention medicine in low- and middle-income settings," the group said in a statement on Wednesday.
More than 189,000 people across 10 countries have already received their first injection of lenacapavir, according to the Global Fund.
The organisation expects 24 countries to have received supplies by the end of this year and, working with the US government, plans to reach at least three million people by the end of 2028.
It is eventually expected to be available in 120 low- and middle-income countries.
Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for nearly two-thirds of people living with HIV globally, with adolescent girls and young women disproportionately affected.
South Africa has the world's largest HIV-positive population, with nearly eight million people living with the virus. It is among the countries expected to receive the cheaper injection.
Some 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV last year, while 570,000 died from HIV-related illnesses, according to the WHO.

The rollout comes amid concerns that sweeping cuts to US foreign aid under President Donald Trump's administration could undermine decades of progress in tackling HIV in Africa, where many countries rely heavily on international funding for prevention and treatment.
The UN aims to end Aids as a public health threat by 2030.

articles.title: Myanmar refuses to comply with parts of ICJ genocide ruling
articles.summary: A landmark ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) convicted Myanmar of genocide against its Rohingya minority.

blocks.text: Myanmar will not comply with "inappropriate" parts of the genocide ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), its leader Min Aung Hlaing has said in his first public comments since the court decision.
The ICJ's landmark ruling last week found Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority in a 2017 military crackdown that killed thousands and forced more than 700,000 to flee.
Myanmar denied committing genocide, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups. It is the first state to have been found in violation of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
Min Aung Hlaing said "the term 'genocide' had seriously affected the country's reputation", state media report.

"Myanmar would take actions appropriate for a responsible country but would not comply with requirements it considered inappropriate," the country's coup leader-turned-president said at a meeting on Wednesday, according to state media.
The statement did not specify which parts of the ruling the country objects to.
The genocide case, brought by The Gambia in 2019, centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.

The ICJ determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were violently killed during the operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world.
The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The ruling is final and cannot be appealed.
The ICJ ordered Myanmar to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure should be determined at a later date.
The court also ordered Myanmar to stop ongoing violations and immediately investigate those suspected of breaking the Convention.
But the ICJ does not have the power to enforce these demands. Instead it has to rely on the UN Security Council and political pressure to make its rulings stick.
While the ruling was largely symbolic, it was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups who have long called attention to the suffering faced by the Rohingya.
More than a dozen countries have acknowledged the ICJ ruling, and the UK has announced sanctions on several senior Myanmar military leaders.

Myanmar has been devastated by civil war since Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup to oust civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021. The move turned Myanmar into an international pariah, and its military regime has faced sweeping international sanctions.
Since then, Min Aung Hlaing has been trying to reintegrate Myanmar into the international community, but it remains largely shut out of key diplomatic arenas.

articles.title: Hamas political official and wife among eight Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza
articles.summary: The killings are the latest from a series of near daily attacks by Israel against what it says are Hamas targets.

blocks.text: A Hamas political official and his wife were among eight Palestinians killed in three Israeli air strikes across the Gaza Strip on Thursday.
Local sources told the BBC a residential apartment in Deir al-Balah was targeted at dawn, killing Khaled Abu Nada - the deputy education minister - and his wife, Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada.
A Hamas Civil Defence spokesman said that rescue teams and medical personnel had transferred eight bodies to Al-Aqsa Hospital in central Gaza and Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.
In a joint statement, Israel's prime minister and defence minister said the operation was "part of a series of targeted killings" against Hamas officials.
Thursday's strikes also reportedly killed three Palestinians on al-Nafaq Street, east of Gaza City. Their identities have not yet been established, eyewitnesses said.

In a separate strike on Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, three Palestinians working for Hamas's security services were killed. They were identified as Yasser al-Lahham, Iyad Ahmed and Ibrahim al-Mashal.
In a post X, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed the death of Khaled Abu Nada and said about 80 Hamas officials have been killed in the last month.
"No one in Hamas's leadership will succeed in evading us," he said, adding that the military would "continue to pursue our enemies and protect the security of Israeli civilians".
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had carried out a strike on a "senior" Hamas operative, and would provide further details later.

The attacks came a day after Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 47, the head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, his wife and their two teenage daughters were killed in Israeli air strike on their apartment in Shati refugee camp in Gaza City.
On Tuesday, the overall commander of Hamas's internal security service was among 10 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes.

Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,772 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title: Israel ‘officially sanctions’ torture of Palestinian prisoners to extract confessions, report concludes
articles.summary:
Public Committee Against Torture in Israel examined 42 complaints against Shin Bet interrogators over past decade

Israel has institutionalised the use of torture to extract confessions from…
articles.byline: Emma Graham-Harrison and Lorenzo Tondo in Jerusalem

blocks.text: Israel has institutionalised the use of torture to extract confessions from Palestinian prisoners, sometimes documenting abuse in official records or granting advanced approval for “special measures” in interrogation, according to a report from the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel (PCATI).
This dangerous practice risked leading to irreversible miscarriages of justice, as Israel moved to implement a racist new death penalty law that targets Palestinians, the report said.
PCATI examined 42 cases in which Palestinians filed complaints about the use of torture by Shin Bet interrogators over the last decade.
More than three-quarters said they confessed after the use of “torture or other illegal methods”, and one in 10 provided incriminating statements about other people under torture.

“When it comes to Palestinian detainees, the Israeli legal system officially sanctions torture as a tool for extracting confessions, regardless of whether the content of those confessions is true,” said Sari Bashi, the executive director of PCATI.
“Torture as a tool of interrogation is particularly egregious given initiatives to impose the death penalty in Israel for the first time since 1962.”

Over the years, in hundreds of testimonies, Palestinian detainees have consistently described interrogations employing extreme sleep deprivation, physical violence such as slapping and kicking, threats, sexual violence and being held in stress positions.

Some of this abuse is also laid out in the official records of Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security service. PCATI details the case of a Palestinian lawyer arrested in February 2019 who was subjected to extreme sleep deprivation.

During an interrogation period lasting 27.5 days, or 660 hours, he was questioned for more than 552 hours, an average of 20 hours a day, with one session lasting nearly 48 hours. Some of the remaining 108 hours were spent travelling to and attending detention hearings.

In a 1999 ruling, Israel’s supreme court explicitly prohibited sleep deprivation as a deliberate interrogation method. Despite this, the lawyer was convicted of involvement in shooting attacks based on information extracted during this period.
The state inspector for complaints about Shin Bet interrogations (Mavtan) ruled that the interrogations took place in accordance with procedures, PCATI said.
More than 1,680 torture complaints were filed between 2001 and 2024 with Mavtan. None have led to an indictment.
Other cases are indirectly documented in Israeli judicial records, although judges rarely accept testimony about torture of Palestinians, PCATI said.

In one case, a detainee’s false confession, made under torture, was used as evidence by prosecutors. The man was released after his lawyer presented proof that he was not present at the scene of the crime, PCATI said.
Sleep deprivation was the most frequently used form of torture in complaints examined by PCATI, but more than half included the use of stress positions and other forms of physical violence.

Israel is a signatory to the UN convention against torture, but its legal system has effectively codified the use of violence and abuse where it is deemed “necessary” to extract life-saving information, PCATI said.

In a “necessity interrogation” or “military interrogation”, Shin Bet officials torture detainees “after consulting with their superiors and following an internal procedure for documenting their decisions and conduct”, the report said.

“[A] supposedly narrow exception ballooned and developed into a sprawling system of legal and administrative exceptions that swallowed the so-called rule, enabling the use of violence while maintaining the appearance of prohibition,” it continued.

There is no publicly available information on the scale of “necessity interrogations” inside the Shin Bet, PCATI said. They are an urgent concern as Israel moves to end a de facto moratorium on the death penalty, which had stood since the 1962 execution of the Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann.

“The death penalty is always wrong, because it’s cruel, irreversible and negates the right to life. No one should be executed, particularly not in a system tainted by systematic violence,” Bashi said.
In March, the Knesset passed a racist law allowing the execution of Palestinians convicted of terror charges over deadly attacks, but not Jewish Israelis who commit similar crimes.
In the occupied West Bank, where Palestinians are tried in military courts, execution is now the default punishment for a defendant found guilty of deadly terror attacks.
The legislation drew fierce international criticism, including from the UN’s high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, who warned that it would constitute a war crime if enacted.
A separate law empowers a special tribunal to impose death sentences in cases arising from the 7 October 2023 attacks.
Even in rare cases where courts have excluded confessions obtained under torture, Israeli case law allows prosecutors to use information derived from them as evidence to secure convictions.

PCATI said that as detention conditions worsened after October 2023, rights groups documented a sharp rise in violence by Israeli prison guards and soldiers, including beatings, attacks with dogs, electric shocks, threats and rape.

At least 103 Palestinian detainees have died in Israeli custody since 7 October 2023. Of 10 postmortems reviewed by Physicians for Human Rights Israel, five showed signs of physical assault and six showed evidence of medical neglect.
The Israel Prison Service said “all prisoners are held in accordance with the law”. The Shin Bet and Israel’s justice ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: Germany news: Cologne court awards record damages in Catholic sex abuse case
articles.summary: A court has awarded the highest damages ever in Germany to a victim of sexual abuse linked with the Catholic Church. An alleged spy and suspected terrorists are also making headlines in Germany on…

image.caption: The court in Cologne has ordered the Catholic Church to pay out record damages to an abuse victimImage: Thomas Banneyer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: November 26, 2026
Court awards record damages in Catholic sexual abuse case

The archdiocese in the western city of Cologne was ordered on Wednesday to pay a woman who was sexually abused by a priest for years €550,000 ($601,865) in damages — the highest amount a German court has ever awarded to a victim of abuse in theCatholic Church.
That amount will, however, by offset by the €360,000 that the Catholic Church's Independent Commission for Recognition Payments has already paid to the claimant.

The woman had previously had her claim rejected by the Cologne Regional Court, which, although it accepted that the victim had been severely sexually abused by a priest in the 1970s and 1980s, argued that the archdiocese could not be made responsible for the crimes because the man had acted "more or less as a private individual."
The higher regional court has now overturned that ruling at an appeal, saying that the priest had approached the claimant "under the cover of his church work" when he was a deacon.
It said he used his standing in the church to be allowed to take in foster children, of whom the claimant was one.
The priest was sentenced to 12 years in prison in 2022.

articles.title: Russia-Ukraine war extends to the Baltic and the Mediterranean
articles.summary: By attacking Russian vessels around the world, Kyiv is trying to up the pressure on Moscow and also sending out signals to its Western allies. What is the impact on global maritime trade?

image.caption: The Russian corvette Merkury was attacked by a Ukrainian drone called Sea BabyImage: Security Service of Ukraine/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: First there was an attack on a Russian cargo vessel, the Sparta II, off the Finnish coast, then on the Russian corvette Merkury and a dry cargo vessel that was allegedly carrying weapons off the coast of Libya. These spectacular Ukrainian operations in regions far from the Ukrainian capital Kyiv have caused a stir. They came shortly after several suspected Russian missiles crashed in Poland, not far from where an international military exercise was underway.
Intelligence agencies have long warned that Russia was preparing some form of provocation along NATO's eastern flank.
What are the risks of Russia's war in Ukraine escalating further and drawing in other regions?

It is no secret that Russia has long since expanded its operations beyond Ukraine: With military provocation, hybrid operations and acts of sabotage, Moscow has attempted to put pressure on the countries that openly support Ukraine.
And Ukraine has also targeted Russia's military and economy beyond its borders.

Since the summer, attacks by both Russia and Ukraine have increased in the Black Sea. Not only have Russian and Ukrainian cargo ships been targeted, but also vessels from other countries, particularly Turkey.

Furthermore, in the past few years, Ukraine has managed to deal significant blows to Russia, deep within Russian territory, thanks to aerial and maritime drones. It has targeted military airfields and other strategic targets such as oil refineries, including one in Omsk, Siberia, as well as military vessels in the eastern Black Sea.

blocks.caption: The Russian cargo vessel Sparta II was attacked off the Finnish coast Image: Finnish Border Guard/Handout/Lehtikuva/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ukrainian attacks in Baltic Sea region

Russia has access only to a very narrow strip of the Baltic Sea coast, which is flanked by Finland and Estonia. Even ahead of the attack on the Sparta II, Ukraine had struck in the area multiple times, targeting oil terminals in the region around St. Petersburg, in Ust-Luga and Primorsk.
Russia uses the Baltic Sea to transport supplies to its Kaliningrad exclave and to export oil and other goods to the rest of the world, with the help of its "shadow fleet."

Ukrainian special forces are also said to have carried out operations against Russian military facilities in Syria, well before the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. They are also reported to have lent support to local Tuareg fighters in Mali who were able to inflict heavy losses on the Malian army and allied Russian mercenaries.
Kyiv is thus attempting to harm Russia's military and economy worldwide, even if in military terms this does not help Ukraine directly.

The Russian corvette that was sunk was part of Russia's Black Sea Fleet but because of Turkey's blockade of the Bosporus and the Dardanelles, it would not have been allowed to return to the Black Sea. Instead, it was escorting Russian cargo ships in the Mediterranean. Primarily, the attacks send a political message: Russian ships can no longer feel safe — anywhere in the world.
Black Sea drone strikes put key global trade route at risk
Could war become omnipresent?

"We are not speaking about random shadow vessels which simply transport oil above the price cap and as a result bring revenues for the Russian treasury," security expert Elisabeth Braw from the Atlantic Council told DW. Sparta II was suspected of carrying military equipment, which Moscow denies.

"Ukraine is showing that it knows exactly, and secondly that it's able to hit them wherever and whatever waters they are in," Braw continued. "And this is something I don't think Ukraine has been able to do at the beginning of the war."

Officially, Kyiv's goal is to disrupt Russian logistics and supply routes, but military experts and politicians also see the attacks as a clear political signal to Western allies. They suspect that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is sending a clear message of strength with an eye toward possible future peace negotiations.

In an interview on the German news outlet Tagesschau, security expert Joachim Weber from the University of Bonn suggested that Zelenskyy was paying less attention to the US, out of a sense of disappointment. He said that Ukrainian attacks in distant maritime areas were a sign that there was less inhibition and that Ukraine was ready to expand the conflict geographically to increase pressure on Russia, despite the risks.

Weber warned that war could become omnipresent if there was an increase in attacks on civilian vessels or ships that were considered suspicious in international waters. He said that Russia was providing more military escorts for the ships of its shadow fleet. "The likelihood that an accidental exchange of fire between armed forces, coast guards or anyone could occur is rising."

Braw pointed out that violations of the Law of the Sea were not only rising with regard to the Russia-Ukraine war but also in relation to other conflicts and playing out in "the South China Sea, the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea."

She said about 90% of global trade today was conducted via the oceans and she feared that others might conclude it was not "really to their advantage" to follow the rules of international maritime law.
She added that they might find it "beneficial in the short term to violate maritime rules" for short-term gains. "That would make the world's oceans significantly less safe for everybody."
This article was translated from German.
How Ukraine fights in the Black Sea without a navy

articles.title: Funeral boss 'The Undertaker' seen in police surveillance amid Toronto mafia probe
articles.summary: Police records obtained by CBC News show Toronto-area funeral home president Luigi Vescio Sr. has been on the radar of Canadian and Italian investigators for nearly a decade. He and his family…

image.caption: Luigi Vescio Sr. is seen in a promotional video released by his limousine firm, and in 2019 police surveillance images. (Phantom Limousine Service; York Regional Police)

blocks.text: Toronto·CBC Investigates

Police records obtained by CBC News show Toronto-area funeral home president Luigi Vescio Sr. has been on the radar of Canadian and Italian investigators for nearly a decade. He and his family business were sanctioned by the U.S. last week amid allegations Vescio played a “senior” role in the mob.
Luigi Vescio Sr., sanctioned for alleged ties to 'Ndrangheta syndicate, has been on police radar since 2019
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 26, 2026 4:00 AM EST | Last Updated: 2 hours ago

When the U.S. slapped financial sanctions on a family-owned chain of Toronto-area funeral homes last week — alleging the company's president played a "senior" role in the Italian mob — the dramatic move likely surprised some clients.
But police records obtained by CBC News show Luigi (Lui) Vescio Sr. has been on the radar of Canadian and Italian investigators for nearly a decade.

Police in Ontario captured surveillance images of Vescio meeting in 2019 with visitors from Italy — purportedly leading figures in the notorious Calabrian criminal syndicate known as the 'Ndrangheta. Months later, Italian authorities sought his arrest on a charge of mafia association.

A news release issued last week by the U.S. Treasury Department identified Vescio, 55, as a key player in the criminal group's Canadian wing. The statement said the 'Ndrangheta in the Toronto area has "strengthened in recent years, becoming so powerful that they dictate events in Italy from across the ocean."

From left, Luigi Vescio Sr., his wife Rose and their children Laura and Luigi Jr. All four were recently sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department over alleged ties to the Italian criminal syndicate known as the 'Ndrangheta. (Vescio Funeral Homes)

The Treasury Department said the 'Ndrangheta in Canada is involved in drug trafficking, money laundering and murder. It named five other men reported to be leaders of the group in the Toronto area, including the purported top boss, Angelo (Don Angelino) Figliomeni.

The statement did not specify how the Canadian-born Vescio's businesses are suspected of fitting into the alleged conspiracy. One location in Vaughan, Ont., came into the spotlight in 2019 for hosting a Hells Angels funeral, attended by bikers from across the country.

Washington also sanctioned Vescio's wife Rose and their adult children Luigi Jr. and Laura "for acting on behalf" of Luigi Sr., who is also known as "The Undertaker." All three family members are listed as owners of Vescio Funeral Homes' three locations in the Toronto area, while Luigi Sr. serves as president.
The Vescio Funeral Home in the Maple district of Vaughan, Ont., north of Toronto. (Pelin Sidki/CBC)
The Vescios and their company did not respond to requests for comment. The allegations against them have not been tested in a Canadian court and the U.S. did not provide evidence for its findings.
No one answered when a reporter knocked on the door of the family's Vaughan home. Signs posted in front of the light brown brick house warned of cane corso dogs "on duty."

In a brief interview posted on social media last year, a smiling Vescio — who has tattoos covering his head and neck — said "we own service-oriented businesses," including the funeral homes and a limousine rental firm.
"I started [in the industry] when I was 15, and still pluggin' away," he said in the interview.

items: U.S. sanctions Italian mafia's alleged Canadian branch, including Toronto-area funeral homes

blocks.text: Pictured during surveillance operation

According to Italian police files and York Regional Police intelligence reports reviewed by CBC News, Vescio was seen picking up high-ranking Italian mob figure Vincenzo Muià at Toronto Pearson Airport on March 31, 2019.

Muià had travelled from Italy to confront other figures about the 2018 ambush killing of his brother in Siderno, Calabria, and to apparently seek permission to strike back against those he believed were responsible, the files say.
Luigi Vescio Sr. is seen in a 2019 police surveillance image, carrying a brown envelope outside one of his family's funeral homes. (York Regional Police)

Police noted that during his two-week visit, Muià stayed at the Vescios' five-bedroom home, which has a wine cellar, an in-ground pool and a black-and-white portrait from the movie The Godfather hanging in the den.
Records show investigators kept a close eye on Muià and his associates, including Vescio, during the trip.

items: Mafia fugitive or innocent son? Italy seeks to extradite Ontario man over mob ties

blocks.text: A York police photo included in the surveillance report shows Vescio holding a brown envelope in the parking lot of one of his Vaughan funeral homes. In a separate image, he's seen with Muià and other suspected mob figures outside an Italian restaurant in Toronto.

Luigi Vescio Sr., far right, is seen with other men observed in a police surveillance operation in the spring of 2019. York Regional Police captured images of Italian mob figure Vincenzo Muià and his associates during his two-week visit to the Toronto area. (York Regional Police)

Italian authorities even managed to listen surreptitiously to Muià's conversations with Vescio and others after bugging the Italian's mobile phone — effectively providing them with a live microphone by his side at all times.
The eavesdropping became a key sticking point in Canada's efforts to deport Vincenzo (Jimmy) DeMaria, another one of the purported 'Ndrangheta leaders now facing U.S. sanctions.
Long investigation into alleged Italian mobster could collapse
That came after Project Sindacato, a multimillion-dollar York police probe targeting the 'Ndrangheta, collapsed in 2021 following accusations that investigators illegally intercepted phone calls.
What do the sanctions mean?

The Trump administration moved to sanction 'Ndrangheta members last week because it said the organization provided "essential logistical and operational support" for major Mexican drug cartels, which the U.S. and Canada classify as terrorist groups.

The sanctions ensure the Vescios and their firms can't deal directly with U.S. banks or clients. In effect, it will mean they'll also be cut off from Canadian financial institutions, said Jessica Davis, president of Ottawa-based Insight Threat Intelligence.

"Because of the inter-linkages between the Canadian and U.S. financial systems, any Canadian financial institution doing business with those sanctioned entities is now going to look at them and say, 'your risk rating has really escalated,'" Davis said.
Staff at the funeral homes told callers on Monday that it's "business as usual," while avoiding talk of the ongoing turmoil.

Vincenzo (Jimmy) DeMaria, left, and Angelo (Don Angelino) Figliomeni are among several individuals and firms sanctioned in Canada by the U.S. Treasury Department, amid allegations they hold leading roles in the Toronto-area branch of the 'Ndrangheta. (U.S. Treasury Department)
By Tuesday, however, there were signs of trouble. Employees answering the phones at two locations confirmed the funeral homes could not process card payments.
Davis, a former CSIS analyst, said unless it can operate as a cash-only business, it's likely any such sanctioned entity would be forced to close.

items: U.S. sanctions Canadian money-exchange businesses allegedly connected to Iranian regime, Ryan Wedding

blocks.text: The Bereavement Authority of Ontario, the funeral industry regulator, declined to comment directly on Vescio Funeral Homes, but said families can reach out if they have concerns about prepaid arrangements.
"All prepaid funds for arrangements are held within a third-party trust fund," spokesperson David Brazeau told CBC News in an email.
Both the RCMP and York police — which the Treasury Department said helped in the sanctions case — declined to comment directly on the Vescios or the sanctions.
With files from Carly Thomas
