articles.title: Guinea orders residents to clean up the capital months after deadly rubbish dump collapse
articles.summary: The capital's main rubbish dump has been closed since the disaster, leading to rubbish piling up in the streets.

blocks.text: Guinea has ordered residents to do a mass clean-up of the capital, Conakry, months after a rubbish landfill collapsed, killing dozens of people.
Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah on Wednesday announced a deadline of 31 December to clear rubbish in the city and its suburbs, which has seen an increase in illegal dumping in recent months.
In August heavy rains caused a landslide at the capital's main waste dump, with the rubbish collapsing onto homes killing 31 people and injuring others.
The site in the city's Dar es Salaam area was subsequently closed permanently, which has led to piles of rubbish accumulating outside homes and on the streets.
At a public forum on sanitation, Sanitation Minister Aboubacar Camara said Conakry was generating about 3,000 tonnes of waste every day.
He said much of the garbage was ending up in the streets because of weaknesses in the collection system.
The prime minister called on local authorities to become more involved in organising waste collection, saying this could become a way to create jobs.
"The state will do its part, but the municipalities must also organise themselves to ensure waste collection and provide jobs for young people," the prime minister said.
"Conakry must be completely clean by the end of December," he added, relaying a directive from the country's president, Mamady Doumbouya.
He cited measures the government was taking to improve waste collection and recycling, including a national sanitation fund that would guarantee financing for the sector.

Camara said talks had been finalised with a waste collection operator, with a plan for equipment to move waste from transit and sorting centres to a new disposal site in Baretodé, outside the capital.
The August tragedy at the Dar es Salaam landfill was not the first - 10 people were killed at the same site in 2017.
The government had ordered people living close to the site to move, but many residents chose to stay.
According to the prime minister, the government now plans to transform the closed waste site into an urban park.

articles.title: New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause, BBC understands
articles.summary: Text of the treaties will be published this afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.

blocks.text: The government and the EU are set to publish the texts of two treaties that were agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.
The treaties will be published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation which is designed to enact the bulk of the deal.

The BBC understands the deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.
Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal and Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay.
The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the long-term UK-EU relationship.
The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
Two of the three legal texts will be released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.
New assessments of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country are also expected.

Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost to agricultural exports.
The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.
Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."

"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."
The BBC understands that a plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.
The treaty text will also contain finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules.
Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, will also be detailed in the legislation.
Such powers could enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny.
Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week, the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".
Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.
Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.
Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

articles.title: Thirteen dead as mine disaster highlights illegal hunt for gold
articles.summary: Indonesian authorities say another 13 are missing in the illegal gold mine, which flooded on Monday.
articles.byline: Gavin Butler, BBC Indonesia, Aditya Nugraha

blocks.text: It's been three days since Rani last saw her father as he left for work on Monday. Early on Tuesday, she received news that he was trapped underground.

Rais, 50, had been working as an illegal gold miner in Bogor, Indonesia's West Java province. On Monday night, he and 25 other miners were digging in an open-pit mine about 100m (328ft) deep, when torrential rain caused a nearby river to overflow and flood the two shafts.
Authorities on Thursday confirmed that 13 people had died and their bodies were recovered from the site. At least 13 more are thought to still be missing.
Search-and-rescue operations are ongoing, with personnel using ropes to access the depths of the dark, narrow and slippery mine shafts, which are continually being flooded from below.
Above ground, ambulances and medical personnel are ready and waiting to transport victims.

"We are coordinating with all search and rescue personnel involved in the operation to monitor water conditions and assess access to the mine shaft," Desiana Kartika Bahari, head of the Jakarta Search and Rescue Office, said in a statement on Wednesday.
"The depth of the shaft, narrow access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely."
Small-scale gold mining is banned in Indonesia, but remains widespread in rural parts of the mineral-rich archipelago.

Multiple studies show that over the past ten years the illegal industry has rapidly flourished, often in correlation with rising gold prices. In early 2026, those prices reached an all-time high – spurring a gold rush that prompted mine operators across the country to expand their operations.

This included state-owned mining company Aneka Tambang (Antam), which owns the business permit for the area in which this week's flooded mine is located. Antam have said the mine was not theirs and was operating without their authorisation.

On Wednesday, while rescue operations there were underway, West Java Regional Police separately announced that they had uncovered 24 cases of illegal mining across the province between October and November alone.

But Bisman Bakhtiar, Executive Director of the Center for Energy and Mining Law Studies, told the BBC earlier this year that the actual number of illegal mines in Indonesia is higher than the government's figures.
"[The government figures are] what's been recorded. That means there must be more than that," he said, noting that law enforcement operations have had little impact on the sector.
"It's still very massive and very big because this has been going on for a very long time."
Others allege that the illegal industry is underpinned by corruption.

Laode M Syarif, former deputy chairman of the Corruption Eradication Committee, said that unofficial mining is difficult to eradicate because every illegal mine has "backing", usually from "police and military or high-ranking officials in local and provincial governments".
"As long as these backers are not dealt with firmly, illegal mining will continue," he said.
In many cases, though, the allure of these mines is simple: they offer an economic lifeline to people with few other viable prospects.
Despite the value of gold having dipped in recent months, countless illegal miners throughout Indonesia are still eagerly digging for paydirt.

But the lack of regulation and poor construction in the pits also means accidents are relatively common – whether from landslides, floods, or exposure to hazardous gases, all of which have claimed lives in recent years.
Earlier this year, in the same area as this week's flooded mine, 11 illegal gold miners reportedly died after a carbon monoxide leak inside a shaft.
Elsewhere, in West Sumatra, nine people were killed at an illegal gold mine in May after heavy rain triggered the collapse of a 30-metre cliff, burying 12 miners in total.
There are numerous reports of other such incidents across the Indonesian archipelago. But the illegal nature of the small-scale gold mining sector obfuscates the true number of casualties.

Even this week, when asked how many miners were in the pits in Bogor when they flooded, M Adam Hamdani, head of emergency and logistics at the Bogor Regency Regional Disaster Management Agency, said the total casualty figure "is still unclear".
"Some say 20 people, others say 29 people," Hamdani told Indonesian news outlet Detik. "The problem is that no one reported it and no one wants to report it."
The Indonesian Ombudsman on Thursday urged law enforcement officials to conduct a thorough investigation of the incident and to address the larger systemic issue behind it.

"This should be a momentum for all parties to resolve the [illegal gold mining] problem comprehensively, not just taking action after the incident or closing the holes discovered," said Abdul Ghoffar, a member of the Indonesian Ombudsman.

"We need to uncover the entire [illegal gold mining] chain," he continued. "We must not allow only the miners in the field to be seen and prosecuted, while those who control the activities, provide capital and facilities, store, and market the mined products remain untouched.
"Law enforcement must target the actors and networks that keep this illegal activity going."
As rescue operations continue and more bodies are recovered, the picture is becoming less murky. But even if there are survivors among those who remain missing, time may be running out.
More than three days since the shafts flooded, the relatives of the anonymous men in the mines are desperately waiting to hear whether their loved ones survived.
As she waits for news of her father, Rani says: "I hope he's found soon."

articles.title: DR Congo demands answers over Ugandan general's threats
articles.summary: Gen Kainerugaba threatened a rebel takeover of a mineral-rich area in DR Congo in controversial X posts.

blocks.text: The Democratic Republic of Congo has summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the president's son.

In a series of X posts, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to support a rebel takeover of Walikale, a mineral-rich territory in eastern DR Congo. He insisted that Uganda's military involvement was purely driven by security concerns.
The DR Congo's foreign ministry summoned Uganda's envoy to explain the remarks, describing them as "particularly serious" and damaging to diplomatic relations.
The Ugandan government has yet to respond.
The diplomatic row comes despite close military ties between the neighbours.
Their forces have been conducting joint operations against the Islamic State-linked Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) in eastern DR Congo since 2021.
Uganda has also recently been involved in efforts to mediate between the Congolese government and an armed group led by former warlord Thomas Lubanga in Ituri province.
In his posts, Gen Kainerugaba accused the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), an armed group operating in eastern DR Congo, of targeting members of the Bahima ethnic community.
The Bahema are a traditionally cattle-herding community mainly based in DR Congo's north-eastern Ituri province.
They have historical and cultural ties to the Bahima people of neighbouring Uganda.
He also threatened a rebel takeover of Walikale, in North Kivu province, while defending Uganda's military presence in DR Congo.
Walikale is rich in mineral resources , including some of the country's largest tin deposits and several major gold mines.
Gen Kainerugaba's X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, has since become inaccessible.
It is unclear whether he deactivated it, as he has done in the past, or whether the platform had suspended it.
During the same week he declared: "My tweets in Uganda are directives that must be obeyed."
The posts followed reports that a DR Congo military aircraft had allegedly been shot down by rebels, with foreign mercenaries reportedly among those on board.
Gen Kainerugaba criticised the reported presence of foreign mercenaries in DR Congo.

"These remarks, which are particularly serious, have caused a major media incident and undermine the necessary restraint that must prevail in relations between sovereign states," the DR Congo foreign ministry said in a statement on Wednesday.
"The Congolese government expects the Republic of Uganda to clarify its official position and take the necessary measures to prevent such transgressions from recurring in the future".
The ministry added that DR Congo remained committed to regional peace and stability but would defend its dignity and institutions against "any form of provocation or interference".
It is not the first time Gen Kainerugaba's social media posts have strained relations between the two countries.
In February last year, he threatened to seize the eastern DR Congo city of Bunia, claiming that members of the Bahima ethnic community were being attacked.
In 2024, DR Congo also summoned Uganda's diplomatic representative after the general made threats against foreign mercenaries operating in eastern DR Congo.
The 52-year-old general, widely seen as a potential successor to his father Yoweri Museveni, has become known for his provocative social media posts.
In 2022, he sparked a diplomatic row with neighbouring Kenya after threatening to invade the country and capture its capital, Nairobi, prompting his father to apologise forn the remarks.

articles.title: Desperate appeals from women on death row in Iran after protests
articles.summary: Female protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, a rights group says.

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied by family
Twin sisters Romina (left) and Taraneh Rahimi were arrested in late January, their cousin says
ByBy Soroush Pakzad
BBC News Persian
Taraneh Rahimi is on death row in Iran.
In recent weeks, the 21-year-old has been unable to walk properly after her legs were beaten, and an ear-infection caused by an untreated head injury has affected her balance, her cousin says.
She is "keeping her spirits up" but "there are days she breaks down in tears," Masoud Nourmohammadi tells BBC News Persian.
He says Taraneh and her twin sister Romina were arrested after joining the anti-government protests that swept the country in January.

When the twins' mother first saw them in prison, their faces were so swollen and bruised, and their hair pulled out, that she could only recognise them by their voices, Nourmohammadi says, speaking from the US.
He says Taraneh signed a confession after interrogators threatened that her sister would be raped in front of her.
Taraneh is one of six women who have been sentenced to death this year in connection with the January protests, according to the UN's human rights rapporteur for Iran, Mai Sato.

The figure for men is much higher. However, women protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, as part of a "horrific rise" in politically motivated executions, Amnesty International's Iran researcher Raha Bahreini says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, January's protests began over economic grievances and spread to become Iran's largest since the 1979 Islamic Revolution

blocks.text: Image source, Anonymous/Getty Images
January's protests began over economic grievances and spread to become Iran's largest since the 1979 Islamic Revolution
The Iranian embassy in London told the BBC that claims of an increase in the use of the death penalty in protest-related cases were "misleading".

It categorically rejected allegations of the use of torture and any allegations that the death penalty has been imposed solely for peaceful protest, which it said is a "legitimate, and protected right".

It said death sentences in relation to the "riot in January 2026" were issued in cases involving "intentional murder" or "Moharebeh (the taking up of weapons with the intent to threaten or wreck the people's lives or property)".
The twins were seized in late January, Nourmohammadi says.

It was two weeks after the end of the protests, which began in late December over economic grievances and grew to become Iran's largest against the clerical establishment since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (Hrana) says it has identified more than 7,000 people killed in the crackdown that followed, most of them protesters, but believes the true figure is much higher.

The Iranian government accuses the US and Israel of fomenting the unrest, blaming "terrorists" and "rioters" for the deaths, which it says totalled 3,117 including some members of the security forces.

The twins' family did not find out where they were being held for more than three months, their cousin says. They were tried over protests in Isfahan, in an area of the city where a member of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) security force was killed.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Taraneh loves horses and would like to set up her own breeding centre one day, her cousin says

blocks.text: Image source, Instagram
Taraneh loves horses and would like to set up her own breeding centre one day, her cousin says

Court documents have not been published, but the BBC has seen part of a sentencing document which says Taraneh was convicted of moharebeh, which is a capital offence under Iran's Islamic Penal Code. The offence included "drawing a bladed weapon with the intent to endanger people's lives", according to the document.
Romina was sentenced to 25 years in jail for the lesser charge of aiding and abetting moharebeh, according to Sato, the UN rapporteur.

Nourmohammadi, who has been in contact with relatives and others in Iran familiar with the case, says both women deny all the charges against them and that there is no evidence Taraneh had a "bladed weapon".
Sato says the sisters were part of a case in which 10 people were sentenced to death, but that there was "no clarification of the acts attributed to each individual".

According to sources familiar with the case, the twins' lawyers have submitted a complaint alleging they were tortured and sexually abused during interrogation, but the investigation into it is being overseen by an official they accuse of torture.

blocks.caption: Image caption, This image of Mahboubeh Shabani, sentenced to death in September, has been shared with human rights groups

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied to human rights groups
This image of Mahboubeh Shabani, sentenced to death in September, has been shared with human rights groups
Voice messages from other women on death row contain a mixture of desperation and defiance.
Mahboubeh Shabani - widely reported to be 33 and a civil engineer - was sentenced to death in September under Iran's espionage law after transporting injured protesters, according to rights groups.

She called for help for herself and other prisoners from jail in the city of Mashhad in north-eastern Iran: "Everyone is in a terrible place mentally, especially those whose sentences have been finalised," she said.

Also jailed in Mashhad is Najmeh Amini, reported to be 23, who was initially arrested in the wake of the January protests, and later sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, according to rights groups.
"As long as I am alive, I have one hope, and that is to see a free and prosperous Iran before my life ends by the noose," a voice message attributed to her says.

In addition, Mojdeh Hashemi Bazargani - reported to be aged 27 - is also facing execution, according to rights groups. They say she was convicted of charges including "espionage", after being arrested in April, during the current war between Iran and Israel and the US.
The US-based Iranian rights group Tavaana has shared audio it says is of a phone call she made from prison, describing being beaten in the head, neck and body and made to sign a confession.
The woman in the recording says: "They accused me of espionage. They say you've been paid for it. If I had been paid for espionage, I would have a car or a house. I have nothing."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Najmeh Amini has been sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, rights groups say

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied to Hrana
Najmeh Amini has been sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, rights groups say
Amnesty International describes the charges in all three of these cases and also the twins as "politically motivated".

In response to the BBC's questions, the Iranian Embassy in London said "any allegations of the use of torture in connection with the mentioned cases are categorically rejected". It did not comment further on individual cases, but said "confessions obtained under duress have no legal validity".
At least 39 people have already been executed in connection with the January protests, according to Sato.

She notes a "sharp" increase in arrests and sentences across both men and women, and sees the rise in death sentences for women as an "escalation and expansion" of an "established pattern of repression".
Iranian human rights lawyer Musa Barzin, who is based in Turkey, says "it appears that factors such as gender or age now carry less weight in determining the severity of punishment".
Official detail on cases is often scant and some may go unreported.

However, Sato says as well as the six women she identified as being arrested in connection with protests, a further three have received death sentences this year - for "blasphemy" and "corruption on Earth charges, in relation to the war in March" and "espionage and moharebeh".
In comparison, these nine sentences are more than Hrana recorded for women for similar offences over the whole decade to 2025 - with no more than three in any one year.

The death sentences in three of the cases Sato identified as being linked to the protests have since been overturned – though two of those have been sent for retrial. She says she is concerned by an "increasingly frequent pattern" where overturned death sentences are later "reimposed by a parallel branch of the judiciary once public attention has subsided".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Taraneh (left) and Romina both say they gave baseless confessions after being tortured

blocks.text: Taraneh (left) and Romina both say they gave baseless confessions after being tortured
Sato says there was a "turning point" for women in Iran during the 2022 protests over the death of Mahsa Amini, who died in custody after being detained over an alleged breach of Iran's dress code.
Women "were at the forefront of challenging state policies and structures of control," says Sato. "Their political agency, visibility and leadership have made them targets of state repression."

The Iranian embassy said judicial proceedings in Iran are conducted in accordance with the Constitution and rule of law. It adds: "Cases involving the death penalty have included charges such as serious criminal offences, violence, terrorism, espionage, cooperation with hostile intelligence services and Moharebeh."
Iran executes more people per head of population than any other country, according to UN experts. Human rights groups say last year saw the highest number in decades.
Hrana recorded 2,003 executions in the year to October 2026. The vast majority - including 47 women - were for crimes such as murder and drug trafficking.
Nourmohammadi says the family are trying as best they can to support the twins.
Romina enjoys music and often asks relatives to play songs over the phone, he says.
Taraneh loves horses and has always wanted to set up a horse breeding centre, he says, and they tell her they plan to help her do so in the future: "That's how we try to give her hope."

articles.title: Can Rassvet, 'Russia's Starlink' change the course of the war in Ukraine?
articles.summary: SpaceX's US Starlink satellite system has played a key role in countering the Russian military in Ukraine, but now a Russian counterpart is under development. What could this mean for Ukraine in…

image.caption: Electronic warfare is an important component in Russia's war against Ukraine Image: Alexander Polegenko/picture alliance

blocks.text: Both Russian and international media refer to the satellite communications network Rassvet (Dawn) as the "Russian Starlink," a satellite internet service operated by the US company SpaceX. Rassvet, which was developed by the Russian aerospace company Bureau 1440, operates in low Earth orbit. Interest in the system surged after the Russian military lost access to Starlink terminals, which until then had ensured communications and internet access in the battle zone in Ukraine. On the front, for example, Starlink helps drone pilots and commanders receive images from drones equipped with cameras. Military personnel also communicate together thanks to Starlink.

Though Russia does not fall within Starlink's area of coverage, the Russian military managed to acquire "illegal" terminals through third countries and was thus using the same system as the Ukrainian army.

In early 2026, SpaceX, in coordination with the Ukrainian Defense Ministry, introduced a "whitelist," which registered all devices on Ukrainian territory authorized to operate on the Starlink network. Any terminals being used by Russian forces were subsequently deactivated and reports of serious communication problems on the front then began to appear in Russian social media channels.

In May, the US news channel Bloomberg reported that the Ukrainian army had recaptured about 400 square kilometers (ca. 155 square miles) of Ukrainian territory since Russian forces lost access to Starlink.
Starlink disruption exposes Ukraine's dependence on satellites
What is Rassvet?

Two first launches of serial Rassvet satellites took place in March and July 2026. According to information from Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) published by the Reuters news agency in early November, Russia has started using Rassvet for military communications over Ukraine and to carry out attacks. The system is reportedly being used to improve strike accuracy, expand capabilities of reconnaissance drones and to strengthen resilience against electronic warfare.
HUR spokesperson Andriy Yusov also told Reuters that "the constellation is currently insufficient to provide uninterrupted coverage of Ukrainian territory."

Georgiy Trishkin, a rocket analyst and operator of Telegram channel Tekhassky Vestnik (The Texas Herald), told DW that Russia aims to have a functioning "sovereign" alternative to Starlink — consisting of 292 satellites in orbit — running by the end of 2027.

According to Serhii Beskrestnov, aka Flash, an advisor to the Ukrainian president, the main danger posed by the Rassvet system is that it could allow the Russian army to control drones over Ukrainian territory. He also pointed out on the platform Facebook that the Ukrainian military cannot use Starlink to control drones over Russian territory, since the US service does not work there.

blocks.caption: Starlink terminals are used by both the Russian and Ukrainian armies for communications Image: Lev Radin/picture alliance

blocks.text: SpaceX remains far superior to Rassvet in tech terms

Inspired by the Starlink model, the Russian military also wants to be able to equip drones with terminals, which will enable connectivity in more remote parts of Ukrainian territory. Bureau 1440 unveiled some initial models last month, but according to Trishkin, the similarities between Rassvet and Starlink stop at the "basic features and concept."

"When it comes to details, these are completely different projects. No one can currently match SpaceX's technological edge — and especially its lead in production technology," he said, pointing out that while the Starlink constellation comprised over 10,000 satellites, Rassvet would not have more than 300 in its first phase.

He added that Bureau 1440 would struggle to make enough of the kits used on the ground. While SpaceX can manufacture about 15,000 per day, this would be a "remarkable achievement even over the course of a year" for the Russian company. He also said that the terminals produced by Bureau 1440 were much more expensive than those by Starlink as they relied "on foreign components."

"Right now, no one can beat SpaceX in terms of price, volume and quality of service," Trishkin said. "The next step for the company is mobile satellite services, where it's making very rapid progress. Will Bureau 1440 be able to respond? Unlikely for the time being."

SpaceX's Starlink was primarily designed as a civilian service, while Starshield is more for government and military sectors. According to DW's sources, Rassvet was likely designed to support battlefield communications and thus does not currently require as many satellites as Starlink. Ukrainian military expert Oleh Starikov said that if Rassvet continues to develop as it has then it could fulfil the mission put to it by the Russian military. He added that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk was developing a system that would work around the world, whereas Bureau 1440's satellites sufficed for Russian military purposes.

But he also underlined the massive expansion of Russia's satellite network generally, which — on January 1, 2022, before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine — comprised 102 satellites according to Dmitry Rogozin, who at the time was general director of the Russian space agency Roscosmos. In September of this year, Rogozin's successor Dmitry Bakanov said that the number almost quadrupled.
Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown?
Did SpaceX throttle Starlink in Ukraine?

Recent restrictions to Starlink services in Ukraine have brought the issue to the fore again. In mid-November, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Starshield had been throttled in Ukraine. "Unfortunately, our units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield's operations over the territory of Ukraine for several days now — along the entire front line and in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine," he said, adding that the restrictions occurred at speeds of 161 km/h and higher.
Restrictions on the use of Starlink were first put in place on October 14 and then lifted, according to US President Donald Trump, on October 23.
When asked by DW whether the Ukrainian military could gain access to Rassvet, Trishkin said it was "only a matter of time" before terminals fell "into foreign hands and are subsequently examined."
This article was originally published in Russian.

articles.title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies aged 65
articles.summary: The musician, who co-wrote some of the band's biggest hits, had been treated for prostate cancer.

blocks.text: Taylor's guitar lines - full of glassy, powerful riffs - were often a highlight of their songs, from the choppy opening of Girls on Film to the sleazy scuzz of Hungry Like The Wolf.
"Andy was there at the very beginning of our story," said his bandmates Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes, John Taylor and Roger Taylor (his bandmates were unrelated, despite sharing the same last name).
"From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.

"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.

"Our thoughts are with his wife Tracey, his children Georgina, Isabella, Bethany and Andrew, and grandson Albie. They all loved him deeply and we ask that their privacy be respected at this very difficult time."
Sir Rod Stewart, who wrote five songs with Taylor for the 1988 album Out of Order, paid tribute to his "dear pal".
"We made some good music together and at the same time had some outrageous fun," Sir Rod posted on Instagram.
The following year, the guitarist decided to quit Duran Duran, after a miserable experience performing at Live Aid.
"We'd reached rock bottom and we had absolutely nothing to say to each other," he wrote in his autobiography, Wild Boy.
"We drove to the venue through streets packed with excited rock fans, but inside the bus the atmosphere was as if we were on a way to a funeral."
He went on to play on Robert Palmer's Addicted To Love, and released a solo album, Thunder, in 1987.
After a period writing and producing albums for other artists, he rejoined Duran Duran in 2000, lasting for just one album (2004's Astronaut) before parting ways again.
In 2022, when the band were inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Taylor was notably absent from the ceremony, despite public plans for a reunion.
When the group took the stage, singer Simon Le Bon read a letter from the guitarist, in which he revealed his diagnosis with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.
Nonetheless, he contributed to the following year's Halloween-themed album Danse Macabre, marking his final collaboration with the band.
"Andy never took the easy musical route," said Le Bon in a personal statement marking his friend's death.
"His overdrive, overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later.
"There's a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart. It'll never close up; I won't let it. I will miss him & love him for all my days."
Taylor is survived by his wife, Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982.
"For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first," she wrote in her statement.
"Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home."
She continued: "Andy faced the last few years with so much courage and determination. He never gave up, fighting until the very end, never losing his love of life.
"The kindness and support shown to him by fans from all over the world throughout his illness brought him immense comfort and strength, and for that we will always be grateful."

articles.title: ‘Trapped in grief’: wife of Japanese journalist detained by Russia pleads for his release
articles.summary:
Yuki Imai being held in Moscow on allegations he conducted ‘espionage’ while working for a newspaper in Sakhalin island in Russia’s far east

The wife of a Japanese journalist who has been…

blocks.text: The wife of a Japanese journalist who has been detained in Russia for more than a month on suspicion of spying has issued an emotive appeal for his release.

Yuki Imai, a reporter for the Hokkaido Shimbun, was arrested in mid-October as he was preparing to return to Japan from a two-year assignment at the Japanese newspaper’s bureau in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, on the island of Sakhalin in Russia’s far east.

Russian authorities alleged that Imai had been “conducting espionage activities” on the island, collecting information about Russian defence capabilities he intended to pass on to Japanese intelligence. Both the newspaper and Japan’s prime minster, Sanae Takaichi, have denied the claims.

His detention has inflamed tensions between Tokyo and Moscow and prompted Takaichi to request Imai’s release during a meeting with the Russian leader Vladimir Putin at last week’s Apec summit in China.

The arrest comes amid rapidly deteriorating ties between Japan and Russia, triggered by Tokyo’s support for Ukraine and a longstanding dispute over islands in the Kuril chain near Sakhalin that are known in Japan as the Northern Territories. Japan claims the four islands closest to its territory – the nearest is less than 4km from Hokkaido – which Russia has administered since the dying days of the second world war.
In a statement released to media organisations through the Hokkaido Shimbun, Imai’s wife, Nozomi Imai, said her husband’s plight meant his family were “trapped in grief”.

“Since his detention, his parents and I have spent every day worrying about him” she said in the statement, published in Japanese, English and Russian. Recalling the moment she saw TV footage of her husband being taken away by Russian authorities, she said: “I could hardly breathe. It felt as if my heart were being ripped apart.”

She added: “No one could remain calm after seeing a beloved family member with his arms bound behind his back. In the video, I could even see the souvenirs in his suitcase – the gifts he was bringing home for us. I could not sleep even for a moment that night. When morning came, it still did not feel real. I could not even cry.”

Imai, 34, has barely seen his infant daughter, who was born during his posting to Russia. “He had been so looking forward to coming home,” Nozomi Imai wrote. “During his posting, our daughter was born. She is now 21 months old, and he loves her more than words can say. He had even said excitedly that he wanted to be the one to pick her up from daycare on the very day he got home.”

blocks.caption: Sakhalin island in Russia’s far east. Photograph: Gribov Andrei/Alamy

blocks.text: Japanese diplomats have been permitted to visit Imai only twice since he was detained, although he has had several meetings with lawyers appointed by his employer.

Japan’s ambassador to Moscow, Akira Muto, said he had met the journalist at Lefortovo detention centre in Moscow this week and that he appeared to be in good health. Japanese embassy officials were also granted access to Imai at the end of October.
The Hokkaido Shimbun said Imai had been engaged in “ordinary news gathering” on Sakhalin, adding the newspaper did “not conduct reporting or gather information based on government directions”.

Shortly after his arrest, Takaichi denied Imai had been spying. “There is no such fact,” she told reporters, adding that “the protection of Japanese nationals is extremely important right now, and we intend to focus our efforts on that.”
Concerns are growing that Moscow will seek to make an example of Imai in protest at Japan’s support for sanctions imposed after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Russia’s Federal Security Service, which is investigating Imai, has not commented publicly since it announced the reporter’s arrest. His detention is scheduled to expire on 12 December but could be extended, the Kyodo news agency said.

The Hokkaido Shimbun said Imai, whose grandfather was born on Sakhalin, was an admirer of Russian culture who had used his position to promote grassroots exchanges.He even hosted Russian visitors at his home in the Hokkaido city of Nemuro.
Nozomi Imai, who said she and her husband had met as students through their shared love of Russian films and novels, said his detention was taking a toll on his ageing parents.

“They worry whether they will ever see their beloved only son again in their lifetime,” she wrote. “Yuki Imai is not only a journalist. He is a beloved son, husband, and father. Please – please return this precious papa to his little daughter.”

articles.title: Watch: BBC confronts German man suspected of supplying migrant gangs with small boats
articles.summary: Marvin Reuter is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.

Nearly a third of small-boat crossings to the UK, in the first four months of 2026, allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.
The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.

We confronted the 35-year-old at his business, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.

articles.title: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds
articles.summary: Nearly a third of crossings in early 2026 allegedly involved boats or engines from the German man's firm.

blocks.text: Watch: BBC confronts German boat dealer Marvin Reuter
ByJessica ParkerBerlin correspondent and Tom BealBBC News Investigations
A German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.
Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.
The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.
His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.
We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.
Reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

The BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.
Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.
Evidence has been gathered through the confessions of alleged accomplices and covert jail-cell recordings of an alleged gang chief - as well as the two deadly crossing attempts.
Image source, Getty Images
A press photo from 2021 - migrants in a boat from Marvin Reuter's firm (logo circled)
At least 82 boats from Reuter's firm reached the English coast in just over two years to May, according to French investigations.
There are also press photos dating back five years showing the MaReBoote logo on dinghies crowded with migrants.
In 2021, Reuter told the Sun and Guardian he felt "frustrated" and "anxious" that his vessels had ended up in the hands of smugglers.

There was no suggestion, at that time, that authorities suspected him of wrongdoing as a German detective reportedly told the Sun: "This would be like if somebody buys a Mercedes and does something in another country which is wrong. The Mercedes seller can't help that."
It is not exactly clear when police suspicions were aroused.
French prosecutor Samuel Finielz would not comment on the details of the investigation but confirmed the head of a German company is currently the subject of a European Arrest Warrant.
The warrant was issued in May this year and relates to alleged offences dating back to December 2024.
While selling boats is "perfectly legal" it becomes illegal, said Finielz, "when one is fully aware that they will be used by networks involved in illegal immigration or human trafficking".
Case files we have seen say that German police had learned from UK authorities that 29% of detected crossings this year, up to the end of April, involved boats and/or engines linked to MaReBoote.
In France, five other men have already been charged as part of the investigation - an Iranian, three Iraqis and a Syrian.
In one of the two fatal incidents where Reuter's equipment is suspected to be involved, one of those who died was also Syrian.
Suliman al Husein would have just turned 20 when he died, according to a birth date listed in the files.
News reports at the time say he suffered a cardiac arrest after likely being crushed on a packed dinghy during a failed launch, west of Calais, in January 2025.
He was the first migrant to die in the English Channel that year. His body was found on the floor of the boat which, investigators allege, bore the MaReBoote logo.

blocks.caption: Image caption, One night in May, French police stopped a car and seized boating equipment and fuel cans

blocks.text: One night in May, French police stopped a car and seized boating equipment and fuel cans
The case against Reuter also stems from a chance arrest when French police pulled over a vehicle with German plates, near the northern port city of Boulogne-sur-Mer.
The BMW, which was towing a trailer, was spotted overtaking another vehicle at speed in the early hours of a morning in May this year - police records say.
Inside the car were two German nationals who - according to a subsequent search - were transporting jerry cans of fuel, a boat engine, pumps and a rolled up inflatable dinghy.
The men claimed they had been paid up to €1,000-a-time (£830) to make several, similar drops to "foreigners" on the coast, interrogation records show.
"Of course I knew that it wasn't legal," one is said to have admitted under questioning. "The money made me turn a blind eye."

items: Take a look at BBC Verify's UK migration tracker - the latest numbers on net migration, visas, asylum and small boats

blocks.text: Both men, who have since been convicted for smuggling offences, allegedly implicated Marvin Reuter as the man who had hired and paid them for this work.
Police files say both the BMW and the boat it was carrying had MaReBoote logos on them.
Marvin Reuter was arrested in Germany in May and later released, pending extradition.
On the day of his arrest, German police also seized more than 30 dinghies and 9,000 life jackets. Equipment which, we can now reveal, was allegedly linked to Reuter.
The BBC was previously granted access to see this haul, held in a police warehouse at a secret location in western Germany.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Part of the haul of dinghies and life jackets shown to us by German police

blocks.text: Part of the haul of dinghies and life jackets shown to us by German police
Meanwhile, further evidence has been gleaned from the bugging of a jail cell of a suspected gang chief, who is being held in pre-trial detention in France.
Recordings captured the inmate talking about buying nautical equipment from a German firm run by a man with Reuter's first name: Marvin - according to files we have seen.
The MaReBoote company address was also discovered on the alleged smuggler's phone, the case files say.

blocks.caption: Image caption, We confronted Marvin Reuter at his company premises. We have blurred his face because of German privacy rules

blocks.text: We confronted Marvin Reuter at his company premises. We have blurred his face because of German privacy rules
When we confronted Reuter last month at his business in the town of Werne, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, he told us to leave and drove off.
He then returned a short time later and said he was reporting us to the police. He did not answer our questions.

We approached him in writing before and after this encounter including a detailed request for comment. In response to that request, he did not address the specific allegations but accused us of harassment.
It is understood Reuter's lawyers have challenged his extradition, citing overcrowding in French prisons as one reason. Their client should face any allegations in Germany, they argue.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Reuter's firm is based in Werne, near Dortmund

blocks.text: Reuter's firm is based in Werne, near Dortmund

In Germany, it became explicitly illegal to aid smuggling to the UK at the end of last year after a prior BBC investigation exposed the country's role as a storage hub for gangs. Before then, some anti-smuggling laws in Germany had no longer applied to the UK because of Brexit.
The raid that saw the seizure of equipment that was allegedly linked to Reuter marked the first time the new law had been used.
Small boat crossings have dropped significantly in 2026, with British authorities citing law enforcement as a "key factor". However, illegal migration into Europe has also been falling.

The UK National Crime Agency's (NCA) deputy director for organized immigration crime, Dan Cannatella-Barcroft, praised Germany's "commitment" to tackling people-smuggling but acknowledged the country would remain "an important piece of the puzzle".

While a gap in the law has been closed, Germany's proximity to France, wider transport links and the fact that some of the Kurdish-dominated gangs are based there, means it is expected to stay as a transit point in the illegal small-boats trade.
The "vast majority" of small boats equipment in the past few years has come through Germany, Cannatella-Barcroft told the BBC - much of it made in China and having been routed through Turkey.

articles.title: Trump tariff threat ‘unacceptable’, says Brazil, as China denounces levies as baseless
articles.summary: Brazil indignant about proposed tariffs on sugar and aircraft, while Beijing says new levies amount to ‘political manipulation’

blocks.text: Brazil has said it will not bend to the new US tariff “threat” and China accused Washington of “political manipulation” in the wake of Donald Trump’s latest economic salvo against 14 major trading partners.

Brazil’s government said on Wednesday: “Brazil will not yield to this type of threat”, adding in its statement that the “unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the framework of the ongoing bilateral negotiating process”.
It voiced particular indignation at US proposals for higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.

It added that Brazil would continue to negotiate “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products”.

Brazil was particularly singled out for in the announcement after trade talks stalled. The Trump administration claimed on Wednesday that the new tariffs would be consistent with trade deals that the US reached last year with dozens of countries.

The new tariffs are being imposed under a law which allowed the president to target countries the US had found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told CNBC that many US trading partners had adopted “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base.”
The administration will seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing on 25 January, suggesting the final duties won’t take effect until February or March.

China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. The US said China would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%. The US and China last year reached a trade truce but that is set to expire on 10 January 2027.
A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China was ‌a source of ⁠excess capacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.

“The so-called issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements secured between Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

Earlier, China’s foreign ministry restated its opposition while calling for the US to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

Greer told CNBC that the administration is proposing a “broad exemption” for $30bn worth of Chinese goods in line with the deal. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this – they know what we’re proposing,” Greer told CNBC. “I think a lot of this is baked in.”
Some US analysts criticised the duties as too weak to change China’s trade practices.

China “is a bigger source of excess production than the rest of the world combined,” said Derek Scissors, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Yet Wednesday’s proposal “barely raises existing tariffs on China and will make no difference to the country’s trade behaviour.”
Vietnam’s trade ministry said it was ⁠working with the US to complete its trade deal as soon ⁠as possible and would coordinate with relevant US agencies.
It added it was “preparing ​and submitting ​rebuttal comments on the ​preliminary findings as well as on inaccurate submissions ​and allegations ‌made by ​interested ​parties.”

In response to the US announcement, the Indian government denied it had any structural excess capacity in ⁠any sector, ⁠adding that it remained committed to an early conclusion of ⁠a trade deal between the two countries. Greer has said the tariff ⁠on Indian imports would be capped at 17% if a trade deal was struck.
Taiwan was also singled out for new tariffs, but Taipei on Thursday said it was confident it would keep its existing ⁠15% tariff rate.

Taipei and Washington signed trade deals in January and February of ‌this year, which secured preferential treatment for semiconductors and other tech product which account for ​over 70% of Taiwan’s exports to the US.
Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the European Union, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, and Thailand.
Tokyo’s top government spokesman, Minoru Kihara, said it was “regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced”.

Trump’s latest round of tariffs may be here to stay despite the Democrats’ electoral sweep in the US midterms. Some Democrats will likely support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. And Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.
However Democratic Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will take over the finance committee next year, said he would “use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariffs chaos.”

“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs,” Wyden added. “Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution.”
With Associated Press and Reuters

articles.title: France's political mainstream risks presidential vote debacle with no clear candidate
articles.summary: Hard-right and hard-left candidates dominate the polls ahead of next year's presidential election.

blocks.text: France's political mainstream faces wipe-out at the presidential election in April-May 2027, unless it acts fast to choose who it wishes to stand.

With every poll confirming the dominance of hard-right and hard-left leaders Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, candidates of the middle-ground – the old "legacy" parties – are being squeezed out of the game.
In theory any contender from centre-right or centre-left who was chosen in the first multi-candidate round of voting in April should be in a strong position to win in the play-off a fortnight later.
That is because at their separate ends of the spectrum both Le Pen and Mélenchon have more people who oppose than support them.
But personal rivalries, lack of preparation and differing political visions have so far put paid to any hope of a meaningful challenge.
"The game in the centre is totally blocked," says political writer François Fressoz at the left-leaning Le Monde newspaper. "The partisans of reason have lost their reason."
On the left – the old Socialist Party and its acolytes – there is at least agreement on a candidate: European Parliament MP Raphaël Glucksmann.

His problem is that allies who he might once have counted on – Greens, Communists and other small left-wing parties, not to mention many Socialist voters – are being pulled inexorably into the Mélenchon orbit.

In the last two weeks, Green party leader Marine Tondelier, a majority of Communist parliamentary deputies and one-time Socialist presidential hopeful Benoît Hamon have all thrown in their lot with the leader of France Unbowed (LFI).
Another prominent figure of the left – François Ruffin – has also withdrawn from the race, bowing to the unbowed Mélenchon's now almost total command of the field.

So with the soft-left emasculated, the main hope for an alternative to Le Pen and Mélenchon has to be focused on the right. But here the prospects – which until recently seemed bright – are now clouded with gloom.
"A Mélenchon–Le Pen duel in round two is not yet inevitable," says Guillaume Tabard, political analyst at the conservative Le Figaro newspaper. "But it is looking increasingly probable."

In recent weeks the poll ratings of the main centre-right hopeful Edouard Philippe – a former prime minister under President Macron – have fallen sharply, and he is now consistently placed behind Mélenchon in the first round of the vote. Marine Le Pen is way ahead of both.

Other candidates for command of this centre-right "space" are circling. They include another former Macron prime minister, Gabriel Attal; the leader of the right-wing Republicans (and former Macron interior minister), Bruno Retailleau; and now – a surprise new challenger – the mayor of Cannes, David Lisnard.

Lisnard, who stands on a liberal economic platform of less state and lower taxes, has emerged from nowhere to become the man of the hour. Membership of his micro-party Nouvelle Energie (New Energy) has shot up to more than 100,000, and he is being taken seriously as a possible Philippe replacement.

But this very multiplicity of names – not to mention others like judoka Teddy Riner, journalist Natacha Polony and former prime minister Dominique de Villepin – betrays the essential weakness of the centre-right challenge.

According to veteran commentator Nicolas Baverez, "If you want to win an election, it's quite simple: you need a strategy, a programme, and activists. Right now in the space between Le Pen and Mélenchon we have none of that: there is a total vacuum.
"The most glaring absence is digital. Mélenchon especially, but Le Pen too, are running extremely effective social media campaigns. In the middle… nothing."
Guillaume Tabard agrees that the lack of a shared platform is proving a serious handicap.
"In recent weeks we have seen Marine Le Pen issue her manifesto proposals for reforming pensions. We have seen Jean-Luc Mélenchon publish his programme in a best-selling book," he says.
"What do we have in between? Arguments about names and polling figures and whether or not there should be a primary. It's not, to put it mildly, an encouraging start."

For Fressoz, "There is no-one in the centre who is taking up the fight. When Le Pen makes her proposals about pensions, there is no-one saying, 'Hang on, that doesn't add up!'. Macron – who did after all take her on and beat her – is said to be furious."

Any mention of Macron, though, is most unwelcome for the camp that nominally is his heir. Philippe, Attal and Retailleau all served under a president who Baverez now calls "as toxic as Trump", so deep is his unpopularity in the country. Lisnard, by contrast, makes much of his refusal to serve under Macron – but he faces another handicap.

According to Fressoz, "Lisnard has shot up in the polls because he is on the right of the right, and there is always an appetite for a figure who is not Le Pen, but who speaks her kind of language on immigration.
"But Lisnard is an economic liberal, and in France that is a minority taste. He'll have his moment but then he will deflate."

With five months to go to until the election, all is not lost for the mainstream. Optimists in its ranks say that come the new year, opinion polls will start settling behind one or other centre-right candidate, and the others will feel obliged to step aside.

Talk of a centre-right primary – as occurred ahead of the 2017 election – is beginning to ebb. The two strongest candidates, Philippe and Lisnard, are opposed. Lisnard says he supports one but his conditions are designed to be unacceptable to the rest. Retailleau and Attal are in favour – but that, says Tabard, is "mainly as a way to keep their hopes alive."

In theory then it is possible a name will emerge in January or February, and start pulling behind him (or less likely, her) the mass of voters who do not want a disruptive radical as France's next head of state.
Possible, but hardly a good bet.
For Fressoz of Le Monde, "After years of Macron's 'neither left nor right', the left and right are once again shaping French politics. But now it is the extremes who are in control."

Le Pen and Mélenchon have both already run three times for the presidency. Their visions were defined long ago, their strategies laid, their activists trained. Polarisation is their friend, so is the social tension of recent weeks, and both are undisputed masters in their own camps.
The 2027 dénouement has been in their sights for years. That is their massive advantage.

articles.title: US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space
articles.summary: The Starmind constellation aims to be the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for AI computing power.

blocks.text: US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.
The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, will "support America's booming super intelligence economy".
Its approval comes as communities across the US have pushed back against the expansion of data centres on the ground.

Space X believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".
"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.
Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites has to begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.
The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.
Its unclear if a million satellites will be launched or if SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.

Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).
Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.

The solar-powered satellite system "promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilisation—one that can harness the full power of the sun", the FCC statement said, in a reference to a hypothetical society, proposed by an astronomer in the 1960s, capable of harnessing the entire energy output of its home star.

The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.
The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.

New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.
Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.
Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.
Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.

articles.title: A renovation to upgrade these Hong Kong homes ended in an inferno that killed 168
articles.summary: A year after one of Hong Kong's deadliest fires, families left behind are still waiting for justice.
articles.byline: Grace Tsoi, Phoebe Kong, Yvette Tan

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
The fire was one of Hong Kong's deadliest in decades
ByGrace TsoiBBC World ServicePhoebe KongBBC Chinese Reporting fromHong Kong and Yvette Tan
It was a sunny Wednesday afternoon on 26 November last year, and Mrs Lau was attending a dance class at an activity centre close to her home.
At around 14:45 she heard the faint sounds of fire engine sirens - but didn't think much of it.

It was only a while later, when she started receiving calls from a friend, that she found out that Wang Fuk Court - the eight-block apartment complex she had called home for the past 40 years - was ablaze. And her husband - a wheelchair user - was trapped inside their home.
"I grabbed my things quickly and ran down without even putting my shoes on properly," Mrs Lau, who wanted to be identified only by her surname, told the BBC.
When she got there, the building had been cordoned off by police.
She called her 74-year-old husband but he told her not to worry - he hadn't heard an alarm so it was probably a small fire, he said.

Mrs Lau could only watch helplessly as the blaze tore through Wang Fuk Court at a peak speed of about 10m (33ft) per second - an "unprecedented" rate, a final report released by an independent committee in relation to the deadly blaze that killed 168 people found.
It was a tragedy that was entirely preventable but happened as a result of a series of human errors, fire safety failures, alleged fraud and suspected corruption, said the report.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Lau Man Kwong took care of his grandson before his death (blurred at source)

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied
Lau Man Kwong took care of his grandson before his death (blurred at source)
"It was ferocious… I saw the fire jump [from one building to another] - then a huge fireball burst. It was truly hell on Earth. How could anyone possibly escape?" said Mrs Lau.
She tried calling her husband again. This time, there was no answer.
The body of Lau Man Kwong was eventually found by rescuers - he had locked himself inside the toilet.
"He was wearing his slippers, sitting on the toilet and clutching his identity card," said his wife, who added that she escaped death "by the narrowest margin".
"I would have held onto my husband and died with him.
"He was such a good person. I just don't understand why he had to die in such a terrible way."
Mr Lau and his wife moved into Wang Fuk Court in 1983 - the year the building was completed.
She recalls an idyllic life - a family with three children who were able to grow up close to the sea and spend weekends playing at a nearby park.
"All three of my children adored my husband… He could be very stern, and I was the only woman who could make him laugh."
No way out
In 2024, mandated renovations began in Wang Fuk Court.
In Hong Kong, all buildings over 30 years old have to undergo an inspection - and any necessary renovations as a result.

Like many building complexes in Hong Kong, Wang Fuk Court had a management committee that oversaw things like building repairs. As many as 57 construction companies submitted bids. But the company that won, Prestige Construction and Engineering (PC&E), submitted the most expensive bid at HK$336m ($42.8m; £32.4m).

Residents, many of whom were over 65, had to bear the cost. The hefty bills triggered protests but eventually, the contract was signed. But once the renovations began in July 2024, residents were unhappy.
Among the complaints was that workers constantly smoked on site, dropping cigarette butts everywhere.
The 1,154 page report suggested the fire was caused by a lit cigarette.
Watch: Christy says she still sends WhatsApp messages to her husband who died in the blaze

There were also complaints about most of Wang Fuk Court's eight buildings having their windows taped over with foam boards to stop debris falling in - blocking daylight or any sort of view at all, for months.
All eight buildings were also covered in a protective mesh netting and bamboo scaffolding.

The report also found that after typhoons damaged the original scaffolding nets in 2025, cheaper non-fire-retardant replacements were chosen - something that was done as a "cost-saving measure at the expense of the safety of the residents".

Residents had filed nearly 140 complaints to six government departments, including the fire services and the buildings departments, in and after 2024, but these were largely ignored, the report went on to say.
It also revealed that a staff member of the estate's property manager, ISS, had turned off the power supply to the fire alarms in all eight buildings - which is why no alarms rang on the day itself.
ISS later told the BBC it had "reviewed and reinforced its procedures [and] staff training" in Hong Kong, adding that it takes the findings of the report "very seriously".

But for those who did manage to flee their homes - the emergency staircase turned out to be another death trap. Windows were removed from some fire escape stairwells to create temporary openings for workers - letting in smoke and cutting off vital escape routes.
Dozens, including Christy's husband, died in such stairwells.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Christy's daughter celebrated her ninth birthday the day before the fire

blocks.text: Image source, Lam Yik / BBC Chinese
Christy's daughter celebrated her ninth birthday the day before the fire

Christy, who wanted to be identified only by her first name, says her husband was at home alone when the fire broke out. She only found out about it when her friends sent her messages about it. By the time she made it to the apartment complex, it was already cordoned off.
She found out later that he had died of smoke inhalation in the stairwell, something she says that is at least of some consolation to her.
"My husband's body would have been burnt and he would have been in more pain if he was at home. At the very least… his suffering was minimal."
Christy says her family had just celebrated their eldest child's ninth birthday the day before - they had saved some leftover cake in the fridge to eat the next day. Their father never got to eat it.
Both children have been deeply affected by the loss of their father.
Her youngest child, a seven-year-old boy, had "covered his ears and yelled" when he was first told what had happened to his father.
He now often comforts his mother, saying he will take care of her as he is the only man in the family.
"He hides his emotions. A seven-year-old child should not behave this way, and I feel heartbroken," says Christy, who has herself been diagnosed with PTSD and depression.
Her daughter has "extreme thoughts" she says, and channels her emotions through art.
She turned 10 on Wednesday, but this year, there was no birthday celebration in sight.
Her birthday, she says, will now instead be a day to commemorate her father.
Bid-rigging and rubber stamps
Wang Fuk Court's problems date back to before the renovations began.

The management company hired to oversee and supervise the project, Will Power, conspired with PC&E to defraud residents in Wang Fuk Court, according to the city's Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC).

Although PC&E was found to have breached safety requirements and violated building department rules for multiple previous projects, homeowners at Wang Fuk Court were told that they had a clean record.

The ICAC alleges that this was part of a lucrative scheme, with Will Power's director Wong Hap-yin, along with other individuals, laundering over $5m in suspected proceeds from the tendering process from Wang Fuk Court, among other housing projects.

Once PC&E cinched the contract, Will Power's registered inspector - an individual meant to oversee the renovations - merely rubber-stamped the documents, without having actually conducted any inspections personally, the report added.
Will Power has been since liquidated and PC&E could not be reached for a response.

Both companies - Will Power and PC&E - and seven individuals have been charged with 25 counts of offences including including manslaughter, conspiracy to defraud, attempting to pervert the course of public justice and tax evasion.
Four of them are still in custody but none of the cases have gone to trial yet.
The report said both companies involved were the "main culprits responsible".

But it also directed heavy criticism at authorities, saying that "no government department took effective ownership of various fire safety issues and complaints about fire hazards fell into a vacuum".

One expert, Prof John Burns of Hong Kong University, had called the event the "largest governance crisis" that authorities have faced since 2020 - a reference to the controversial National Security Law that was passed in that year.

On the day the report was released, almost one year after the fire, Hong Kong's housing chief Winnie Ho resigned and the city's top leader John Lee apologised for the first time, promising that a "large number" of reforms would be rolled out.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Homeowners at Wang Fuk Court (pictured) were told their construction company had a clean record

blocks.text: Homeowners at Wang Fuk Court (pictured) were told their construction company had a clean record
A shell of a home
Five months after the fire, Mrs Lau was allowed into her flat for the first time to collect any personal belongings that might have remained.
In her first visit, she was given just three hours to retrieve 40 years' worth of belongings.
Pictures taken from the visit show a home that has been utterly burned out - with every surface blackened and soot covering the floor.
"I almost fainted when I saw what had become of my home. I don't understand how the home I had built, such a warm and beautiful home, could end up like this," said Mrs Lau.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The frame of Mr Lau's wheelchair was one of the few things left in their burnt home

blocks.text: The frame of Mr Lau's wheelchair was one of the few things left in their burnt home

Her children, who came with her, described the house as a "war zone". Among the rubble, they found broken pieces of a piggy bank that Mr Lau had dutifully filled with coins every day for the past 20 years.
"Everyone in our family knew it was his favourite possession. The piggy bank died with him," said Mrs Lau.
Mrs Lau and her daughter have since rented a place nearby to live - and she is worried about how she is going to afford a new house.
The government has said it will spend $867m (£663m) to acquire affected flats - but Mrs Lau says it is not nearly enough to buy a similarly sized flat in the area.
Still, her family was in a better position than many others, she said.
"Should I say that we are fortunate?
"I lost my husband but many families lost multiple family members... Babies less than a year old died. "
Stories have emerged of some of the other victims - a six-month-old who died alongside her 68-year-old grandmother when the fire broke out.
The bodies of an Indonesian domestic helper and the elderly person she worked for were found huddled together.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Mrs Lau's son has since bought new piggy banks in memory of his father

blocks.text: Image source, BBC Chinese / Phoebe Kong
Mrs Lau's son has since bought new piggy banks in memory of his father
As for Christy, she says she is planning to file a lawsuit against those responsible for the fire - but acknowledges that even if she wins, she "can't [get] my husband's life back".
"I share things that happen in our daily life, as if he still existed," she says. "I often write to him, 'I miss you so much. Are you doing well on the other side?'"
It's a similar story for Mrs Lau, who says she can't go anywhere without seeing her husband.
"Every day, something reminds me of him," she said.
"I still find it very hard to accept that my husband is gone, my home is gone, and so many of my neighbours are gone…. This place was my roots. I never imagined it would also mark an ending for me."

articles.title: Palestinian journalist killed by Israel in Gaza wins Rory Peck prize
articles.summary:
Mariam Dagga shares award with two of her colleagues from AP for ‘powerful coverage’ of human cost of war

Mariam Dagga, the Palestinian war correspondent who was killed at the age of 33 in…
